Before it, everything crossed by ferry. The Mississippi had always been the delta's fact of life. The bridge was the first argument that you could ignore it.

The Mississippi here isn't a river in any ordinary sense. It's the last 100 miles of a watershed that drains 41 percent of the contiguous United States — water that fell as rain on the Rockies, on the Appalachians, on the Iowa cornfields — all of it arriving here, slowing, spreading, depositing. The delta that New Orleans sits on didn't exist 7,000 years ago. The river built it, load by suspended load, and the river would reclaim it tomorrow if the levees weren't holding it in place. We're riding across land younger than the pyramids, built from the interior of a continent, held together by engineering and ambition.

We're crossing into Orleans Parish now — into the city proper. The parish and the city have been one entity since 1870, which makes New Orleans unusual: a place where the political boundary fits the geographic reality. The poverty rate here runs nearly 23 percent, which sits against a median income of $51,000 and an economy built on education, health, and the arts and hospitality that drew people here in the first place. The city was built on this impossible ground — below sea level, surrounded by water, sitting on mud that's still moving — and it's been arguing with geography ever since. That argument isn't resolved. It's just ongoing.

The whole leg has been a transect. We started in desert basins — country where the rivers don't reach the sea, where the rock is ancient and bare and the distances are staggering. We moved east through the managed wildlands, past the ghost towns and the old mail routes, following the phantom of the Butterfield line and the road that preceded every railroad. The land got wetter. The sky got lower. The Cenozoic sediments thickened beneath us until the bedrock disappeared entirely under hundreds of feet of river-laid mud. Now we're at the delta's edge — the terminus of the continent's drainage, the city that grew up where the water runs out of land. The track ahead ends at New Orleans Union Passenger Terminal. The river ends at the Gulf. Everything that came from the dry interior ends here.

New Orleans. The station is just ahead. The city sits where the Mississippi's last curve before the Gulf pinched a ridge of higher ground — barely above sea level — and that ridge was exactly where the French planted their colony in 1718. The choice made sense: the highest, driest land for miles. What they couldn't know was that the river's sediment, once leveed and controlled, would stop replenishing what subsidence and erosion were constantly removing. The land sinks. The sea rises. The city holds. We've crossed a continent to get here — from the endorheic deserts where water disappears, to the place where all the water finally arrives. Welcome to the end of the line.

27.text: The great hall's vaulted ceiling — travertine marble, 1925, 110 feet overhead — is already behind us. Eight long-distance routes converge here, including ours, the same way railroad men dreamed it a century ago: the northern tier of the continent, iron spine running west. The station opened in 1925 on the bones of an 1881 predecessor. Out of it come all the great trains. We're one of them now, rolling north through the grid of streets, the city giving itself to us one block at a time.

The ground beneath Chicago is not the dramatic glacial moraine country we'll reach in an hour or so — it's the lake plain, nearly flat, scraped and waterlogged from the last glacial advance. But the bedrock below, if you could bore straight down, is Silurian-age dolostone and limestone, laid in a warm, shallow tropical sea roughly 430 to 445 million years ago — when this latitude wasn't this latitude at all, when the continent was drifting through equatorial waters teeming with crinoids and brachiopods. The Silurian system: a chapter of deep time named for the Silures tribe of Wales, where geologists first identified it in the 1830s. The bedrock here is its expression — dolostone, limestone, shale, and the fossil record of an ancient sea floor. We never see it; it's buried under glacial drift, then fill, then a city. But it's there, 400 feet down, holding all of this up. The Central Corn Belt Plains ecoregion — flat, managed, the land cover that surrounds the metro — runs beneath the city's reach in both directions. Named for what it grows: mostly corn, some hay and vegetables, soil built by glacial deposition and ten thousand years of prairie root. Two-thirds of this land is now developed. We can see that out the window right now: the tight brick two-flats of the Northwest Side, the freight corridors and rail yards, the thinning skyline in the mirror behind us.

To your right, the Yellow Line station at Dempster — a CTA rapid transit terminal that started life as a North Shore Line stop in 1925, the same year Union Station opened. The North Shore Line ran electric interurban trains between Chicago and Milwaukee for nearly four decades before losing the fight to highways and automobiles in 1963. This station survived as a transfer point. The 1925 construction makes it a landmark now — the old interurban infrastructure underneath the modern transit map, like a geological unconformity in the built environment.

Glenview on the left — incorporated 1899, about forty-eight thousand people now, fifteen miles from the Loop. A former naval air station occupied the center of this village from World War II until 1995; the land is a park today. Cook County ends not far ahead. The suburbs thin almost imperceptibly as we go — the spacing between houses increases by perhaps thirty feet per mile, a gradient you only notice across a few miles, not at any single point.

We're in the transition now — Cook County giving way to Lake County, the second-most-populous county in Illinois dropping behind, and a quieter, wealthier north shore opening ahead. Lake County, Illinois: median household income over $104,000, nearly twice the national figure, one of the wealthiest counties in the Midwest. Manufacturing and healthcare, suburbs pressed against Lake Michigan to the east, corn and soy in the few farm patches inland. The lake is just beyond view to our right, three or four miles — and that fact shapes everything here. The Great Lakes watershed is the dominant drainage. Every rain that falls between here and the crest of the divide we'll cross at mile sixty runs east into Lake Michigan and eventually through the St. Lawrence to the Atlantic. But that divide is still ahead; for now we're deep in the basin.

Highland Park on the right: a Lake Michigan shore city, platted in 1869 — the same year the transcontinental railroad was hammered together at Promontory, Utah, a continent away, and the same year that rail speculation was platting dozens of towns across Illinois. In 2022, a Fourth of July parade shooting killed seven people in Highland Park's downtown. The city has thirty thousand residents and a long commuter rail history. The built landscape out the right window — older commercial blocks, residential streets lined with mature oaks — looks like a place that has stood here long enough to accumulate weight. And it has. A hundred and fifty years of the same cycle: train brings suburb, suburb grows, city becomes established, city endures.

The land out both windows is doing something subtle you might miss if you're not watching for it. The wetlands are increasing — low spots between drumlins, potholes left by glacial kettle formation, willow thickets around still water. Lake County, Illinois, is about a third wetland. The last glacier — the Lake Michigan Lobe of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, which retreated about twelve thousand years ago — left this terrain kneaded and dimpled, a till plain with poor internal drainage. Farmers have tiled and drained it for a century and a half, but enough of the original hydrological chaos remains that the wetlands keep appearing between the cornfields. Corn and soybeans and hay are the crops; the fields appear in the windows between the suburbs as we go north, small-scale agriculture persisting in the gaps of the metropolitan fringe.

The fossils of the bedrock below us date to about 432 million years ago: Caryocrinites ornatus, a crinoid — a sea lily, anchored to the seafloor by a stalk, waving its feathery arms to catch plankton — and Eospirifer radiatus, a brachiopod, a two-shelled animal that filtered the same shallow water. Neither looks like anything alive today. They're not quite like their modern descendants. They're the Silurian versions: forms from the period after the great Ordovician extinction wiped out perhaps 85% of marine species, and before the Devonian diversification that followed. A recovery fauna, experimenting its way forward. The rock that holds them is under everything out this window right now — under the subdivisions, under the wetlands, under the county roads. Half a billion years of context, invisible.

Waukegan to the right — the county seat of Lake County, the tenth-largest city in Illinois, a majority-minority city now. Its first recorded European presence: 1829, a fur trade outpost on the lake. By the 1880s it was an industrial harbor town, a Great Lakes port for manufacturing. The Abbott Laboratories headquarters is here. The author Ray Bradbury grew up in Waukegan; he called it Green Town in his novels — the Midwestern town of memory, summer, and wonder. "Something Wicked This Way Comes" is Green Town. The industrial lakefront of his childhood is still there, largely, though the factories have turned over. A town that contains both of those things at once: the Bradbury novel and the real harbor. They're not contradictory.

About ten miles ahead we cross the state line into Wisconsin — a political line that corresponds, roughly, to something real in the landscape. The ecoregion we've been in since Chicago, the Central Corn Belt Plains, is giving way. Watch for the shift: the till plains of northeastern Illinois become the Southeastern Wisconsin Till Plains, a related but distinct region — the glacial topography here is a little more pronounced, the drumlins slightly more emphatic, the soils a bit heavier with clay. And the watershed divide is just ahead: at mile sixty, the drainage tips. Rain to the south of that divide flows to Lake Michigan and the St. Lawrence. Rain to the north finds rivers that run west into the Mississippi system — a continental seam written in the slope of the land, invisible from a train window but geographically as significant as the Appalachians.

Zion, on the right — founded in 1901 by a faith healer named John Alexander Dowie, who built it as a theocratic city-state. No doctors, no theaters, no pork. Dowie planned the streets in a grid radiating from a central tabernacle, with every street named for a figure from scripture. The theocracy collapsed in 1906 when Dowie suffered a stroke, was deposed by his own church, and died the following year. The city remained. The street grid — Ezekiel Avenue, Enoch Avenue, Elijah Avenue — is still there, a theocratic town plan that outlasted its theocrat by over a century. Zion also hosts a nuclear generating station, now closed, on the lake. Dowie would not have approved of that either. Twenty-four thousand people live here now, going about ordinary Illinois lives on streets named for prophets.

The state line is behind us now — Wisconsin ahead. The Illinois period of this leg is closing. We've come through the second-most-populous county in the country, then the wealthy North Shore, then the industrial harbor cities of Lake County, and now the lower-density agricultural edge of the metropolitan fringe. At around mile fifty, the bedrock makes a subtle shift — from the broader Silurian system undivided to the Waukesha Formation, a slightly younger Silurian dolomite, medium-grained, light to medium gray, locally cherty, dated to about 431 to 429 million years ago. A difference of perhaps two million years in the rock. Negligible to a human. A distinct formation to a geologist, because the depositional environment shifted, because the sea that laid it down changed character slightly — deepened, maybe, or warmed. The Waukesha Formation outcrops in quarries across southeastern Wisconsin; it built the stone walls and foundations of the farms we're starting to see.

Kenosha on the right — Wisconsin's fourth-largest city, nearly a hundred thousand people on the southwestern shore of Lake Michigan. The name is Potawatomi, likely meaning "place of pike" — the fish, not the weapon, though the distinction gets lost in the sources. European settlement began in 1835. By the late nineteenth century it was a manufacturing city: furniture, then automobiles. American Motors Corporation built cars here until 1988. The Chrysler plant that followed closed in 2010. The bones of a manufacturing city are visible in the building stock: the solid brick commercial blocks, the workers' bungalows, the rail spurs. Kenosha has also produced pre-Clovis archaeological evidence — human presence here predating the conventional first-Americans timeline of thirteen thousand years. The lake was different then; the geography was different. People were here. The city sits on that compressed deep time without necessarily advertising it.

The cropland opening up around us — corn, soybeans, hay — marks Kenosha County proper: two-thirds cropland, which is a different character than the Lake County, Illinois, we've left behind. The metropolitan fringe has thinned. The agricultural Midwest is reasserting itself. And the divide we've been approaching is now very close — at mile sixty, the drainage tips west, into the Mississippi watershed. We've been in the Great Lakes basin since Chicago. In a few minutes, the rain that falls to our right will find rivers that run to the Mississippi, the Gulf of Mexico. The rain to our left will still drain toward Lake Michigan. Both things will be true simultaneously, just a mile or two apart, out this window. The great continental water divide, invisible in a flat agricultural field, doing its slow silent work of separating the continent's two great drainage halves.

Somers ahead — a village of eight thousand, Kenosha County. The terrain here is gently rolling till plain, the Southeastern Wisconsin Till Plains ecoregion fully established now: a landscape shaped by the same glacial lobe that built the country to our south, but with a slightly different character — the soils a little more clay-heavy, the topography a bit more expressive, the wetlands beginning to appear more insistently between the fields. The bedrock below remains Waukesha Formation dolomite, the gray Silurian stone, and that formation will carry us for some time to come. Over the next hour or two, the elevation holds nearly flat — we won't climb much until much later in this leg, far to the west. For now, the land is doing what the lake plain does: lying patient and low, organized into fields, carrying its deep-time geology invisibly underneath.

The ground beneath these cornfields is dolomite — gray, slightly cherty, laid down in a shallow tropical sea about four hundred thirty million years ago, when Wisconsin sat south of the equator and nothing walked on land. The Waukesha Formation. We're riding over reef debris, essentially: the compressed skeletons of a lost ocean. Above it, glacial till smoothed everything flat, and then came the corn. The buried rock is invisible but it's doing work — the dolomite holds groundwater that feeds the wells of every farm we're passing.

We're still firmly inside the Great Lakes watershed right now. Every drop of rain that falls on these fields drains eventually to Lake Michigan — and from there to the St. Lawrence, the Atlantic. That's the water world we've been inside since we left Chicago. It won't last much longer. Around mile one hundred we'll cross an imperceptible ridge, a glacial moraine so low you'd miss it on foot, and everything on the far side will drain west toward the Mississippi instead. Two oceans' worth of drainage separated by a few feet of elevation. That crossing is coming. For now, watch the fields — the soil darkens as we move north, glacial clay working up through the topsoil.

The bedrock shifts here, almost on cue. We're rolling onto the Racine Formation — also Silurian dolomite, but a few million years younger and coarser-grained, thick-bedded, and fossiliferous. The fossils here are the reason to pay attention: conodont animals, eel-like creatures no longer than your thumb, left behind their tiny phosphatic teeth in this rock. Two species — Wurmiella polinclinata and Walliserodus curvatus — both about four hundred forty million years old. The rock was already a reef when they were alive. We're traveling through the record of a vanished tropical sea one limestone layer at a time.

The track here follows the old Chicago and North Western right-of-way, pressed close to the Lake Michigan shore — and that proximity was not accidental. The railroad engineers of the 1840s and 50s who pushed lines up this coast were threading a needle: lake to the east, marshy lowlands to the west, and a narrow band of firm glacial gravel in between. The train dictated where the towns went. Racine County — the county we're crossing now — was organized in 1836, two years before Wisconsin achieved territorial status. The French named the Root River running through it: racine, "root." The county is older than the state it's part of. Settlement came first by water, then the rail lines fixed it in place permanently, stringing one lakeshore community after another into what eventually became the continuous Milwaukee metropolitan edge.

Out the right window, the city of Cudahy — about eighteen thousand people, packed into a tight lakeshore grid south of Milwaukee. It bears the name of Patrick Cudahy, a meatpacker from Chicago who moved his operations north in 1892 and built a company town almost from scratch: he platted the streets, built the workers' cottages, put up the plant. The same year, 1892, the Homestead Strike was tearing through Carnegie Steel in Pennsylvania — the industrial Midwest was in open conflict over what a factory town owed its workers. Cudahy's version was paternalistic but functional. The meatpacking is gone. The grid and the houses remain.

There's a pattern along this lakeshore that repeats itself: a founding industry that recruited a specific immigrant wave, ran for a generation or two, then departed — leaving a neighborhood, a set of surnames, and a Catholic parish that outlasted everything else. German and Polish workers in the packinghouses; Danish and Italian craftsmen in the machine shops. The Lake Michigan shoreline towns from Kenosha north to Milwaukee absorbed successive waves of European labor from the 1880s through the 1920s. The factories are largely gone now — education and healthcare are the employment base today, as they are across most of the post-industrial Midwest. But the neighborhood bones hold.

St. Francis — nine thousand people, incorporated as a city only in 1951, one of the last Lake Michigan suburbs to formalize its boundary. It sits on a narrow shelf between the rail corridor and the water. The name comes from a seminary established here in the nineteenth century; the institution shaped the character of the place far longer than most founding institutions do. Small cities like this one tend to be invisible from the train — we're moving fast, the platform is a flash — but they're where a significant fraction of the metropolitan population actually lives: not downtown, not the outer exurb, but this middle distance, close enough to the lake to feel it.

Milwaukee is just ahead. As we approach, watch the industrial archaeology out both windows: the old brick warehouse districts, the rail yards that once handled grain and livestock and manufactured goods pouring in from the hinterland. Chicago may have been the capital of the interior railroad network, but Milwaukee was its essential northern node — the place where the Wisconsin farm country met the Great Lakes shipping lanes. Grain elevators, tanneries, breweries: the city's nineteenth-century economy was written in bulk commodities. The iron road made it, and the iron road is bringing us into its station now.

Milwaukee. The station is a brief stop — a moment to feel the city's weight. Nearly a million people in the county, the most densely settled place in Wisconsin. The name is Algonquian, probably from the Potawatomi — Millioke, "good land" or "gathering place by the water." French traders knew it by the 1670s. The first permanent American settlement came in 1835; the city incorporated in 1846, the same year the Mexican-American War began and the same decade that the railroads were transforming what it meant to be interior. Milwaukee's harbor made it a grain-shipping junction; its railroads made it a manufacturing center. Both roles are diminished now. But the gathering-place function persists.

As we pull out of Milwaukee and move west — and we are turning west here, following the rail corridor inland away from the lake — we're beginning the long climb toward something geographically consequential. Waukesha County ahead of us has a median household income nearly double that of Milwaukee County we're leaving. The numbers tell a familiar story: post-industrial core, prosperous suburb. But the landscape tells a different one. We're moving away from the lake's moderating influence. The air will be drier. The terrain, though still glacially smoothed, starts to show more topographic texture — moraines, kettle lakes, drumlins. The glacier that shaped all of this retreated about twelve thousand years ago. It left its fingerprints everywhere: those small rounded hills, the ponds tucked between them, the gravelly ridges that the old-timers called "hogbacks."

Elm Grove — a small Waukesha County suburb, prosperous and quiet. The land cover shifts noticeably here: sixty percent developed, forty percent forest, a reversal of the cropland-dominant counties we've been riding through. The elms for which it was named are largely gone — Dutch elm disease swept through the upper Midwest in the 1960s and 70s and took most of the street canopy. The oaks replaced them, which is its own ecological story: oak savannas were the original vegetation of this part of Wisconsin before European settlement and fire suppression transformed the landscape.

We're approaching the watershed divide now — that quiet moraine somewhere around mile one hundred where the continent tips. East of it, water finds Lake Michigan. West of it, water finds the Fox River, then the Wisconsin River, then the Mississippi. It is one of the fundamental lines on the continent, and it crosses our tracks without ceremony, without a sign, without a sound. You won't feel the train crest it. But after we cross it, every drop of rain falling on these fields is destined for a different ocean — the Gulf of Mexico, a two-thousand-mile journey south. The divide between the Great Lakes basin and the Upper Mississippi watershed is the geography that explains why this part of Wisconsin was so strategically contested: whoever controlled the portages between those drainage systems controlled the fur trade, the military routes, and eventually the rail corridors.

Look left — Waukesha, the county seat, seventy-one thousand people along the Fox River. The name is Potawatomi: Wau-ke-sha, probably "little fox." First surveyed in 1834, when Wisconsin was still part of Michigan Territory, before there was a Wisconsin or a state or even a settled American presence this far north. But Waukesha's particular story is water — not the Fox River, but the mineral springs. In the 1860s and 70s, Waukesha became a spa town. Physicians were prescribing its spring water for a range of ailments, and the wealthy from Chicago and beyond came north by rail to drink it. Dozens of hotels, a bottled-water industry, a minor resort economy — all built on the chemistry of groundwater percolating through that Silurian dolomite we crossed near mile sixty. The springs declined, the resort economy faded, but the rail connection that brought the spa visitors turned Waukesha into a commuter suburb when the automobile age arrived. The geology gave the water, the water built the railroad relationship, the railroad built the modern city.

Between Waukesha and Delafield, the bedrock does something we should mark. Around mile one hundred ten, the Silurian dolomite — the reef rock, the fossiliferous shallow-sea formation we've been riding over since Chicago — gives way to something older. Late Ordovician sedimentary rock, laid down between about four hundred fifty-eight and four hundred forty-four million years ago. That's fifteen million years older than the Silurian above it, formed before the great reef systems of the Silurian had even begun to build. In the Ordovician, the seas were deep and cold. The organisms fossilized in the rock beneath us lived in a marine world so foreign from our own that it barely registers as Earth — no land plants, no insects, no vertebrates on land. Just the sea, and the slow rain of shell and sediment to the bottom. This is the first time this leg we've stepped back past the Silurian into that older world.

Delafield — seven thousand people along the Bark River, western Waukesha County. The Bark River drains these kettle lakes and flows west, eventually reaching the Rock River, which reaches the Mississippi — we've crossed the divide and the water knows it. Delafield was settled in the 1830s, part of the same wave of New England migrants who came west after the Erie Canal opened in 1825 and made Wisconsin reachable in weeks rather than months. The town's character has always been shaped by its lakes — kettle lakes left by the glacier, clean and cold — and by the rail corridor that made it a weekend destination for Milwaukee's professional class in the late nineteenth century. That pattern, lake plus rail equals resort town, is one of the recurring formulas of the upper Midwest.

As we push toward mile one hundred twenty, we're well inside the Southeastern Wisconsin Till Plains now — the ecoregion that replaced the Central Corn Belt Plains we started the segment in. The moraines are more pronounced, the relief more rolling. The forest patches are thicker. We're moving through a landscape that the last glacier sculpted in some detail: this far north, the ice lingered longer and pushed harder, piling up ridges and basins in patterns that make the terrain genuinely varied. The bedrock below us is Ordovician — older than anything we've crossed today — buried under a hundred feet or more of glacial drift. The drift is what farmers work with; the rock is irrelevant to the plow. But it shapes the groundwater, which shapes the springs, which shaped the spa towns, which shaped the rail routes. The connections run downward as well as across the map. We'll carry this thread west — the buried geology and the water it holds are still doing work far ahead of us.

The fields out both windows are doing something we've been watching since Chicago — laying a kind of orderly midwestern grid over ground that is anything but simple underneath. The soil here sits on Late Ordovician rock, limestone and shale laid down in a shallow sea about 450 million years ago. The corn doesn't know it. But the bedrock does.

We're in the Upper Mississippi watershed now — every raindrop that falls on this ground will eventually find its way to the Mississippi and then to the Gulf. That won't change for another sixty miles. Around milepost 180, almost imperceptibly, the land tips the other way, and water begins moving toward the Great Lakes instead. You won't feel the divide when we cross it. It will look like more Wisconsin farmland. But it's one of the continent's organizing lines — the kind of boundary that decided where the fur traders portaged, where the Ojibwe traveled, where the earliest European maps went blank.

Off to the right, the town of Ixonia. Population just over five thousand. The name is one of those invented Wisconsin place-names — no Greek or Latin root that anyone can agree on, proposed at a town meeting in 1846, the same year Wisconsin Territory was busy organizing itself as the Mexican-American War began on the other side of the continent. Two very different frontiers, moving at the same historical moment. Here, the frontier was paperwork and county lines. Out southwest, it was artillery.

The geology makes a quiet shift around milepost 140, where the bedrock transitions into the broader Paleozoic record — rocks laid down across a 290-million-year span that opens all the way back to the first complex animal life. But before we get there, a word about what Paleozoic actually means, because it's going to be part of our story for a while.

Paleozoic: from the Greek for "ancient life." It runs from about 541 million years ago — when hard-shelled animals suddenly appeared in the fossil record in an explosion of forms — down to 252 million years ago, when the largest mass extinction in Earth's history wiped out something like ninety percent of all marine species. Within that span, this part of Wisconsin was repeatedly covered by warm, shallow tropical seas. The land we're crossing was once near the equator, riding on a tectonic plate that hadn't yet finished drifting north. The fossils in the roadcuts nearby are the shells and reef structures of creatures from that tropical ocean: brachiopods — Atrypa reticularis, Leptaena rhomboidalis — filter-feeders that carpeted the seafloor about 433 million years ago. And older still, gastropods like Macluritella, coiled shells from 487 million years back. They're in the rock right outside. The corn grows on top of them.

Watertown, off the right window — just under 23,000 people now, which probably doesn't suggest a city that once challenged Milwaukee for regional dominance. In the 1850s and 1860s, Watertown was the largest German-speaking city in the United States outside of New York. German Forty-Eighters — liberals and intellectuals who fled after the failed revolutions of 1848 — poured into Wisconsin. Carl Schurz, who would become a U.S. Senator and Lincoln's ambassador to Spain, lived here. The German immigrants founded the first kindergarten in the United States here, in 1856. Then the railroads shifted their trunk lines, and the city that had the geography stopped having the advantage. The Iron Spine chose other routes. Watertown remained; it just stopped becoming.

The land between Watertown and Richwood is quietly beautiful in the midwestern way — gentle rolls, woodlots, dairy operations, the occasional barn with faded paint. We're crossing from Jefferson County into Dodge County, counties whose borders mean little on the ground but a great deal in the county seat records. Dodge County was organized in 1844 from Wisconsin Territory, back when organizing a county from territory was an act of ambition, a way of saying we intend to stay.

Ahead, the unincorporated community of Richwood — one of those places that appears on maps because the post office needed an address, not because there's much to mark. The town of Shields surrounds it. Most people here grow corn.

The Crawfish River threads through this landscape — we'll cross it near Fall River in a few miles — and it's worth knowing something about the rivers of this part of Wisconsin, because they're all doing the same thing: draining the meltwater legacy of the last ice age.

Twelve thousand years ago, the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered this ground under a mile of ice. When it retreated, it left behind a churned and rearranged landscape — the kettle lakes we saw farther east, the moraines, the till plains, the rivers that hadn't yet settled into stable channels because the old drainage patterns had been erased and new ones were still being carved. The Crawfish River is one of those new rivers. Young, in geological terms. Still adjusting.

The Ho-Chunk people — whose territory this was for thousands of years — knew these rivers as travel routes and fishing grounds long before European contact. The 1837 and 1842 treaties opened Wisconsin to settlers and required the Ho-Chunk to relocate west of the Mississippi. Many refused. They came back. They were removed again. They returned again. By the time Wisconsin became a state in 1848, there were Ho-Chunk communities still living in the state — by persistence and refusal, not by the treaty's permission. That history is present in the county names, in the river names, in the land itself, even when the signs don't mention it.

Columbus — we're stopping here. The station dates to 1906, built when this was Milwaukee Road territory. The Milwaukee Road was one of the great overreachers of American railroading — a company that spent the first half of the twentieth century building west and electrifying mountain passes and positioning itself as the premium northern transcontinental, and spent the second half slowly going bankrupt. The Milwaukee Road folded in 1980. The line we're riding here became Amtrak's. The 1906 station still stands. Columbus, Wisconsin, has a population of about five thousand — about what it had in 1906. The railroad didn't make it grow much. But it made it stay.

Columbus sits in Columbia County, which was organized in 1846 — the same year as the Mexican-American War, the same year the first Smithsonian Institution building broke ground in Washington. The county has about 58,000 people today, which is not many for a county this size. The county seat is Portage, which is where we're heading. Between here and there, the landscape opens into something wider and wetter.

Off the right, Fall River — a village of about 1,800 along the North Fork of the Crawfish River. The Crawfish is a tributary of the Rock River, which flows south into Illinois and eventually the Mississippi. Every drop of rain in Fall River today is Mississippi-bound. Twelve miles from now, that will no longer be true. We're approaching the divide.

The watershed divide between the Mississippi basin and the Great Lakes basin runs roughly through this part of Columbia County — not a ridge you'd notice, not a line you could point to on the ground. Wisconsin's topography here is so flat and glacially reworked that the continental divide between two massive drainage systems looks like a cornfield. But cross it we will, around milepost 180.

This is one of the things the fur traders and explorers understood very precisely and we've mostly forgotten: water divides are the organizing facts of a continent. Before the railroad, before the highway, before the automobile, water was the only corridor for moving people and goods across this country. The canoe route from the Great Lakes to the Mississippi ran through Portage — through the portage, the carry-over, the short stretch of land where you lifted your canoe and walked from one watershed to the other. That's not metaphor. That's exactly what happened, and it happened for centuries.

Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet made the portage in 1673, paddling up the Fox River from Green Bay, carrying their canoes roughly a mile and a half across to the Wisconsin River, and then floating south to the Mississippi — the first Europeans to reach the upper Mississippi overland from the east. The portage they used is now the city of Portage, Wisconsin. The city is named for the act of carrying a canoe. And that act, that geographical fact about where the two watersheds nearly touch, is why there was a fur trading post here, why there was a fort here (Fort Winnebago, built 1828), why there was a canal project here (the Fox-Wisconsin Waterway, started in 1838, completed sort of, abandoned eventually), and why there is an Amtrak stop here today. Geography compels. The iron spine runs where the water-routes once ran.

Out the left, the land is shifting — more wetland now, more open water visible at the edges of fields. Columbia County is roughly 28% cropland and 28% wetland. That's an unusual balance. The wetlands are glacial remnants, low spots where meltwater pooled and stayed, where peat accumulated, where cattails replaced corn. We're starting to see what Wisconsin looked like before the drainage tiles went in — before farmers systematically drained the wet prairie in the second half of the nineteenth century to make it farmable. Some of those wetlands came back. Others are still farmed, but barely, in wet years.

The Wisconsin River is just ahead — Portage sits at the bend where the Fox and Wisconsin approach each other. The Wisconsin flows southwest from here to join the Mississippi at Prairie du Chien, about 100 miles downstream. We're about to cross it. After we do, we'll have our feet, conceptually speaking, in two watersheds at once — the Fox-Wisconsin corridor has always been a hybrid place, a seam.

John Muir grew up near here, in Marquette County, just to the north. He worked farms in this landscape as a young man in the 1850s and 1860s, before he walked a thousand miles south and eventually found his way to Yosemite. What formed him — the wetlands, the glacial lakes, the moraines — is the same landscape we've been watching for the past hour. He wrote about these Wisconsin meadows with the same intensity he later brought to the Sierra Nevada. The scale was smaller. The attention was just as fierce.

Portage — we're coming in now. Ten thousand people in a city whose entire existence is an explanation of the continent. The name says it plainly: this is the carry-over, the place where the watersheds nearly touch. The Fox River flows northeast from here into the Great Lakes system. The Wisconsin flows southwest to the Mississippi. Between them, a mile and a half of ground — and for two centuries, that mile and a half was one of the most important pieces of real estate in North America.

The canal the engineers attempted here — the Fox-Wisconsin Waterway — was meant to be the inland passage from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico. They started digging in 1838. The project dragged on for decades, underfunded, interrupted by the Civil War, finally limping to a kind of completion in the 1870s, by which point the railroad had already made canals obsolete. The railroad won. We're riding the proof of it.

Around milepost 180, we cross the Great Lakes watershed divide. After that, rain falling on our roof drains toward Lake Michigan, not toward the Gulf. It's a small distinction from the window. It's a massive shift in the story of the continent.

The fields out both windows have been telling the same story for a long while now — corn, soy, a barn, a woodlot, then corn again. Beneath all of it, Paleozoic seafloor. Those sedimentary rocks down there were laid in warm shallow seas when this latitude was closer to the equator, somewhere between 250 and 540 million years ago. We can't see them — the glaciers buried everything in till and outwash — but they're down there, holding up the whole agricultural plain we've been crossing since Chicago.

We're still in the Great Lakes watershed — every stream and ditch out there eventually drains northeast toward Lake Michigan, then down the St. Lawrence to the Atlantic. That's about to change. Around mile 190, without any fanfare, we'll cross a low, subtle divide and slip into the Mississippi watershed instead. Water falling on one side of that line makes its way to the Gulf of Mexico, 1,500 miles south. The divide itself won't look like anything — no ridge, no bluff, just a slight shift in which way the ditches drain. That invisibility is the whole point: this is glacial lake-bed country, flat ground rearranged by ice, and the old topography is gone. The watershed boundary runs across a plain so level that it took nineteenth-century surveyors weeks to find it.

Coming up ahead, the town of Lewiston — 1,200 people in Columbia County. Small enough that you'd miss it in a blink, and in a sense that's the story of every town on this line west of Milwaukee. The railroad chose the route; the towns grew where the railroad stopped or watered its engines or needed a section house. Lewiston never became a city. Most of them didn't. The ones that thrived got a county seat designation or a grain elevator at the right moment; the ones that didn't became what Lewiston is now — a quiet residential scattering on a grid that still has the ghost of ambition in it.

Right around here we cross that invisible water divide, and something else shifts almost simultaneously — the ecoregion. We've been rolling through the Southeastern Wisconsin Till Plains since we left the Milwaukee basin, a landscape shaped by the last glacial advance: moraines, drumlins, lake-bed flats. Now we're entering the North Central Hardwood Forests. The difference isn't dramatic from the window, but it's real. The glaciers didn't fill every corner of Wisconsin the same way, and ahead, the forests get thicker and the wetlands wetter, the soils a bit sandier and less productive for row crops. Oak, aspen, birch start mixing into the woodlots. This ecoregion stretches northwest all the way across Minnesota, a band of transitional forest between the corn belt and the boreal north. We're at its southeastern edge right now.

Wisconsin Dells. If you've seen roadside billboards for the last hundred miles, you've seen the name. The town is the waterpark capital of the Midwest — something like twenty million visitors a year, which sounds absurd for a city of 3,000 people. But the original attraction wasn't the waterparks. It was the Dells themselves: a gorge cut by the Wisconsin River through Cambrian sandstone, the walls rising in columns and arches that genuinely startled nineteenth-century travelers. The railroad made the Dells famous. Trains brought tourists from Chicago starting in the 1870s, photographers followed, and the images of those sandstone towers — strange, almost desert-looking formations in the middle of Wisconsin — went national. We're at the station stop here, so take a look out both windows at the country around town. That pale, buff-colored rock showing in cuts and outcroppings: that's what the Dells are made of.

The sandstone around Wisconsin Dells deserves a moment. We're crossing a geological boundary right now — the bedrock is shifting from general Paleozoic sedimentary to specifically Cambrian rock, which means some of the oldest sedimentary stone in North America. Around mile 200, the formations beneath us date to 490 to 540 million years ago. The fossils found in strata like these nearby — small brachiopods and gastropods with names like Schizopea and Sinuopea — lived in the Cambrian sea that covered this region when the first complex animals were diversifying. The tracks of trilobites. The earliest reef-builders. A sea full of creatures with no predecessors, evolving fast, 490 million years ago, on what is now a Wisconsin dairy county.

The bedrock shifts here to Cambrian sandstone — 490 to 540 million years old. That's the base layer of the Paleozoic, right at the explosion of animal life. The sandstone started as a beach and shallow seafloor, grains of quartz rounded by surf and current, compacted over hundreds of millions of years into rock. Wind and water have been cutting it ever since. What made the Dells is what makes canyons everywhere: differential erosion, the rock splitting along joints while softer layers wash away, leaving columns and fins. The Wisconsin River did the cutting during the great meltwater floods at the end of the last ice age, and it did it fast — geologically fast, meaning a few thousand years. The gorge you'd see from a boat on the river is younger than the pyramids, geologically speaking, even if the rock itself is older than any animal with a spine.

Juneau County begins around mile 204. The population density drops — 26,000 people spread across a county bigger than Rhode Island. Poverty runs higher here than in Columbia County to the southeast, nearly 15 percent. The land cover tells you why: 40 percent wetland, 40 percent developed, which in rural Wisconsin means small towns and scattered farms. The crops are hay, corn, soybeans — but the yields are lower, the soils sandier, the drainage more complicated. This is marginal agricultural land by Midwest standards. The farms that persist here are the ones that adapted — dairy, specialty crops, outdoor recreation. The ones that didn't adapt left behind the usual archaeology of rural attrition: a closed co-op, a grain elevator with weeds growing through the loading dock, a Methodist church with eight families.

Lyndon Station, ahead — a crossroads rather than a town, the kind of place that existed to serve the railroad and now exists in a different way, as a dot on county maps and a cluster of houses on a county road. The name says everything: this was a railroad station point, a place where the line paused. When the trains ran on steam and needed water and coal every thirty miles or so, places like this had a function. Diesel changed the calculus. The stops lengthened, the section houses emptied, the stations closed. The town stayed, barely, because people already lived there and the land was paid for.

The railroad's relationship to these small Wisconsin towns is the same story playing out all across the northern tier, from here to the Pacific. Land grants. The federal government gave the railroads roughly 174 million acres of public land to incentivize construction — every other section in a checkerboard pattern on either side of the track. The railroads then platted towns on their land, sold lots, and advertised in Germany and Scandinavia for settlers. The towns that got a depot thrived; the ones the line bypassed withered before they started. This was the 1865-to-1900 era: the great cattle-drive trails and the Santa Fe trade were running their last years in the Southwest, Chicago was becoming the railroad metropolis of the interior, and here in Wisconsin the same iron logic was arranging the landscape. You can still read the railroad's decision-making in which towns exist and which don't, a century and a half later.

Mauston, the county seat of Juneau County — 4,300 people, 70 miles northwest of Madison. The seat was set here in 1857, just as the county was being organized and the railroads were starting to push through. County seats had advantages: the courthouse generated traffic, legal business kept lawyers and clerks employed, and the county government meant the town wouldn't simply fold when an economic wave passed. Mauston held. Juneau County itself, formed in 1857, was named for Solomon Juneau — the fur trader and co-founder of Milwaukee, one of those figures who bridge the French-Canadian voyageur era and the American commercial expansion that followed it. By 1857, Juneau himself was already dead, and Milwaukee was a city of 45,000. But his name went on the county, a small monument to the world that the railroads were replacing.

There's a pattern to these county seats that you notice if you ride enough train miles through the rural Midwest. They all have a courthouse square, a main street that was once the commercial spine, a few blocks of Victorian commercial architecture behind painted or aluminum-sided facades, and then almost immediately — fields. The boom was real. Between 1870 and 1910, Wisconsin added half a million people, most of them in exactly this kind of county. Then the demographics shifted: farm mechanization reduced labor needs, young people moved to Milwaukee or Madison or Chicago, and the county population stabilized or fell. Mauston's 4,300 today is probably close to what it was in 1920. That's not failure — it's a kind of equilibrium, a county seat that found its floor and stayed there.

Camp Douglas, ahead — 647 people, and a name that opens onto an unexpected story. The village is home to Volk Field, an Air National Guard base, and there's been military presence around here since the Civil War, when a Union training and prisoner-of-war camp operated in this area. The original Camp Douglas was in Chicago — one of the largest Civil War prison camps in the North, holding Confederate prisoners in conditions that killed thousands. This Wisconsin town shares the name but not the infamy, connected through a chain of frontier-era naming conventions. What's here now is a Guard base that periodically fills the sky with training flights, a small village built on the outer edge of federal land, and a sign that tells you the population was 601 in 2010 and 647 in 2020. Forty-six people. The county is counting.

Watch the landscape out both windows for the next few miles. The terrain here is part of what geologists call the Driftless Area — a region of Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, and Illinois that the Pleistocene glaciers somehow missed, or touched only lightly. While the ice sheets that created the Great Lakes were grinding and flattening everything to the east and south of us, this corner of the upper Midwest kept its ancient stream-cut topography: valleys, ridges, coulees, bluffs. The Driftless Area is an anomaly, a patch of older landscape in a region otherwise remade by ice. We're at its edge, and if you look carefully you'll start to see the hint of more topographic relief — not dramatic, but the flat is breaking.

Oakdale, left window — 302 people, Monroe County, the smallest populated place we've named all segment. The village sits inside the Town of Oakdale, which is the standard Wisconsin configuration: a village incorporated within a town (the township), both governing the same territory with overlapping jurisdictions. It's an administrative structure inherited from New England via the Northwest Ordinance, transplanted to the upper Midwest in the 1840s and 1850s and never replaced. Oakdale the village: a few streets, a church, probably a tavern. The town around it: farms, wetlands, the county road grid. Monroe County to the west has more forest than Juneau, a third of its land cover, and the terrain is starting to feel it — the tree lines thicker, the fields fitting themselves into whatever flat ground the topography offers.

As we push toward mile 240 and into Monroe County, the large arc of this journey starts to clarify. We've crossed the Great Lakes watershed boundary, entered the Mississippi basin, watched the Paleozoic seafloor give way to Cambrian sandstone, moved from the glacially flattened till plains into the edge of the Driftless country. Each of those crossings happened without ceremony, announced only by a slight change in the land — the rock in a roadcut, the angle of a ridge, the direction a creek runs. That's the gift of a long train ride: you move slowly enough to notice the gradients. Over the next few hours, the elevation will start working more deliberately, the watershed boundaries will multiply, and eventually the land will start doing things that require an explanation in plate tectonics rather than glaciology. We're not there yet. But the Midwest is beginning to let go.

The train slows into Tomah — a grid town platted in 1855, the same decade the railroad was threading its way across Wisconsin, making and naming settlements as it went. The name itself came from a Menominee chief, Thomas Carron, whose French nickname "Tomah" the founders borrowed to give the place a sound of the country it displaced. Nine thousand people here now, surrounded by the broad wetland flats of Monroe County. Watch for the depot as we ease through — these small Wisconsin stations were the commercial pulse of the county for a century before the highway took over.

Monroe County is running past us now — a third wetland, a third forest, the rest field and pasture. Hay, corn, soybeans, the same rotation that covers most of the upper Midwest, but here the land is noticeably flatter and wetter than the till plains we left behind in eastern Wisconsin. That's the Driftless character: no glacier scraped this country clean and left behind the well-drained till that makes the east side of the state so productive for row crops. The drainage here is slower, the wetlands persist, and the forest holds on in the draws and coulees — narrow valleys carved by streams that found the Paleozoic limestone and sandstone and cut down through it over millions of years.

We're near the high point of this stretch — just over 1,100 feet. It doesn't feel dramatic. There's no pass, no cliff, no obvious ridge. But this quiet rise is a water divide: rain falling on one side eventually reaches the Wisconsin River and the Mississippi; rain on the other drains north and east toward the Great Lakes. On a long train you learn to read these invisible lines. The Mississippi basin we're about to enter is one of the great drainages of the continent — from here west and south, everything flows toward the Gulf of Mexico, and the river itself will be our companion all the way to La Crosse.

The bedrock underfoot through all of this is Paleozoic sedimentary rock — limestone and sandstone and dolomite laid down in shallow tropical seas between 490 and 540 million years ago, when this part of North America sat near the equator. Those seas were full of life. Paleontologists working the bluffs along the Mississippi here have pulled out Dikelocephalus minnesotensis, an Early Ordovician trilobite, and a gallery of early cephalopods — Ellesmeroceras, Burenoceras, Clarkoceras — coiled and conical shells from a world 486 million years in the past, when the first animals with complex eyes and active hunting were just beginning to figure out the ocean. They're locked in the bluffs we're about to descend through. You won't see them from the train — they take a hammer and a careful eye — but the formations they came from are the walls of the valley ahead.

What the railroad found when it surveyed this route in the 1850s and 1860s was a natural corridor: the coulees and valleys carved into that Paleozoic limestone gave a gradient the steam locomotives of the era could actually climb. The railroad didn't carve this landscape — the rivers did, over tens of millions of years — but the railroad followed the rivers because the rivers had done the grade work already. That's the logic repeated across the entire northern tier of the country: iron follows water because water chose the lowest path first. Chicago, growing into the railroad metropolis of the interior in those same decades, needed a line to the Northwest, and this river corridor was the answer.

Bangor town — population 617. A small La Crosse County settlement, part of the La Crosse metropolitan area in the statistical sense but rural in every visible sense. These small places on the Mississippi corridor have a particular rhythm: a founding in the land-rush years, a generation of growth tied to the railroad, and then a long, quiet hold. Not ghost towns — still here, still occupied — but the ambition of the 1870s reduced to a sustainable steadiness. Most of the county's 120,000 people are concentrated in La Crosse itself, just ahead.

La Crosse County is running past on both sides now, the land shifting — two-thirds cropland, a third pasture, the wetlands mostly behind us. The Mississippi is getting close; we can feel the terrain dropping and compressing toward the river corridor. La Crosse County was organized in 1851, the same year the federal government was signing the Fort Laramie Treaty with the Plains nations far to the west — a treaty that would be broken within a decade as the railroad and the settlers it carried pushed through. Here in Wisconsin the displacement was earlier and more complete; by 1851 the Menominee and Ho-Chunk had been largely confined to reservations, and the county was being organized for Euro-American settlement.

The railroad reached La Crosse by the mid-1850s, and what it found there was one of the finest natural settings on the Upper Mississippi: the confluence of the Black and La Crosse Rivers with the main stem, a broad flood plain, bluffs rising behind, and river traffic from St. Louis and St. Paul already moving through. The combination of river and rail made La Crosse briefly one of the most important transshipment points in the upper Midwest — lumber from the Wisconsin pineries, grain from the farms spreading west, all of it moving through this narrow gap in the bluffs.

Look left — this is La Crosse, the largest city on Wisconsin's western border, 52,000 people pressed between the Mississippi and the bluffs that rise 500 feet behind the city. The river here is braided and wide, split into channels by islands, the kind of river geography that made steamboat captains cautious and river pilots valuable. Mark Twain knew this reach of the river. The railroad displaced the steamboat era but never erased it; the grain elevators and the terminal infrastructure still reflect a city built on moving things. La Crosse was platted in 1841 — early, by Wisconsin standards — as a fur-trade outpost, and grew fast once the railroad arrived. This is our station stop; the doors will open here.

Now we cross the Mississippi. This is the moment the segment has been building toward — not because the river is a surprise, but because crossing it means crossing a line that runs through American geography with unusual clarity. On the Wisconsin side: the Driftless Area, the Paleozoic blufflands, the upper Midwest's characteristic mixture of wetland and small-farm landscape. On the Minnesota side: we enter Winona County, where the land is 71 percent water and wetland by cover type, and where the river occupies a broad valley it carved through glacial outwash. The Mississippi here runs between bluffs 400 to 600 feet high, some of the most dramatic river scenery in the interior of the continent.

This corridor is one of the great migratory flyways of North America — the Mississippi Flyway, used by hundreds of millions of birds twice a year. In fall and spring the backwater lakes and islands below the bluffs fill with waterfowl: canvasbacks, scaup, tundra swans moving between the boreal breeding grounds and the Gulf Coast wintering areas. The bluffs we're threading now have been a navigational landmark for those birds, and for people, for a very long time. The Ho-Chunk and Dakota people used these bluffs as territorial markers. French voyageurs in the 1600s named the river La Crosse for a game played on the bottomlands. The names stack up the way the geological strata do — one era laid over another.

Dakota, Minnesota — 295 people, a name that tells you plainly who was here before. The Dakota nation held the upper Mississippi valley for centuries before American expansion; the Dakota War of 1862 and its brutal aftermath — mass executions, forced removal — compressed that presence into reservation land farther west and north. Towns named Dakota, like this one, were often named by settlers who arrived after the displacement, borrowing the name of the people they had displaced. It's a pattern repeated across the Minnesota map. The town itself is small and quiet, sitting on the river terrace below the bluffs.

Winona County running past us now: the bluffs to the right rising in steps of Prairie du Chien dolomite and St. Peter Sandstone, the same Ordovician sequence we saw in Wisconsin, but here exposed in walls rather than buried under wetland. The valley floor is wide — the Mississippi ran much larger at the end of the last ice age, carrying meltwater from the Laurentide ice sheet, and the broad flat terraces we're crossing are the legacy of that swollen river. The current channel is narrower, contained within that oversized valley.

We're in the Western Corn Belt Plains now, or close to it — the ecoregion boundary runs through this stretch, and by the time we reach Winona in a few miles we'll have crossed it fully. The land will continue to feel like river country for a while yet, but the underlying shift is underway: from the bluffland character of the Driftless to the flatter, more agricultural terrain of the upper Corn Belt. The elevation has been dropping steadily — we're nearly 300 feet lower than the summit at Tomah — and it will continue to drop as we follow the Mississippi corridor northwest toward the Twin Cities.

Lamoille — a small populated place in Winona County, the valley widening slightly around it. The name is French, one of the quiet reminders that this river corridor was a French trade route two centuries before it was an American railroad corridor. The Great Northern Railway that eventually ran through here followed the same logic the French voyageurs had — the river is the easiest path through the bluffs, and whoever controls the corridor controls the movement of goods. We're following a route of continental commerce that is at least 350 years old. The bluffs ahead are the same Paleozoic limestone, but we're reading them differently now: not as geology to explain, but as walls of a corridor we're committed to, following the river northwest.

The bluffs crowding both sides of the river — they're Paleozoic limestone and dolomite, laid down when this whole region sat under a shallow tropical sea, somewhere between 490 and 540 million years ago. We've been riding over that rock since Wisconsin. It's not dramatic to look at, but if you know what you're looking for, the layering in those cliffs tells time in a way that no clock can. Each band is a different sea floor, a different extinction, a different world.

The Mississippi is doing what it always does here — braiding through its own backwater, splitting into channels and sloughs and islands that don't quite know which bank they belong to. This is the upper river, still young in its behavior, still arguing with the glacier's leftovers. The channel we're following hugs the Minnesota bluffs on the left. Wisconsin sits just across the water to our right, though you'd be forgiven for losing track of which state is which — the river doesn't care.

Homer sits just ahead of us, one of the older white settlements in this corner of Minnesota. It was a going concern in the 1850s, a river landing, a mill town with ambitions. Then Winona, a few miles downstream, got the railhead. Homer got the silence. That's the story of almost every small river town we've been passing — the railroad chose one and left the others to slowly thin out, the way a forest reclaims a field, quietly and without ceremony.

Here's the chain that made this valley: water carved the gap through the bluffs, the gap gave the railroad a grade it could manage, the railroad came in the 1870s and platted towns at every strategic landing. Winona was already there — founded in 1851, barely a year after Minnesota opened to white settlement — but the rail line locked in its primacy. Every town upstream and downstream felt the gravitational pull of wherever the trains stopped and loaded. The Mississippi corridor had been a highway for ten thousand years; the railroad simply inherited the alignment and hardened it into steel.

We're pulling into Winona. Take a moment to look at the bluffs closing in from both sides — Sugar Loaf, the tall isolated column on the left, is a remnant of the same Paleozoic limestone we've been crossing, carved by the river and the melt of the last ice age. The town itself is built on a river terrace, sand and gravel left by glacial floods. In the late nineteenth century Winona was one of the wealthiest cities per capita in the country — white pine from the northern forests came downriver in vast log rafts, was milled here, and shipped out by rail. The lumber barons built mansions you can still see from the train. The pine is gone. The mansions remain.

The white pine story is worth sitting with. By 1900, the forests that had fed the Winona mills for thirty years were essentially gone — stripped from northern Minnesota and Wisconsin at a pace that even the loggers knew was unsustainable. What replaced them was agriculture: the cutover land was sold to immigrant farmers, Scandinavians mostly, Poles, Germans, who broke the stumps and tried to farm ground that wasn't really farmland. Many failed. Some stayed. The towns that had grown up around the mills shrank back to river-landing size. Winona kept its rail connections and its institutions — a state university, a cathedral, the bones of civic ambition — and survived. The mill towns upriver did not.

Minnesota City, just ahead. Population 202 at the last count. It was platted in 1852 by a German utopian community — the Turners, freethinkers who imagined a rational, secular colony on the Mississippi. The experiment collapsed within a few years, as utopian experiments tend to. What's left is a quiet river-edge settlement, a few hundred people who like living between the bluffs and the water. The name Minnesota City suggests grand ambitions. The population suggests what became of them.

The fossils in this limestone are extraordinary, and we're riding right over them. Dikelocephalus minnesotensis — named for this state — is a trilobite from about 490 million years ago, found in the rock of these bluffs. It lived in that shallow tropical sea, crawled across the muddy bottom, and died, and the mud compressed around it over half a billion years. Now it's in the cliff face you can see from the window, if you know where to look. The Cambrian-Ordovician boundary runs through this valley. Time made physical, right there in the rock.

Minneiska — the name is Dakota, a reminder that this river corridor was Mdewakanton Sioux territory for centuries before the treaties of the 1850s extinguished those claims, or tried to. The town itself is tiny, 97 people, tucked between the bluffs and the river. The Dakota name survived the displacement of the people who gave it. That's a pattern we'll see again and again on this route: the names persist as the cultures that made them were pushed west, pushed north, pushed off the map entirely.

The Fort Laramie Treaties of 1851 and 1868 attempted to codify indigenous land boundaries across the northern plains. Both were broken, systematically, as settlement pressure and gold strikes made the agreements inconvenient. Along the upper Mississippi specifically, the Dakota were removed to reservations in the 1850s, then expelled from Minnesota almost entirely after the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862. Entire communities gone within a decade. The towns that replaced them — Minnesota City, Minneiska, the string of small river settlements we're passing — were platted in that same decade, on ground cleared partly by treaty and partly by force.

Look for the brick building in the unincorporated community of Weaver, coming up on the left — the Mercantile, built in 1875, Italianate details pressed into the facade, now on the National Register of Historic Places. 1875 is a specific moment: the Northern Pacific was driving west across Dakota Territory, the Chisholm Trail cattle drives were at their peak, barbed wire was just being patented. Here in Weaver, someone was confident enough in the river-landing economy to build in brick and put up decorative cornices. That confidence wasn't wrong exactly — the building is still standing — but the economy it was built for, the river freight and the mill traffic, was already beginning its long decline. The railroad was winning.

This is the essential drama of the Mississippi valley corridor: for decades, river and rail competed for the freight. Steamboats had ruled the upper river since the 1820s. By the time our railroad was built along the Minnesota bluffs in the 1870s, the steamboat era was already fading — rail was faster, more reliable, less subject to ice and flood and snag. The river towns that had grown up as steamboat landings found themselves suddenly positioned along a rail line instead, and the ones that got a station thrived and the ones that didn't began the long, slow process of becoming scenic. We're passing through the scenic ones now. The valley is beautiful in a way that has a lot to do with the economy not quite working out.

Out the right window, across the river in Wisconsin — Nelson, in Buffalo County, a river town of 574 people. The train doesn't stop there; we're on the Minnesota side. But it's worth noting: this stretch of the Mississippi forms the Wisconsin-Minnesota border, and the communities on both banks grew up together, trading across the water, connected by ferry before the bridges came. Two states, one river economy. The divides we keep crossing — water divides, state lines, watershed boundaries — rarely correspond to how people actually live.

The bedrock here is still Paleozoic, still the Ordovician limestone and dolomite sequence we've been on since the segment began. But within those rocks, if you could crack them open, you'd find conodonts — tiny tooth-like structures from eel-like animals that went extinct at the end of the Triassic. Amorphognathus superbus, Belodina compressa: names that sound invented but aren't, formal taxonomy applied to creatures nobody has ever seen alive. They're index fossils, which means geologists use them to date rock — find the right conodont and you know within a few million years when that layer was deposited. The bluffs around us are full of them.

Pepin, right side. It sits on a wide spot in the river — Lake Pepin, technically, a natural impoundment behind a delta fan pushed into the Mississippi by the Chippewa River from the east. Laura Ingalls Wilder was born seven miles back in the woods from here, in 1867. Her family were homesteaders in the big woods of western Wisconsin before they moved to the open prairie. The Little House books begin here, in this river valley, in the decade after the Dakota were expelled. Wilder's childhood stories of wild abundance — the woods, the game, the family independence — are set in a landscape that had been thoroughly reorganized within living memory of her parents. She didn't write about that part.

Lake Pepin stretches behind us now as we move upstream. It's one of the widest natural points on the upper Mississippi, roughly twenty miles long and two miles across at its widest. The Chippewa River fan that created it is still growing — the Chippewa carries sediment from Wisconsin's interior, and every flood pushes that delta a little further into the Mississippi, maintaining the impoundment. The lake fills in, slowly, geologically. In ten thousand years, at current rates, it won't be a lake anymore. It'll be a marsh, then a floodplain, then just another section of river. The Mississippi is always renegotiating its terms.

We've crossed into Goodhue County now, and the land cover begins to shift. Less water, more developed ground, more open fields as the bluffs widen and the bottomland broadens. The crops here are corn and soybeans, same as behind us, but the Ordovician bedrock we've been riding over is still underneath it all, still the same ancient sea floor, and will be for another forty miles before it gives way to something older. The farm looks modern. Under the topsoil, nothing has changed in 485 million years.

The township name comes from a Dakota leader — Wacouta, "Shooter," one of the men who navigated the collision between two worlds along this stretch of the upper Mississippi in the 1840s and 50s. Four hundred people live here now. The bluffs on both sides of the river — those pale limestone walls — are the same Paleozoic seafloor we've been riding through since we left La Crosse. Ancient lime mud, compressed. Five hundred million years of patience, and still standing.

The Great Northern came through here on its drive toward the Pacific — James J. Hill's road, the iron spine of the northern tier. Hill was obsessive about grades. He sent surveyors up every river valley, through every pass, looking for the gentlest possible climb across the continent. The Mississippi corridor gave him the easiest eastern approach, which is why we're here now, threading between these bluffs, following a route that the river itself engineered over ten thousand years of post-glacial cutting. The railway didn't choose this valley. The valley was already the path. Hill just laid iron in it.

Red Wing appears on the left, spreading up from the river bank against the bluff. Named for the Dakota chief Hupahuduta — Red Wing — whose band held this territory for generations before the treaties of the 1850s stripped it away. The city that replaced the village became a stoneware capital: Red Wing Pottery, founded 1877, produced crocks and jugs shipped across the Midwest. The pottery's long closed, the old stoneware commands high prices at antiques markets. Sixteen thousand people live here now. The county seat of Goodhue County, part of the Minneapolis metro. A Mississippi river town still arranged around its waterfront, still legible.

Look at the fields as we pull clear of Red Wing — corn and soybeans running up to the bluff edges, then the limestone walls dropping clean to the flood plain. This is Goodhue County's land: forty percent wetland, forty percent developed, the rest in agriculture. The numbers sound modest, but out the window it reads as a full landscape — productive, managed, old. The bedrock under all of it is still Paleozoic sedimentary, the same broad band of Cambrian and Ordovician seafloor that underlies most of southeastern Minnesota. We haven't changed rock yet. But we're about to. Around milepost 400, the formation shifts — and the story of that rock is worth holding in mind.

Wisconsin side, right window — Diamond Bluff, a town of fewer than five hundred people on the opposite bank. The bluff it's named for catches the light differently depending on the time of day; the limestone faces can read almost white at noon, ochre in the late afternoon. These Wisconsin bluffs are continuous with the Minnesota side — the Mississippi here is cutting through the same plateau, the same layered Paleozoic stack. The river is the seam. The state line is political. The geology doesn't notice it.

We're in the Driftless now — the unglaciated pocket of the upper Midwest, where the ice sheets flowed around rather than over, leaving these sharp valleys intact while the country to the north and west was planed flat and buried under glacial till. The bluffs we keep passing are possible only because no glacier smoothed them. Everywhere else in the upper Midwest, the pre-glacial landscape is buried. Here it's exposed, running.

The land is changing slowly. Corn replaces the floodplain forest in the broader bottoms. The watershed is still Mississippi — every creek we cross is feeding water that will eventually reach the Gulf. But we're approaching the St. Croix. That confluence is a boundary. Past it, the character of the corridor shifts.

The St. Croix comes in from the right — clear water draining the lake country to the north, forming the Wisconsin-Minnesota border for its lower hundred and twenty-five miles before it empties into the Mississippi just south of here. In Dakota the river is Hoġan Wanḳe Kin — something close to "fish-lying river." The lower St. Croix is a national scenic riverway; the bluffs here are protected, which is why they still look like this and not like the developed banks closer to the Twin Cities. We've also just crossed an ecological threshold: the Western Corn Belt Plains begin here, around milepost 390. The Driftless Blufflands we've been riding through give way — not abruptly, but steadily — to a flatter, more glaciated terrain as we push northwest toward St. Paul. The corn belt, in other words, is just getting started.

The Western Corn Belt Plains stretch from here into Iowa and the eastern Dakotas — a biome defined by deep glacially-deposited soils, reliable summer rains just sufficient for corn and soybeans without irrigation, and a flat-to-rolling topography that rewards large-scale row-crop farming. It replaced the tallgrass prairie that covered most of this ground before the 1860s and 70s. The tallgrass is almost entirely gone now — less than one percent of the original extent survives in scattered preserves. What's out the window is the replacement: enormous, productive, ecologically simplified. Corn yields in this belt run to two hundred bushels an acre in a good year. The landscape is engineered as surely as the railway we're riding.

And speaking of the railway — we're approaching the eastern edge of the Twin Cities metro. The Great Northern's original route into Minneapolis and St. Paul ran through exactly this corridor. By the time the line was consolidated into Burlington Northern and later BNSF, these tracks had been carrying freight and passengers for over a century. We're still on that same iron spine.

Cottage Grove sits on the north bank of the Mississippi, ten miles south of St. Paul. It incorporated as a city in 1963 — one of those mid-century suburbs that sprawled outward from the Twin Cities as the Interstate Highway Act remade American geography. The freeway arrived, the rail lines that had once been the only way in or out became freight routes, and the towns along the Mississippi became bedroom communities for Minneapolis and St. Paul. Cottage Grove: fifty thousand people now, Washington County, median household income over a hundred and ten thousand dollars. The wealth gradient between here and Goodhue County to the south is striking. Same river. Different economy.

Just past Cottage Grove, around milepost 400, the bedrock quietly changes beneath us. We cross onto the Shakopee Formation — Early Ordovician, roughly 485 million years old, and a genuinely different rock from the broad Paleozoic band we've been riding through. The Shakopee is a heterolithic unit: thin-to-medium bedded dolostone, sandy dolostone, sandstone, and shale, laid down in a shallow tropical sea that covered this part of the continent nearly half a billion years ago. It contains oolites — tiny spheres of calcium carbonate precipitated around a grain of sand in warm agitated water, the same process you see in the Bahamas today. It contains intraclasts — chunks of already-hardened seafloor ripped up by storms and redeposited. And it contains fossilized microbial mounds: stromatolites, the oldest visible ecosystems on Earth, here preserved in Ordovician dolostone under Minneapolis.

The fossils collected near this stretch of track — conodonts like Amorphognathus superbus and Belodina confluens, brachiopods like Petrocrania reversa, gastropods like Hormotoma gracilis — date to around 457 million years ago, the Late Ordovician. That sea was full of life. Complex life. Reef-builders, filter feeders, grazers. A world entirely without terrestrial plants, without insects, without any creature that had learned to breathe air on dry land — but the oceans already intricate, already old. We ride above it.

The bedrock shifts again around milepost 410 — into Late Ordovician sedimentary, slightly younger, laid down as that ancient tropical sea gradually receded. Above it: glacial till, lake sediments, and then the city. St. Paul is eleven miles ahead. We're entering the core of the Twin Cities metro — Ramsey County, over half a million people, the state capital, the older of the two cities (St. Paul got its growth earlier, when the river was the highway; Minneapolis grew with the railways and the mills). The Mississippi bends here, braids its floodplain, and the bluffs that defined the whole corridor begin to give way to the leveled terrain of a major city built on both banks.

St. Paul station — our stop. Union Depot, actually, the Beaux-Arts terminal that opened in 1926 and served as the city's rail junction until Amtrak contracted to a smaller facility. The Empire Builder pauses here.
