And geologically we're back in Late Cretaceous siltstone and shale, the same broad formation we've been riding over since mile 750, that 100-million-year-old sediment from the closing chapters of the Western Interior Seaway. The prairie rolls slightly here — the first real topographic inflection we've felt since the Red River valley. We have crossed into the Northern Glaciated Plains, where the glacier left its moraine-work unsmoothed by a lake's patient filling. It's a small thing, that roll. But after sixty miles of absolute flatness, the land remembering its own irregular past feels like something.
27.place: Nelson County line / Northern Glaciated Plains

27.text: We've just crested a subtle ridge — you'd never know it from the seat, but the ground under our wheels sits at almost exactly 1,532 feet, which sounds modest until you trace the water from here. Rain falling east of this line finds its way to the Red River, then north to Hudson Bay. Rain falling west drains into the Missouri, then south and east to the Gulf. The Souris-Red-Rainy watershed is behind us now. The whole remainder of this afternoon belongs to the Missouri basin. That shift, invisible to the eye, is as absolute as a continental border.

Below that rolling black soil runs Late Cretaceous bedrock — siltstone, shale, sandstone laid down when a shallow inland sea covered all of this country, maybe 75 million years ago. The glacier came and went and left its drift on top, smoothing everything flat, filling the low spots with lakes. What you see is the glacier's furniture, rearranged. The bedrock is buried so deep you'll never glimpse it from the train. But the farms riding over it — the winter wheat, the soybeans — those are possible because the glacier ground that ancient seafloor into something the root can use.

Petersburg ahead — population 162 at last count. It was platted in 1884, which places it squarely in the great railroad-town wave. The Great Northern was pushing west, and wherever the surveyors staked a siding, a town appeared: grain elevator, post office, church, general store, all within a year or two of the steel arriving. Petersburg got its elevator. It got its church. What it didn't get was a second act when the highway pulled commerce to larger centers. Some of these towns are still breathing, just barely. Petersburg is one of them.

The years 1882, 1883, 1884 appear again and again in Nelson County's founding dates — Petersburg, Michigan City, Lakota, Crary. Every one of them born in a three-year burst. That's not coincidence; that's the railroad schedule. James J. Hill's Great Northern pushed across Dakota Territory with something close to military discipline, grading and laying track through the short construction season, platting towns at regular intervals to capture the grain trade. The towns existed, legally and on paper, before a single family had moved in. The railroad drew the map, then settlers came to fill it. It was the most systematic act of landscape creation in American history — a continent colonized by survey line and siding spacing. Chicago, already the railroad metropolis of the interior, absorbed the grain this whole system produced. The wheat we're riding through today still moves on essentially the same logic, though now by truck to the elevator, then by rail to the terminal.

The locals call this one Michigan — the "City" dropped off somewhere along the way, as small-town formality tends to. Founded 1882, platted 1883. Population at the 2020 census: 263. It's been declining for decades, which is the dominant story of the Northern Plains agricultural town: the machinery got bigger, the farms consolidated, fewer hands needed, the young left for Fargo or Minneapolis, and the town contracted around whoever stayed. The school is usually the last institution standing. Then the school consolidates with a neighbor, and that's often the last chapter.

Here's the arithmetic that explains what we're seeing. In the 1880s, a family farm on the Northern Plains was 160 acres — the homestead quarter-section. You needed neighbors close by to share the labor, the church, the school, the social world. Towns spaced every eight or ten miles made sense. By the 1980s, a single operation might be ten thousand acres. The combines and grain carts and GPS autosteer replaced ten families' worth of labor. Those ten families' houses, their churches, their grain elevators — the landscape is full of them. Some are still upright. Some are foundation outlines in a field. We've been passing the evidence for hours. The economists call it agricultural consolidation. Driving through it, it looks more like a slow withdrawal. What persists: the land itself, the wheat still growing, and — more than outsiders expect — the people who chose to stay.

Lakota is the county seat of Nelson County — which tells you it held on while others thinned. Population 683. It sits about 63 miles west of Grand Forks and 27 miles east of Devils Lake, planted precisely midway between two larger centers, which is how county seats often ended up where they did: far enough from rivals to anchor their own hinterland. Founded 1883, another child of the railroad survey. The county seat designation gave Lakota its courthouse, which gave it a stable institutional weight the smaller towns never got. That one difference — courthouse or no courthouse — has meant the difference between slow decline and actual survival across scores of Plains counties.

We're moving now through Ramsey County — population just over eleven thousand, with Devils Lake ahead as its anchor. Notice the land beginning to carry a little more water: shallow ponds, wetlands catching in the low spots, the glacial terrain pocked and irregular in ways the smoother drift plain behind us wasn't. This is the Coteau du Missouri transitional zone, where the glacial geology left a more chaotic surface. Devils Lake itself — we'll reach it soon — is the largest natural lake in North Dakota. It has no outlet. Water comes in, nothing goes out. Which means it rises and falls with the climate, and for the last several decades it has mostly risen, flooding farmland and roads and eventually requiring entire communities to relocate. A closed basin lake is a barometer. Devils Lake has been reading the precipitation record faithfully for ten thousand years.

Bartlett is listed as unincorporated — which means it never quite achieved the legal standing of a town, or it shed that status as its population drained away. There's a class of Northern Plains community that exists in the records, in the memory of the people who grew up there, and in a few standing buildings, but not in any official census count. Bartlett is one of these. The name persists on the map. The place itself is something more ambiguous.

The railroad that built these towns also destroyed some of them — not through malice, but through the logic of the branch line audit. Every decade or two, a railroad would examine its lightly used branches and ask whether the traffic justified the track maintenance. When the answer was no, the branch closed. The elevator that depended on the branch had no reason to exist. The town that depended on the elevator had no economic anchor. This is how the map was unwritten, town by town, from the 1920s through the 1980s. The Great Northern — which became Burlington Northern after the 1970 merger — ran the trains through here, and its successors still do. The main line survived. The branches, many of them, did not. What we're riding is the survivor.

Crary — founded 1884, named for William Crary, who owned much of the surrounding land before the town was platted. Population 113. The pattern is legible now: landowner's name becomes town name, 1884 founding date, a life measured in grain and proximity to the railroad. William Crary presumably sold or granted that land knowing the railroad would make it valuable. Speculators and landowners and railroad companies often moved in interlocking orbits in these founding years — the railroad needed towns to generate freight, the towns needed the railroad to exist, and the men who held the land sat at the intersection of both needs.

Devils Lake ahead — and the lake itself deserves a moment before we pull into the station. It is a remnant of a much larger glacial lake that covered this basin at the end of the last ice age. As the glacier melted and the climate dried, that lake shrank to its current form. But "current form" is a moving target: Devils Lake has no outlet to a river, so it responds directly to precipitation. In the wet decades of the 1990s and 2000s, the lake rose more than thirty feet, inundating tens of thousands of acres of farmland, swamping roads, forcing the relocation of homes and highways. The state eventually built an outlet to the Sheyenne River to relieve the pressure — a massive engineering intervention to manage a lake that was doing exactly what it had always done, which was reflect the climate back at us. Ten thousand years ago, the basin held a lake perhaps fifty feet deeper than today's. The Pleistocene version makes our current engineering problem look like a minor adjustment.

Devils Lake station — our stop here. The city of about 7,200 is the largest community we'll see until we've crossed more of Dakota. The name comes from the lake, and the lake's name is a translation of the Lakota name — Mni Wakan, "Spirit Water" or "Mysterious Water." The first European-American house went up here in the early 1880s; the town incorporated in 1883, the railroad arrived, and it became the commercial and governmental center of Ramsey County. The Spirit Lake Nation — Dakota people — have lived around this lake for centuries; they're still here, their reservation abutting the lake's south shore. The town that carries the translated name of the Lakota's sacred water sits today in the middle of a landscape those same people shaped for generations before any survey line was drawn. That layering — indigenous name, settler town, railroad grid, all stacked on the same shores — is as precise a summary of the Northern Plains as anything we'll see today.

Pulling west out of Devils Lake, the land holds its elevation — we're still near 1,500 feet, and we'll stay close to this for the next hundred miles. The bedrock below us is shifting almost imperceptibly toward slightly older Campanian-age rock — same Cretaceous sea, slightly earlier chapter, a million or two years deeper in geologic time. You won't see it. The glacier's till is too thick, the farms too continuous. But ahead, somewhere in the next two to three hours, the terrain begins to gather itself for what's coming: the Missouri River country, the Badlands, the first hint that the buried West is starting to push upward through the skin of the plains. We're not there yet. Right now, the wheat fields run to every horizon, the sky is enormous, and the train is threading the long flat logic of the Northern Plains at its most characteristic. Hold that image. It won't last.

Nine people. That's the 2020 census count for Churchs Ferry — a community that once had enough going on to warrant a name, a post office, a place on the railroad map. It sits out there near Devils Lake, which isn't a fixed thing. That lake has been rising for decades, swallowing fields, roads, structures. Churchs Ferry was platted in 1886, same year Rugby was founded down the line — the railroad arriving and towns popping up like seeds after rain. Some held. Churchs Ferry did not, quite. The lake reclaimed its margin. Nine people, and the water still encroaching.

The Great Northern line we've been riding since long before the Minnesota border was James J. Hill's great obsession — built without a land grant, which made it singular among the transcontinentals. Hill called his strategy "scientific railroad building": pick the lowest grades, follow the rivers and the divides, find the wheat country and bind it to the market. Out here in Ramsey and Benson counties we're seeing the result. Every handful of miles along this line, a town name appears — York at mile 860, Knox at 865 — places that exist because the track arrived in 1887 and the railroad's survey crew decided: here is where the grain elevator goes, here is where the farmers come to ship. Not every town survived, but the ones that did are arranged with the regularity of railroad arithmetic. Ten miles between stops, give or take, which is how far a farmer could drive a team of horses to the depot and back in a day.

Seventeen people in York. The post office is likely gone; the grain elevator may still stand, or it may not. Towns like York reached their population peaks somewhere around 1910 or 1920, when the homestead rush was still spilling families across the quarter-sections and the price of wheat made the northern plains feel like a promised land. Then came the 1930s — drought and Depression arriving together — and the numbers began their long slow decline. What remains often isn't abandonment so much as consolidation: the farmers are still farming, the fields still producing, but the children drove to Rugby or Minot to work and stayed there.

We're in Benson County now — one of the poorer counties on this run, with poverty rates near 27 percent, one of the highest we've crossed. That number is partly a reflection of the Fort Totten Indian Reservation to our south, where Spirit Lake Nation holds land that was drastically reduced under the Dawes Act of 1887 — passed the very same year these railroad towns were platted along this line. The Dawes Act broke up communally held tribal lands into individual allotments, with "surplus" acreage sold off to settlers. The timing is not coincidence. The railroad opened the country; federal land policy followed immediately behind, reshaping who held what and on what terms. The landscape out the window — that orderly grid of fields — carries that history in its property lines.

Knox, founded 1887. Twenty-two people now. It has the same origin story as York, the same trajectory. What's worth noting is how the Great Northern strung these places — not at random, but by calculation, every station a potential market, every market a freight customer. Hill's genius was understanding that a railroad without traffic is a railroad going bankrupt, and traffic meant settlers, and settlers meant towns, and towns meant grain. He actively recruited Scandinavian and German immigrants, sent agents to Europe, printed pamphlets in Norwegian. The people who built Knox and York and Rugby came largely from those recruitment campaigns. Their descendants are still here, farming the same general ground, in farms now several times larger than the original homestead quarter-sections.

The bedrock under us is Late Cretaceous — shale and siltstone and sandstone laid down between 100 and 66 million years ago at the margins of the Western Interior Seaway, that shallow inland sea that split North America in two for tens of millions of years. We're not seeing that rock; it's buried under glacial till, the debris the ice sheets dumped here as they melted roughly 10,000 years ago. The till is what makes this farmland so relentlessly flat and so relentlessly fertile — ground-up continental rock, fine and mineral-rich, spread in a thick blanket across the old seabed. The glacier was the last great sculptor here. Before it, this was the sea floor. Before the sea, older mountains that erosion reduced to nothing. That layering — old seabed, glacial overprint, modern cropland — is what we're crossing. The flatness is not emptiness; it's deep time made horizontal.

Rugby claims the geographic center of North America — there's a monument in town marking the calculated point, though geographers argue the exact location depending on how you define the continent's boundary. What's unambiguous is the station. The Great Northern Passenger Depot here was built in 1907, the same year as the McHenry County Courthouse coming up down the line — that was a building year on the northern plains, a moment of institutional confidence when it seemed these towns would keep growing. The Rugby depot was restored in 1987 by a local Lions Club and other community groups; it's on the National Register. We pull in on the left side. Two thousand five hundred people — the largest town we've seen since we left Devils Lake behind. The county seat of Pierce County, which is 100 percent cropland by the land-cover data. Not a scrap of it isn't farmed.

The depot itself — brick, 1907, Great Northern style — is worth a look while we're stopped. Hill's railroad built depots to signal permanence, to reassure settlers that the line wasn't going anywhere, that their investment in land and labor would have a market connection for generations. Most of those depots are gone now, demolished or collapsed. Rugby's survived because someone cared enough in 1987 to restore it. That year of restoration is interesting: 1987 was a hard moment in the farm economy — the agricultural debt crisis of the 1980s was still grinding, land values had cratered, farms were failing. Choosing that particular year to invest in the old depot was a statement about staying.

We're pushing into Pierce County, which grades into McHenry County near mile 900 — and something is about to shift. McHenry County's land cover is 60 percent grassland and 20 percent water, a sudden change from the near-total cropland we've been crossing. That shift is a hint of the divide ahead. Around mile 970, we'll cross from the Souris-Red-Rainy watershed — water draining northeast toward Hudson Bay — into the Missouri watershed, water draining south and east toward the Gulf of Mexico. That's a continental divide, though out here on the plains it doesn't announce itself with a ridge or a peak. It's just a subtle rise, a slight tipping of the land. We're climbing toward it now, roughly 700 feet of elevation gain spread across the next 150 miles, almost imperceptible to the body, visible in the way the land begins to open and the sky seems to expand. The grassland coming into McHenry County is an early sign. The cropland doesn't hold everywhere; the soil thins, the moisture decreases slightly, and the grass comes back.

Coming into Towner — the McHenry County seat — watch ahead for the courthouse, built 1907, Beaux-Arts design by the firm Buechner and Orth, who built a remarkable number of North Dakota courthouses in that same flush decade. Listed on the National Register in 1980. The Beaux-Arts style — formal, symmetrical, classical detail — was a deliberate choice for territorial and early-statehood courthouses across the West. It said: this is not temporary. This is civilization arrived. North Dakota became a state in 1889, eighteen years before this courthouse went up. By 1907 the state was trying to look settled, permanent, institutional — and these courthouses were part of that argument. Towner's population today is under a thousand. The courthouse is still there, still the county seat, still making that argument.

The ground here is reading fine to us — flat, pale, enormous sky — but the rock beneath our wheels tells a stranger story. We're rolling over Late Cretaceous sediment laid down between 100 and 66 million years ago, when a shallow inland sea called the Western Interior Seaway split North America clean in two. Siltstone, shale, fine sandstone — the floor of that vanished ocean, pressed into stone. The glaciers came much later and smeared everything level. What looks like simple farmland is, in geological terms, the bottom of a sea.

The line we're on was James J. Hill's Great Northern Railway — completed to Seattle in 1893, the same year a financial panic shuttered hundreds of American banks. Hill drove his railroad through without a single acre of federal land grant, which made him unusual and proud of it. He believed the line would only survive if the land alongside it filled with productive farms. So he imported seed wheat from eastern Europe, published pamphlets in Norwegian and German, and actively recruited settlers. The towns strung along this route — the ones still on the map and the ones that aren't — are the direct result of that campaign. The railroad made them. It also decided which ones it would keep serving and which it wouldn't.

Denbigh is ahead of us and already nearly invisible — an unincorporated scattering in McHenry County with no incorporated government and no census count worth reporting. It had its moment. Most of the communities along this stretch did. The Great Northern platted them, named them, and sold adjacent lots to homesteaders convinced the rain would follow the plow. It didn't, not reliably. Denbigh persists as a name on maps and not much else. We pass it without ceremony.

The geology is shifting under us, though you'd never see it from the window. Around mile 920 the bedrock transitions into what geologists call Campanian rock — a specific slice of the Late Cretaceous, roughly 91 to 67 million years old. The Campanian stage is when the Western Interior Seaway was at something close to its maximum extent, a body of water stretching from the Gulf of Mexico to what is now the Arctic Ocean. The chalk, sand, and marine mud compressing into stone beneath this prairie were being deposited while Tyrannosaurus rex was still a few million years in the future. What we're crossing isn't just old farmland. It's the floor of a vanished continent-splitting sea, and the rock is getting, if anything, slightly younger as we move west — we're climbing gently toward the higher, later-buried layers.

Granville was founded in 1900 — right at the hinge of the railroad land-grant plat era, when the Great Northern was filling in its branch and spur network across the Dakotas. Population today is about 240 people. It's a genuine town, with a street grid and a grain elevator visible from the tracks, which is the mark of survival out here: if the elevator stayed, the town stayed. If the elevator closed, the town followed it into silence, usually within a generation. Granville's elevator is still standing.

McHenry County has roughly 5,300 people spread across an area larger than Rhode Island. Sixty percent of the land is grassland. The crops that do grow here — hay, wheat, soybeans — are the crops of thin-soil, short-season country. This was never prime agricultural land by Midwest standards; it's the edge of what dryland farming can reliably do. The homesteaders who arrived after 1900 often found that out the hard way, in the drought years of the 1910s and again, catastrophically, in the 1930s. Many left. Some stayed. The ones who stayed often consolidated — bought out the abandoned quarter-sections around them — which is why you see so few farmsteads now and such large fields.

Norwich is another unincorporated community, founded around 1901, the same year the Spindletop gusher in Texas announced the petroleum age. Norwich knew nothing about oil. It was wheat country, dry-goods country, country measured in bushels per acre and miles to the nearest rail siding. It peaked early and declined slowly — the 1996 date in its record likely marks some administrative reorganization rather than any new prosperity. The name itself is borrowed from Norwich, England, as settlers on the northern plains frequently named their towns for the places their parents or grandparents had left behind. A piece of East Anglia, transplanted to McHenry County, ND, and now almost gone.

We've been traveling through the Souris-Red-Rainy watershed since we entered North Dakota — water here flows north and east, eventually reaching Hudson Bay. That is genuinely strange, geographically speaking: the rain that falls on these fields drains into Canada, not the Gulf of Mexico. The continental divide between the Hudson Bay basin and the Missouri basin lies ahead of us, around mile 970. It's not a ridge; there's no dramatic moment. It's a nearly imperceptible rise in the plain — the kind of divide that fooled early explorers who expected a mountain. But cross it and every drop of water is heading a different direction, toward a different ocean shore.

Surrey is a populated place in Ward County — we're just crossing the county line. Ward County holds nearly 70,000 people, most of them in Minot, and the contrast with McHenry County to the east is sharp. This is what a regional city does: it draws population in, keeps the surrounding county alive with services and employment, while the counties without a Minot quietly empty. The Great Northern chose Minot as a division point early, and that single decision — where to put the locomotive shops, where to concentrate the crew changes — compounded over 130 years into the difference between a county of 5,000 and one of 70,000.

Beneath us now, the bedrock has shifted again — from Campanian marine sediment into Paleocene rock, dated roughly 66 to 56 million years ago. The Paleocene is the first geological period after the mass extinction that ended the dinosaurs. The boundary between Cretaceous and Paleocene — called the K-Pg boundary — is one of the sharpest transitions in the entire rock record: below it, dinosaurs; above it, none. The sediment being laid down in the Paleocene here was not marine. The seaway had withdrawn. Rivers and floodplains replaced the inland ocean, and the first modern mammals were beginning to diversify in the world those rivers crossed. The prairie above that rock is young and glacially reworked; the story in the stone below is the first chapter of our own biological lineage's eventual dominance.

Minot coming up — we'll stop here. It's the fourth-largest city in North Dakota, built on the Great Northern's decision in the early 1890s to make this a division point for locomotive servicing. The shops, the roundhouse, the crew quarters — that infrastructure drew workers, workers drew merchants, merchants drew families. The city calls itself "Magic City" for the speed with which it materialized: it went from empty prairie to a town of several thousand in less than a year, 1886–87. That pace wasn't magic; it was the logic of the railroad town, where the company's decision to stop here was worth more than any natural resource. Minot survived because the Great Northern kept stopping. It still does.

While we're stopped in Minot, or just clearing the yards, notice how developed the land looks compared to the open grassland we've been crossing. Ward County is 43% cropland, 28% developed — a very different ratio from McHenry County's 60% grassland. Minot's presence reshapes the surrounding land use. Suburbs, service roads, ag support facilities ring the city. Then, almost immediately east and west, the plains resume their old sparseness. The city is an island of density in a sea of grass and sky, which is itself a kind of geography lesson: without the rail junction, without the institutions it attracted — the university, the air force base, the regional hospital — this particular island would not exist.

If you look to our left, you'll see a coulee cutting through the plain — Gassman Coulee, a valley carved by glacial meltwater drainage thousands of years ago. Coulees like this one are the signature landform of the glaciated northern plains: not river valleys in the usual sense, but meltwater channels, cut fast during deglaciation when the ice sheets were releasing enormous volumes of water and the drainage patterns were still being established. Some coulees carried rivers for a few centuries and then went dry when the drainage reorganized. Gassman Coulee is a reminder that the flat landscape around us is actually a geologically recent creation — the glaciers left only about 10,000 years ago, practically yesterday in the timescale we've been traveling through.

The Plains Indian Wars were still ongoing when the first homesteaders were filing claims in this part of Dakota Territory. The period from 1860 to 1890 — the span usually given to those conflicts — overlaps almost exactly with the period of railroad construction and the first waves of European-American settlement. The Great Northern's predecessor lines were surveying and grading through land that Indigenous peoples, principally the Lakota, Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara nations, had occupied for centuries. The railroad didn't just carry settlers; it was itself a tool of displacement, a physical assertion of a different land tenure. The towns we've been naming — Granville, Norwich, Des Lacs ahead — were platted in the aftermath of that displacement, on land cleared by policy and force. The cheerful boosterism of the Great Northern's settlement pamphlets existed alongside that history, and the landscape holds both.

Des Lacs — French for "River of the Lakes," named by French-Canadian fur traders who passed through long before the railroad arrived. Founded in 1888, which puts it in the earliest wave of Great Northern settlement on this stretch. By 1888 the Plains Indian Wars were winding down; the Dawes Act had passed the year before, opening reservation lands to homesteading. The town today has 185 people. It's remained small but present — one of the communities that found enough local purpose to persist while dozens of others along the same rail corridor have vanished into the grass. The name, at least, preserves the memory of the voyageurs who came through on foot and by canoe, before any of this was American territory at all.

We're now tracking northwest, and the elevation is beginning its long slow climb. We're at roughly 1,500 feet here; by the time we approach the Missouri watershed divide around mile 970, we'll have gained another hundred feet or so — imperceptible in the riding, but real. The Northwestern Glaciated Plains ecoregion begins just ahead, a slightly drier, slightly rougher landscape than the Lake Agassiz plain we've been crossing since Minnesota. The grass will shorten. The wheat fields will thin. We're moving toward country where the sky seems to take up more of the view, not because the land drops, but because the land empties — fewer trees, fewer shelterbelts, fewer farms. The iron road climbs with us, steady, northwest, toward the divide.

Something is quietly happening underfoot that you can't see from the window. Around milepost 970 we cross from the Souris-Red-Rainy watershed — drainage that eventually finds Hudson Bay — into the great Missouri Basin, water that will reach the Gulf of Mexico. The divide itself is nearly invisible here: no ridge, no dramatic pass, just a gentle roll in the glaciated plain and then, by some subtle logic of gradient, the rain that falls a step to one side flows north and east, and a step to the other flows south and west. The continent's plumbing splits without ceremony. James J. Hill, who built this line in the 1890s, understood divides differently — to him they were obstacles to be crossed as cheaply as possible. He graded his track to stay on the flattest corridor he could find, which is why we've been traveling at essentially the same elevation for two hours and will for another hundred miles yet.

A grain elevator flashes by — the tallest structure for miles, as it's been since around 1900 when Berthold was platted. Every town along this line began roughly the same way: the Great Northern surveyed a route, chose a watering or coaling point, and a cluster of hopeful settlers arrived within months of the first spike. Berthold held on. Four hundred and ninety people live here now, which counts as staying power on the northern plains.

We've also just crossed another kind of divide — ecological this time. The Northern Glaciated Plains biome we've been moving through since Minnesota gives way now to the Northwestern Glaciated Plains. The distinction is subtle but real: slightly drier, slightly shorter grass, the cropland beginning to share more space with native grassland. You can feel it in how the fields alternate — wheat and canola, then a stretch of pale buffalo grass, then wheat again. The Pleistocene glaciers retreated here too, but the soils are thinner, the frost comes earlier, and the farmers who broke this ground in the 1900s and 1910s were working at the outer edge of reliable rainfall. Some of them held on. Many left.

Tagus. Or what's left of it. This is the first genuine ghost town we've passed today, though not the last. Founded in 1900, incorporated in 1908 — a complete arc in under a decade. The Great Northern was the artery, and when the line's economics shifted and the cars got better and the roads came, the blood stopped moving through small stops like this. By 1940 Tagus was already fading; by 1976 it was officially a ghost. What you're looking at — or looking for — is the ghost town's essential lesson: the railway both made and erased these places. The Iron Spine gave life and could withdraw it.

Palermo. Population 125, down from a modest peak a century ago. Platted in 1902 — the same year the Reclamation Act passed, launching the federal government into the business of watering the arid West with dams and canals. Palermo didn't get a dam; it got the railroad and a grain elevator and a post office, and that was enough to keep it breathing, barely, into our own time.

The geology here is Paleocene — roughly 57 to 66 million years old — sedimentary rock laid down just after the extinction that ended the dinosaurs. Soft, relatively flat, easy for a glacier to plane and easy for a railroad to grade across. Paleontologists working these badland edges have pulled up Metasequoia occidentalis from this layer — a dawn redwood, a tree now native only to a single Chinese valley, but once growing right here along what were then subtropical river margins. And Averrhoites affinis, a leaf fossil from the same warm world. Fifty-seven million years ago, this exact stretch of ground was warm, wet, forested. It takes a moment to hold that beside the view out the window: pale grass, wheat stubble, the cold geometry of a Quonset hut.

The 1937 concrete deck girder bridge at Stanley — a modest piece of infrastructure, but it's on the National Register of Historic Places, which tells you something about how seriously this region takes its railroad heritage. Built in the depths of the Depression, when the federal government and private railroads were both spending to keep workers employed and rail lines functional. Stanley is our station stop; we'll pause here briefly. The county seat of Mountrail County, though the county's largest city is actually New Town, down by Lake Sakakawea to the south. Stanley sits astride the old Great Northern transcontinental route — a reminder that this line wasn't incidental to the northern plains, it was the reason most of these towns exist at all.

Mountrail County today runs about 9,600 people across a landscape that's nearly half grassland, half cropland. The median income here is above the national rural average — boosted in recent years by the Bakken oil formation that underlies much of northwestern North Dakota. That's an economic thread you'll hear more about as we move west into Williams County, where Williston became briefly the fastest-growing city in America during the fracking boom of the early 2010s. The Paleocene rocks we're riding over contain something besides fossil leaves.

Ross, North Dakota. Population 95. What makes this tiny town historically notable is the community of Lebanese and Syrian immigrants who homesteaded here beginning in 1902 — largely Muslim families who built what is documented as one of the earliest mosques in the United States, a small structure that stood until 1979. Syrian-Americans and Lebanese-Americans on the northern plains, a century ago, working dryland wheat in the wind. The homesteading era brought people here from everywhere: Scandinavians, Germans from Russia, Bohemians — and from the Levant. The plains absorbed them all and then slowly released most of them back, but Ross held a community long enough to leave a mark in the history of American Islam.

The grassland-cropland balance keeps shifting as we push west. This is the margin where the old open range — the unfenced sea of grass that once ran from Texas to Canada — met the homesteaders' wire. Barbed wire, patented in 1874, is what finally closed the range. Before it, cattle grazed freely on a commons; after it, the land was divided into private lots, and the cattlemen and the sodbusters fought over every quarter-section. By the time these Mountrail County towns were platted in 1900-1902, the outcome was already settled: the homesteader's wire had won. The great cattle drives to the railheads had ended a decade earlier, and what remained was grain country.

White Earth — one of the oldest communities in Mountrail County, founded in 1887, the same year the Dawes Act broke up tribal lands across the West into individual allotments, dispersing the collective holdings of many nations into private parcels that could be sold. The act transformed the northern plains permanently. White Earth sits near the White Earth River, a tributary of the Missouri, and its founding date places it squarely in the era when the railroad was threading west and federal policy was reshaping who held the land. A hundred people live here now. The river keeps its name.

Ahead of us, still well over the horizon, is the Missouri River crossing — and beyond it, the land begins its long, slow climb toward Montana. We've been traveling at roughly two thousand feet for hours, the plain nearly level, the sky enormous. The Missouri Basin we've entered will carry our drainage all the way to St. Louis and the Gulf. What changes as we push into Williams County isn't elevation — not yet — it's the economy below the soil. The Bakken shale is underneath us now, and Williston, our next significant stop, is where that underground story broke into the surface most dramatically. The iron road that made these towns a century ago now runs through country that briefly became a new kind of boomtown — the same arc, the same question of what remains when the boom exhausts itself.

Oil changed Tioga. The town platted in 1902 — the same year Congress passed the Reclamation Act, opening the arid West to federal irrigation — but it was drilling that remade it. In 1951, the Clarence Iverson No. 1 well came in, and Williston Basin oil turned this quiet wheat depot into something faster, louder, and richer than anyone in 1902 imagined. What you're seeing ahead is still a working place, population just over two thousand — a modest number for a town sitting atop one of the most productive oil formations in North America. The Great Northern rails brought it. The rock below sustained it.

We're riding the high ground of western North Dakota, approaching a subtle summit near mile 1040 — just over 2,370 feet. Nothing dramatic to the eye, but the water beneath us tells the story. Every drop of rain that falls here drains eventually into the Missouri, which drains into the Mississippi, which drains into the Gulf of Mexico. We're inside the Missouri watershed now and have been since we left the Dakotas' glaciated heart. The ground is Paleocene, laid down in the first ten million years after the dinosaurs vanished — yellowish siltstones and claystones, sediment from rivers and shallow lakes that spread across a warming, flattening continent. That rock is old and quiet. What happened on top of it is not.

Temple is a ghost town. Founded 1906, dead within decades. What's left: a small garage, a couple of outbuildings, a caved-in house or two. In 2003 one of the last two business buildings burned or was demolished — by 2010 the census counted almost no one. This is the pattern out here on the northern plains. The Great Northern laid track, surveyors platted a town every seven or eight miles — the distance a farmer could haul grain to an elevator and return by dark with a horse team — and those intervals became places with names and post offices and aspirations. When the automobile stretched that distance, every other town died. Temple is not unusual. It is the rule.

The railroad made these towns, and the railroad unmade them. James J. Hill's Great Northern — "the Empire Builder," which is what this train is named for — pushed across the northern tier in the early 1890s, one of the last transcontinental lines built without a federal land grant. Hill believed in dense settlement: small farms, short hauls, revenue from volume. So towns came every few miles, each one a bet that the land would fill with families. Some bets paid. Most didn't. When yields thinned and automobiles arrived, the distance between viable places stretched, and the in-between places emptied. What the railroad strung together, mobility quietly unstrung.

Ray arrived the same year as Tioga — 1902 — platted along the Great Northern and still holding on at 740 people. A working farm town: wheat and canola move through here, same as they always did. Williams County raises wheat on nearly half its land, and the rest is grass. The proportion tells you something about the climate — enough rain for grain, but not reliably enough for more. Canola means shorter summers are tolerable; it matures faster than wheat and handles the cold. Ray is what persistence looks like in a place where the economics never became spectacular.

The fossils in the rock under our wheels deserve a moment. Near this stretch, paleontologists have pulled out Titanoides primaevus — a large, clawed, early mammal from roughly 61 million years ago — and Metasequoia occidentalis, the dawn redwood, from about 57 million years ago. The dawn redwood is a tree that still exists; you can plant one in a garden today. But 57 million years ago it grew in forests across North Dakota because this latitude was warmer, wetter, more like what we'd now call the American Southeast. The Paleocene was the age when mammals filled every niche the dinosaurs had vacated. Titanoides was one of the earliest experiments in large mammal body plans — not quite a carnivore, not quite an herbivore, browsing and digging in those warm forests. Nothing about the short-grass country outside suggests the swampy subtropics buried beneath it.

We're near the high point of this segment now — the land crests just above 2,370 feet and will not rise again on this leg. From here, very slowly, the terrain tilts west and north toward the Yellowstone, toward the Missouri's main stem, toward the river Lewis and Clark followed upstream in 1804. Wheelock is barely a named place today. But the elevation matters: everything from here runs toward Montana.

Lewis and Clark mapped the Missouri in 1804 and 1805, passing through this country with thirty-three people in a keelboat and two pirogues — moving upstream against a current that averaged four miles an hour. The Mandan villages they wintered near were the last reliable fixed point before the unknown. What they documented along the northern Missouri corridor — the cut banks, the cottonwood groves, the tributaries — became the first American survey of country that would remain beyond the reach of permanent settlement for another seventy years. The Great Northern tracks we're riding follow the same logic the Missouri taught: the gentlest crossing of the continent, staying north of the worst terrain, threading the passes the river found first. Water wrote the route. The railroad traced the signature.

Avoca is a populated place — which is the census category's polite way of saying it is not quite a town. A name on a map, a cluster of buildings, a place that once warranted a post office or a grain elevator. Williams County has several of these: the skeleton of a settlement system built for a denser population than ever arrived, or that arrived and then left when the oil boom moved on or the farm economics shifted. We pass through without stopping. The train has never stopped here.

The bedrock changes just ahead. At mile 1060 we enter the Bullion Creek Formation — Paleocene claystone, siltstone, sandstone, and lignite, laid down in rivers, lakes, and swamps between about 58 and 57 million years ago. Lignite is the softest coal, barely more than compressed peat, still brown, still showing wood grain sometimes. It formed in those Paleocene swamp forests — the same world that preserved Metasequoia and Titanoides. And lignite is why several of the ghost towns in this county existed at all. Small strip mines opened in the late 1800s and early 1900s, pulling fuel out of the Bullion Creek beds to heat homes and run early power plants. The geology wrote a resource, the resource wrote a settlement, and when cheaper coal and then oil arrived, the settlement was erased. The Bullion Creek Formation is still there. The towns are not.

Williston is our station stop — the largest city in Williams County, the county seat, and a place that has been remade more than once. Founded as a Great Northern depot in the 1880s, it grew steadily on wheat and cattle. Then the Williston Basin oil boom of the 1950s expanded it. Then the Bakken shale revolution after 2008 nearly doubled its population in a decade — roughnecks, man camps, traffic, housing shortages. The boom faded after 2015 when oil prices collapsed, and Williston is settling again into something more stable. That oscillation — railroad town, oil boomtown, contraction, recovery — is the compressed history of the American extractive West in one city of roughly 27,000 people. If you step off here, the wide Missouri is a few miles south.

Just south of Williston, the Missouri makes one of its great bends. The river we've been traveling parallel to — felt more than seen, its drainage shaping the land's grade — is about to become something we'll cross directly as we continue west. The Missouri at Williston is wide and brown and serious. Lewis and Clark noted the Yellowstone joining it a few miles upstream, and that confluence is still one of the most historically loaded spots on the northern plains: two great rivers meeting, the whole drainage of the northern Rockies pouring into the system that will eventually reach St. Louis, then the Gulf. We are in the Missouri watershed, and we have been for hours. But crossing into Montana in a few miles, we begin the slow tilt toward a different drainage — the land that eventually sends its water down the Yellowstone and into the Missouri from the west, rather than from the north and east. The divides are subtle here. The consequences are not.

Trenton sits along North Dakota Highway 1804 — the number is not accidental. The highway follows the route Lewis and Clark traveled upstream, and the date 1804 names the year they passed through. Trenton is an unincorporated community, a CDP, the kind of place that exists at the margin between town and not-town. The connection to 1804 is worth sitting with: this road through an unincorporated community on the high plains carries the number of one of the most consequential journeys in American history. The expedition mapped this country for an American government that had just bought it from France without asking the people already living here. Those people — the Mandan, the Hidatsa, the Assiniboine — had been on this river for centuries. The highway number honors the cartographers. The land remembers longer.

We are approaching the Montana border — roughly mile 1092 — and as we do, the ecoregion is quietly changing beneath us. We're still in the Northwestern Glaciated Plains, the dark-brown prairie of glaciated topography, but ahead lies the Northwestern Great Plains: a different country, less marked by ice, more exposed in its bedrock and coulees, dryer and rawer at the edges. The grass will shorten. The sky will widen. The Bakken oil fields and the wheat fields of Williams County will give way to country that feels less settled, less worked-over, closer to whatever this land was before anyone put a fence on it. The Bullion Creek lignite swamps of 60 million years ago are behind us in the bedrock. Ahead, the rock grows older. The land grows younger in its wildness.

Ahead of us sits Buford — or what's left of it. A name on a map, an unincorporated community, a handful of rooftops lost in the grass. But a mile and a half south of those rooftops stood Fort Union, the greatest fur-trade post on the upper Missouri, where Assiniboine and Crow and Blackfoot traders brought packs of beaver pelts for decades. John James Audubon stopped here in 1843, sketching birds and watching a world he already sensed was vanishing. By 1867 the Army dismantled the fort to build Fort Buford nearby. Erasure built on erasure. The trading post is a national historic site now — preserved, quiet, visited mostly by people passing through on their way somewhere else. Like us.

We're riding the last miles of North Dakota, and the Missouri River is not far to our south — we've been in its watershed for hundreds of miles, since long before the land flattened out and the oil derricks appeared. But ahead, past the state line, that changes. The Missouri bends north and then east through Montana, and we'll cross it. Everything we've seen draining into it — every coulee, every creek-cut badland — all of it eventually reaches the Gulf of Mexico. When we cross into Montana and then over that river, the calculus of water shifts slightly but doesn't break yet; we're still in the Missouri basin, still bound for the Gulf. The true divide comes later, out west, when we climb into the mountains. For now, the watershed is enormous, quiet, invisible — the shape underneath everything.

The Paleocene rock under our wheels is roughly 60 million years old, laid down in river floodplains and shallow lakes just after the dinosaurs vanished. We've been riding over it for the last hour. Inland sea gone, the land rising, the first mammals exploring an emptied continent. You won't see the rock dramatically — it's buried under glacial till and topsoil — but it's there, the floor of everything.

No fanfare out the window — just a fence line, a slight color change in the pasture grass, and we've crossed into Montana. Roosevelt County now. Named for Theodore Roosevelt, who died in January 1919, the same year the Montana Legislature carved this county out of the eastern grasslands. Roosevelt had ranched not far south of here in the Dakota Badlands in the 1880s, a young man who came west to outrun grief after losing his wife and mother on the same day. The land made him a conservationist. The county named for him has a poverty rate over 31 percent — four times what we left behind in Williams County, North Dakota. The iron road connects these places, but it doesn't equalize them.

The land cover shifts as we move west — less of the tilled cropland geometry, more grassland opening up. We're entering the Northwestern Glaciated Plains, the biome ticking over as the last glaciers' outwash gave way to something rougher at the margins. The grass here is short, the sky enormous. Wheat still grows, and hay, and some lentils farther west, but the fields have a more provisional quality now — as if the land is reminding farmers who is actually in charge.

The bedrock is still Paleocene under us, that same 60-million-year-old sedimentary floor. But a few miles ahead, Late Cretaceous rock begins to surface — older by tens of millions of years, siltstone and shale laid in the Western Interior Seaway when this continent was bisected by a warm shallow sea. Time runs backward in the exposed West: the deeper you look, the older the stone.

To the right, Bainville — 271 people, a water tower, the grain elevator that marks every Great Northern Railway town along this line. Named for Charles Bain, the town's first postmaster, a man now almost entirely erased from memory except for this name on a sign. The town celebrated its centennial on July 4th, 2006, a hundred years of surviving on the northern high plains. The railroad made it; without the Great Northern, there's no reason for Bainville to exist at this particular longitude. That's true of almost every settlement we'll pass between here and the mountains. James J. Hill chose the routes; the towns grew where the tracks allowed.

Coming up ahead, on the National Register of Historic Places: Hale's Filling Station and Grocery. A gas station and a store, built probably around 1928 — the tail end of a decade when automobile travel was transforming the American plains, when US highways were being numbered and paved, when a filling station on a prairie road was genuinely essential infrastructure. Eighty years later, the federal government deemed it worth preserving. It's a small, strange monument — not a fort, not a church, not a courthouse, just the place where people stopped to fill their tank and buy bread on the way somewhere. The ordinary made historic by its rarity. Most of its cousins are gone.

Here's the arithmetic of this county. Roosevelt County, Montana: population 10,799. Of those, a significant share are members of the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, whose reservation covers much of the land south and west of us. The poverty rate is 31.5 percent — and on the reservation itself it runs higher. The Assiniboine had been on this land long before Lewis and Clark passed through in 1805, trading at Fort Union, wintering along the Missouri breaks. Then came the Dawes Act of 1887 — the same year Culbertson, just ahead, was platted. The act broke up tribal communal land into individual allotments, with the "surplus" sold to white settlers. The town and the dispossession arrived in the same year. The railroad came, the town was founded, and the land that had sustained a people for generations was legally redistributed. That's the chain: policy to plat to town to county seat.

Culbertson, platted in 1887 — the year the Dawes Act passed, the year the Interstate Commerce Act put railroads under federal oversight for the first time. The Great Northern's predecessor lines were driving west through the northern tier, and every survey crew that staked a townsite was setting a pin in the map that would determine who lived where for the next century. Culbertson has 753 people now, a county road junction, the Missouri River a few miles south. It's survived drought and depression and the slow outmigration that hollowed out dozens of similar towns farther east. Still here.

South of our line, maybe ten miles, the Missouri bends in great slow loops through the Montana breaks — the same river we traced from its confluence with the Yellowstone, the same river that Lewis and Clark poled their keelboats up in 1804, struggling against the current at two miles a day. We'll cross it soon. When we do, we're still in the Missouri's basin, still technically bound for the Gulf of Mexico via St. Louis and the Mississippi. But we're getting to the upper end of that enormous plumbing system. The headwaters are out west, in the mountains we'll reach tonight or tomorrow morning. The Missouri drains a sixth of the United States. Right now, on our left, it's just a line of cottonwoods marking where the bluffs drop away.

The bedrock has shifted under us — Late Cretaceous now, the siltstone and shale of that ancient seabed, surfacing where the glaciers scraped and the rivers cut. Older rock, exposed. The West doesn't bury its past the way the Midwest does.

Brockton — 358 people, a census-designated place on the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes' land. The town sits inside the reservation boundaries, a crossroads community that grew around a Great Northern siding. Two worlds at the same junction: the reservation economy, shaped by treaty rights and federal policy and a history of dispossession that dates to the 1880s; and the railroad-town grid, shaped by James J. Hill's surveyors and the homestead rush that followed the tracks. They've coexisted here for well over a century. Coexistence is not the same as resolution.

We're approaching milepost 1140, and the geology is quietly turning under us — deeper into that Late Cretaceous siltstone and shale, the remnant floor of the Western Interior Seaway. A hundred million years ago, warm salt water covered this ground. Marine reptiles swam overhead. The chalk and the shale that seaway left behind run in a band across the northern plains, and the rivers and glaciers have been cutting into it ever since, exposing layer after layer. Ahead, the Missouri breaks get rougher. The land becomes less forgiving. We're still on the high plains, still riding the same elevation we've held for hours, but the texture of the country is changing — more exposed rock, more coulees, more of the raw bone of the continent showing through. The mountains are still hours away, but the land is beginning to remember they exist.

The ground out both windows is the color of old rope — dried grass over pale clay, stubble from last year's wheat still combing the surface. We're riding through the upper skin of the Western Interior Seaway floor: siltstone, shale, sandstone laid down when this whole basin sat beneath warm shallow water, a hundred million years ago. The Cretaceous is very close to the surface here. Not exposed, exactly, but just under us — a foot or two of topsoil, then the sea's sediment all the way down.

We're still in the Missouri watershed — every drop of rain that falls on this prairie eventually drains east and south, into the Missouri, and eventually into the Gulf of Mexico. That'll change, later today, when we cross the Continental Divide and everything tilts toward the Pacific. But for now the land flows toward St. Louis and the sea. The Missouri's pull is invisible from here — we can't see the river — but the gentle eastward cant of the terrain is there if you watch the drainage patterns, the shallow draws running off to our right. This is how North America tells time: not with clocks but with which way the water runs.

Ahead is Poplar — a small city, fewer than a thousand people, sitting at the edge of the Fort Peck Indian Reservation. It's the tribal headquarters for the Assiniboine and Sioux nations who have lived on this stretch of the Missouri country for generations, and it carries a name that is straightforwardly descriptive: the cottonwoods and poplars along the bottomlands. The reservation spans more than two million acres across northeastern Montana. Two million acres is hard to hold in the mind — roughly the size of Connecticut plus Rhode Island. And yet it represents what remained after a century of treaty reductions. Fort Peck was established in 1871. The Assiniboine had been here far longer.

The Fort Peck Reservation anchors a story that runs the length of this leg and far beyond it — one of the recurring threads of the Iron Spine itself. Every town the Great Northern strung across this country in the 1890s was platted on land that had been Indigenous territory within living memory.

James J. Hill's Great Northern Railway reached this corridor in 1887, pushing west from Minnesota toward Puget Sound. It was the last of the great northern transcontinentals to be built, and Hill built it without a federal land grant — unusual for the era. He chose his route partly by following the Missouri drainage, partly by hunting for the lowest, most direct passes through the Rockies. The line's logic was commercial and hydraulic both.

When the Great Northern came through, it didn't just carry passengers. It carried settlers, offered cut-rate immigrant fares, distributed seed wheat, and literally printed pamphlets advertising the "Great Northern Country" as an agricultural paradise. The pamphlets lied, or at least overstated. Annual rainfall here is around thirteen inches — barely enough for dryland wheat farming in good years, not enough in bad ones. The settlers came anyway. Some stayed. Many left. The reservation communities — Assiniboine and Sioux both — persisted through all of it, through the homestead boom and the dust years and the agricultural consolidation that emptied the surrounding townships. Poplar is still here. A lot of the homestead towns aren't.

Off to the left, three miles east of Wolf Point, you might catch a glimpse of a small airstrip — L. M. Clayton Airport, which has the distinction of being the smallest commercial airport in the contiguous United States. One airline, subsidized under the federal Essential Air Service program, which exists to connect remote communities that markets alone would abandon. It's the twenty-first century version of a very old problem: how do you link a thin-population, wide-geography country? The Great Northern solved it with steel. Essential Air Service solves it with subsidized turboprops. Different era, same question.

Wolf Point. We'll stop here. The station opened in 1893 — the Panic year, when railroads across the country were failing and the economy was in free fall, yet the Great Northern was still building west. Wolf Point became the county seat of Roosevelt County when the county was carved out in 1919, the year Theodore Roosevelt died. Named for the president, for the man who made Yellowstone and the national forest system, whose cattle ranching days in the Badaknds to the east left him with a permanent attachment to this particular stretch of northern plains.

The town itself sits on the Missouri — which we'll cross nearby. The river has been with us for a while now, invisible but present, running roughly parallel before curving south. Wolf Point grew up as a river crossing and a railroad division point. Those two facts explain almost everything about it.

Around mile 1150, something changed underfoot that you wouldn't know from looking at the grass. We rode off the Late Cretaceous bedrock — that ancient seafloor shale and siltstone — and onto alluvium: the river deposits, the gravel and sand and silt that the Missouri and its ancestors have been laying down for the last 1.8 million years. Alluvium is geologically young. It's not rock yet; it's sediment in the process of becoming rock, if you have a few million more years to wait. River gravel, floodplain silt, old channel fills. This is the geology of yesterday, if yesterday means the ice ages and the meltwater rivers that reworked everything in their path.

The Missouri has been a powerful reworker. During the Pleistocene glaciations — the last great ice advances, the most recent ending roughly twelve thousand years ago — the drainage here was profoundly reorganized. Ice sheets pushed river channels southward. Meltwater floods carved coulees into the landscape. The ground we're riding through near Wolf Point is partly that ice-age flood deposit, river gravels laid down when the Missouri was running many times larger than it does today.

Oswego — another small community, unincorporated, on the Fort Peck Reservation, sitting on Route 2 between Wolf Point and Frazer. The name is borrowed from Oswego, New York, on Lake Ontario — the habit of transplanting eastern place-names westward was so ingrained in American settlement that Montana ends up with a New York town name on a Sioux and Assiniboine reservation. The community endures here in the way small reservation communities endure: quietly, largely invisible to the train windows, present in the landscape if not in the tourist literature.

We're still moving through the Missouri's basin, but we're approaching the western edge of Roosevelt County and the beginning of Valley County — a landscape where wetlands make up more than a third of the land cover. That's unusual for eastern Montana. It's partly a result of the Missouri's floodplain topography and partly the legacy of glaciation, which left behind depressions that filled with water and never fully drained. The prairie potholes of the northern Great Plains — critical breeding habitat for North American waterfowl — are a glacial inheritance. The ponds and sloughs we'll pass are old ice holes. Without the Pleistocene ice sheets, none of this would be wetland. It would be dry rolling grass all the way to the horizon.

Frazer — another small community, part of the Fort Peck Reservation, just across the Roosevelt-Valley county line. These small settlements — Poplar, Oswego, Frazer — occur at intervals along Route 2, each one a reservation community with a post office and a school and a gas station, each one outside the frame of the highway-map version of Montana that tourists carry. The reservation is not a relic or a museum. It's a working landscape of more than two million acres, with farms and ranches and government jobs and schools, carrying forward the Assiniboine and Sioux presence through everything the last century threw at it.

We've ridden back onto Cretaceous bedrock here — the alluvium gave way as the river's floodplain narrowed, and underneath us again is that old seabed: shale and siltstone, ninety million years old, the remnant of the Western Interior Seaway. These rocks are not dramatic from the surface — they're covered with grass and thin soil — but if you know they're there, the landscape reads differently. The mild swells and shallow draws are the weathering signature of soft marine sediment, rock that's been dissolving for sixty-six million years since the seaway drained and the dinosaurs ended.

About those dinosaurs: the fossil record of this specific bedrock is remarkable. Edmontosaurus — the great duck-billed hadrosaur, one of the most common large herbivores at the very end of the Cretaceous — roamed ground we're riding through. Tyrannosaurus rex hunted here. Meniscoessus, a small early mammal, scurried under the feet of both of them. These are not abstract evolutionary facts. The bones are in this rock. Ranchers and amateur collectors have been finding them in the eroded coulee walls for a hundred years. Somewhere off to our left or right, there's almost certainly a hadrosaur vertebra half-exposed in a wash.

Out the right window — Milk River Coulee, a broad valley cut by the Milk River, which drains into the Missouri not far from here. The Milk is one of those rivers that sounds minor until you look at a map: it rises in Montana, crosses into Canada, runs through Alberta, returns to the United States, and joins the Missouri near Fort Peck. It's international, binational, its watershed straddling the 49th parallel. The Milk runs through the northeastern corner of Montana's hi-line country, its name coming from the pale silty look of its water. Lewis and Clark noted it in 1805 — Clark called it "the river that scolds at all others." The coulees carved by rivers like the Milk are the terrain here, the main topographic feature: broad, flat-floored valleys with steep eroded walls, cut into the Cretaceous shale by thousands of years of runoff.

The grass out both windows right now is shorter than it looks. Shortgrass prairie — blue grama and needlegrass — cropped by drought as much as by grazing. Beneath it, the bedrock is Late Cretaceous siltstone and shale, laid down when a shallow inland sea covered this whole region a hundred million years ago. That sea is gone, but its floor is what we're riding across. The land feels open and empty. It is. Valley County runs to the Canadian border and holds fewer than eight thousand people.

We're in the Missouri watershed now — everything that drains from these slopes eventually finds the Missouri, then the Mississippi, then the Gulf. We crossed into that drainage hours ago, and we'll ride it a long way yet. The Milk River, just north of us, threads along the Canadian border before looping back to join the Missouri near Fort Peck. It's a river that can't quite decide which country it belongs to.

Nashua ahead — three hundred people, a grain elevator, a bar, a school. It sits at the confluence of the Milk River and the Missouri, which made it a logical stop when the Great Northern came through in the early 1890s. The railroad strung these towns like beads — each one a water stop, a grain platform, a post office. Some grew. Nashua held on. Others down the line didn't get that far.

James J. Hill built the Great Northern across this stretch in 1887, the same year the Dawes Act broke up tribal lands into individual allotments — converting communal territory into parcels that could be sold, homesteaded, lost to debt. The two forces moved together: the railroad offering access, the allotment system releasing land. The towns that appeared along this line in the 1890s were platted onto ground that had been Assiniboine territory within living memory. Hill never received a federal land grant — he was proud of that — but he benefited from the clearing that federal policy had done ahead of him.

The geology shifts here — we've crossed from the old Cretaceous bedrock onto Pleistocene and recent alluvium, the river's own deposit. Gravel, sand, silt, clay. Geologically speaking, it's yesterday. The Milk River built this flat ground by dropping its load every time the current slowed. We're riding across the river's own autobiography, written in sediment.

The Assiniboine people — they call themselves Nakoda — have been in this country for centuries, long before the railroad, long before the survey lines. Fort Peck Reservation sits just south of us, established in 1888, a year after the Dawes Act and the same year the Great Northern survey crews were running their transit lines across the same ground. The reservation boundary and the rail corridor are roughly parallel. That's not coincidence — both lines were drawn in the same decade, by the same federal policy ambition, which was to settle and organize the northern plains into something legible and taxable. The Nakoda are still here. The surveyors' republic has changed shape several times since.

Glasgow on the right — the county seat, thirty-two hundred people, the biggest town for a long stretch in any direction. It was founded in 1887, the year the Great Northern reached this point, and named — according to local tradition — by a railroad official who simply drew a city name out of a hat. Glasgow, Scotland, won. The town grew up around the depot: grain elevators, stockyards, a federal courthouse. Fort Peck Dam, thirty miles south, brought a second wave in the 1930s — ten thousand construction workers flooded the county during the Depression, when there was almost no work anywhere else in America. Glasgow absorbed them, then watched most leave when the dam was finished.

Fort Peck Dam — worth a moment even though we can't see it. Finished in 1940, it's one of the largest hydraulic earthen dams in the world. The reservoir behind it, Fort Peck Lake, stretches 134 miles. The dam was a New Deal project, a make-work enterprise on a continental scale: the federal government employing armies of men to reshape the Missouri's hydrology. It worked, in the engineering sense. The Missouri below the dam flows calmer now, its sediment load trapped behind the earthwork. The river downstream is actually cutting deeper into its bed because the dam catches the gravel that used to replenish the channel. You control a river; the river finds another way to move.

Tampico ahead — or what's left of it. An unincorporated ghost, a water stop that existed to feed steam locomotives. The Great Northern established it in 1909 to keep the boilers running between Glasgow and Hinsdale. When diesel replaced steam in the 1950s, the reason for Tampico evaporated. The water tank came down. The section crew left. The Judith River Formation outcrops near here — Campanian sandstone and shale from about seventy-five million years ago, light brown and fine-grained. The same formation that produces coal seams farther east. Tampico sat above ancient swamp deposits and didn't know it, and it wouldn't have mattered anyway.

The Judith River Formation is one of the great fossil beds of North America, and we're riding right through it. Paleontologists have pulled Tyrannosaurus rex and Pachycephalosaurus from these strata — the bone-headed dinosaur whose skull dome was up to ten inches of solid bone, probably used in head-butting contests the way bighorn sheep use their horns today. Also from these layers: Meniscoessus robustus, a multituberculate mammal — rat-sized, with teeth like a nutcracker — that lived in the shadows of the dinosaurs and survived the extinction that killed them. That's the thing about the Cretaceous end: the small, opportunistic, generalist survivors became us. Every mammal alive today, including everyone in this car, traces back to something like Meniscoessus scrabbling through a world being remade by a bolide impact sixty-six million years ago.

Back onto alluvium — the river's deposit again. The Milk River has been our companion through this whole stretch, running roughly parallel to the tracks, just to the north. It rises in Glacier National Park, loops into Canada through Alberta, then returns to Montana and drains into the Missouri at Fort Peck. An international river that ignores the border. Valley County has thirty-six percent wetland cover, one of the highest proportions in Montana — much of it tied to the Milk River corridor. Out both windows, you'll see the wet margins of that drainage: willow thickets, cattail edges, the darker green that signals standing water just out of sight.

Phillips County begins near milepost 1248 — we're approaching the county line. Named for Benjamin D. Phillips, a rancher and state senator, it was carved out of Blaine County in 1915, which had itself been carved out of Chouteau County in 1912. The northern plains were subdivided relentlessly in the homestead era: new counties, new courthouses, new county seats, all built on the assumption that population would keep growing. It didn't. Phillips County today has four thousand people across five thousand square miles — roughly the area of Connecticut, with a population smaller than a mid-sized high school.

Hinsdale on the right, along the Milk River. Under two hundred people now. It was a Great Northern station, like Tampico, like Nashua — the railroad's grid of every-ten-miles supply points that seeded the northern tier with small towns in the 1890s and early 1900s. Hinsdale got a post office, a grain elevator, a school. The school still runs. The elevator still runs. The post office still runs. That's actually a kind of success out here — many of the towns in this corridor have lost all three.

There's a particular brutality to the way the railroad made and unmade these towns. Hill's Great Northern was explicit about it: towns were platted at regular intervals to serve the line's operational needs, not the settlers' social ones. Water stops every ten miles because that's how far a steam locomotive could run between fillings. Grain platforms every few miles because that's the radius a farmer could haul a wagonload before dark. When the operational need changed — diesel engines, grain trucks, better roads — the railroad's rationale for the town vanished. The town didn't know it yet, but it had already been reclassified as redundant. Tampico, back at mile 1230, was founded 1909 and essentially dead by 1960. Fifty years, one function, then nothing. We've passed five or six of those stories this afternoon.

The Frenchman River crosses our path on the right — small, unimpressive-looking, but worth noting. It rises in Saskatchewan, dips into Montana, and returns to Canada before joining the Milk River. Another international river on this border corridor. Locally it's called the Whitemud River, for the pale clay banks along its course. A tributary of the Milk, which is a tributary of the Missouri, which is a tributary of the Mississippi. We're four rivers deep in the continent's interior drainage. The water passing under that bridge right now will reach the Gulf of Mexico in roughly three months.

Saco ahead — 159 people in the 2020 count, Phillips County now. Another Great Northern stop, another grain platform town. The name comes from Saco, Maine, which suggests the railroad official naming towns on this stretch either had a map of New England or a list of eastern postmasters who wanted their hometown commemorated. The Claggett Formation outcrops near here — dark gray Campanian marine shale, eighty million years old, from the deeper water of the Western Interior Seaway. The sea that covered this ground was deeper here than in some stretches to the east. What's out the windows now — shortgrass, sky, a water tower — sits directly on top of a sea floor that no longer exists.

We're climbing, though it doesn't feel like it. Since Glasgow we've gained a hundred feet of elevation, and over the next two hours we'll gain another two hundred and fifty more as the plains tilt upward toward the Rockies. The land shifts too — from Valley County's grassland-and-wetland patchwork to more open, drier rangeland as we push west into Phillips County. The crops change: less wheat, more hay, some barley. The sky gets bigger, which seems impossible, but it does. The Bearpaw Mountains will appear to the south before long — an island range, a laccolith complex, rising out of the plains like a misplaced idea. We'll get there.

The ground beneath us right now is Campanian shale — eighty million years of compressed seafloor, the dark gray kind that weathers brown at the edges. We've been on it for a while. What's about to change, in another thirty miles or so, is that the sea floor gives way to something much younger: river gravel, sand, the ordinary debris of the last two million years. From deep time to the very recent — one of those quiet shifts the window shows you if you're watching for it.

The Great Northern ran this line in the early 1890s, staking it along the Hi-Line — the northernmost practical rail corridor across Montana, pressed close to the Canadian border. James J. Hill's engineers chose it for grade, not scenery. The Missouri watershed tilts just enough that a locomotive can hold speed without burning the firebox down. Every town we'll pass through in the next hour exists because the railroad decided to stop there, take on water, unload freight. The railroad didn't follow settlement — it preceded it, dragged it into being.

Off to the right, you'll catch a glimpse of the Sleeping Buffalo area — a name that outlasted almost everything else here. There's a large sandstone boulder nearby that the Assiniboine people recognized as a sleeping buffalo long before any railroad surveyor set foot in Phillips County. The settlers who came after mapped it, named a hot springs resort for it, built a little recreation economy around it. Twelve people live in the census-designated place today. The boulder endures. The resort is quieter now.

Here's something worth sitting with as the grassland rolls by: in 1890 — the very year Malta was platted down the tracks — the Census Bureau declared the American frontier officially closed. No more continuous unsettled territory. The West had been filled in, at least on paper. But out here, the numbers tell a different story. Phillips County today, 130 years later, holds about four thousand people in an area larger than the state of Connecticut. The frontier closed on a map. On the ground, it never quite ended. What you see from this window is what "closed" looks like: grass, sky, a fence line running to the horizon, and the occasional hawk riding a thermal.

Look left — that cluster of buildings set back from the road is East Malta Colony, a Hutterite community. Ninety-seven people, communal ownership, German dialect, a theological lineage running back to sixteenth-century Austria. The Hutterites arrived on the northern Plains in the late nineteenth century, pushed out of Russia when the Tsar rescinded their exemptions from military service. They found in Montana something they'd been seeking for three hundred years: enough land, enough distance, enough tolerance.
