The station opened in 1893, the same year the Great Northern achieved its Pacific endpoint: this was one of the first waypoints on a completed transcontinental. Libby's other history is harder: the W.R. Grace company mined vermiculite here from 1919 to 1990, and the vermiculite deposit was contaminated with asbestiform tremolite. For decades, dust from the mine drifted through town. The EPA declared Libby a Superfund site in 2002. The cleanup has been extensive and ongoing. Both histories are real: the railroad town that persisted, and the mining town whose legacy is still being reckoned with. We're here for only a few minutes; the town has been reckoning for decades.

Pulling out of Libby, we follow the Kootenai east and then the line begins to describe the slow arc that will take us toward the Idaho border — still about thirty-five miles ahead. The bedrock stays Mesoproterozoic for now, that same ancient sedimentary package that has underlain almost everything since we entered Lincoln County. But the land is changing in a way the rock doesn't capture: we're descending, slowly, consistently. Over the next 150 miles the elevation will drop more than 1,200 feet. The forest will thin. The river valleys will open. The Pacific drainage we're in will begin to feel less like mountain country and more like the country of a big river — because that is exactly what it is becoming. The Columbia system is pulling us downstream, toward a different world than the one we woke up in this morning.

The Mesoproterozoic sedimentary rock holds under us, patient as ever — limestone and shale and dolomite laid down when this continent was still assembling itself, when the oxygen in the atmosphere was only beginning to reach modern levels, when the most complex life on Earth was a mat of cyanobacteria at the bottom of a warm sea. We're riding across a billion years of quiet time. Forty miles ahead, around milepost 1780, the bedrock shifts to Quaternary — material deposited in the last 2.6 million years, a geological eyeblink. That transition, when we reach it, will mark a real change in how the land looks and feels. For now, we're still on deep time.

The roar reaches you before the sight does. Kootenai Falls — the largest undammed waterfall in the Northern Rockies — drops about ninety feet in a series of cascades, the river compressed between ancient walls of Mesoproterozoic argillite and quartzite that have been standing here for more than a billion years. The Kootenai people call this place sacred. It is. The railroad had to thread a ledge cut into the canyon wall to get through — there was simply no other way. Look at the rock faces: those thin parallel bands of deep grey and rust are the original seafloor sediment, laid down when this part of North America sat beneath a shallow inland sea, before the Rockies existed, before the Atlantic existed. A billion years compressed into a cliff face outside our window.

Edwin H. Beckler surveyed this canyon for James J. Hill's Great Northern Railway in the early 1890s. What he found was a route that required blasting ledges into solid Precambrian rock for miles — but it was the only viable northern passage. Hill wanted the shortest possible line to Puget Sound, and the Kootenai River canyon gave him just enough room. The Great Northern's tracks were laid here in 1891 and 1892, opening the line to Seattle in 1893 — the very year of the great financial panic that bankrupted competing railroads all across the West. Hill had built lean; he survived. We're riding his geometry still.

Troy sits at the junction where the Kootenai River swings south, and it owes its existence almost entirely to the railroad — platted in the Great Northern boom years as a division point and timber-shipping junction. Lincoln County was created in 1909, named for Abraham Lincoln, and Troy was already its working town. Today the county's median household income is around $44,000; poverty runs nearly seventeen percent. The big timber mills that once anchored the local economy are mostly gone. Troy persists, a few thousand people in the valley bottom, surrounded by the same billion-year-old rock the railroad crews had to negotiate around.

We're still rolling through some of the oldest exposed rock in the American Northwest — Mesoproterozoic sedimentary and volcanic rocks, between one and 1.6 billion years old. Look for the intercalated bands where mafic volcanic flows interrupt the sediment layers: dark, fine-grained rock sandwiched between the lighter argillite and quartzite. This is where an ancient rift system tried and partly failed to tear the continent apart, flooding the seafloor with basaltic lava between pulses of sediment. The Rockies we think of — the Laramide mountains, the big lift — didn't happen until about 70 million years ago. What we're reading in these walls is five times older than that.

Yakt is barely a bend in the road — a cluster of buildings where a Great Northern flag stop once served the ranches and small homesteads that filled in the valley after the railroad came through. Places like Yakt exist because the train stopped. When it stopped stopping, the logic of the settlement dissolved. This is the recurring pattern on this line: the railroad creates the town, and the railroad's changing economics slowly unmakes it.

Somewhere in the next several miles, without drama, we cross from Montana into Idaho — from the Pacific Northwest's Kootenai drainage into Boundary County, the northernmost county in the state. The state line here is a surveyor's abstraction; the land doesn't know it. The Kootenai River crosses the same line at nearly the same place. But notice the county name: Boundary County. It names itself after the thing that defines it — the 49th parallel, the US-Canada border, drawn in 1846 by the Oregon Treaty before either of these states existed, before the railroad existed, before any of these towns were platted. The border is the oldest human mark on this landscape by a generation.

Out the right window: Moyie Springs, population around 820, sitting where Moyie River meets the Kootenai. The Moyie comes down from Canada through deep limestone gorges — same Mesoproterozoic carbonate rock we've been reading for the last thirty miles. The Kootenai Tribe of Idaho has its reservation just downstream from here, one of the smallest reservations in the country by land area, home to fewer than two hundred tribal members. The Kootenai people have been in this drainage for thousands of years; the county surrounding them was only formally organized in 1915. That chronological ratio — millennia of indigenous presence against a century of county government — is the ratio that the landscape keeps showing us.

Around mile 1780 the rock changes — and it's a change worth noting because it marks a real boundary in deep time. We leave the Mesoproterozoic behind and roll onto Quaternary deposits: sand, gravel, glacial till, and glacial flood sediments, all younger than about 2.6 million years. This is the first time on the leg we're formally introducing Quaternary rock — technically the youngest stratigraphic period, covering everything from the onset of the ice ages to yesterday. What you're looking at out the window isn't ancient seafloor anymore. It's the wreckage of glaciers. The Cordilleran Ice Sheet — the great ice mass that covered western Canada and spilled south into the northern states — draped this valley with drift and outwash as it retreated, roughly 12,000 to 14,000 years ago. The flat valley floor ahead isn't natural flatness; it's the smoothed, filled surface left when the ice let go.

Bonners Ferry — county seat, largest city in Boundary County, population about 2,500. The name is literal: Edwin L. Bonner ran a ferry here across the Kootenai River in 1864, the same year as the Sand Creek Massacre out on the Colorado plains, the same year Sherman was burning toward Atlanta. The Idaho goldfields had just opened; miners and supplies needed to cross. Bonner's ferry was replaced by a bridge, the bridge by a railroad bridge, the railroad town by the modern highway town. The valley floor here is wide, flat glacial outwash — the Kootenai River meandering across a plain it didn't carve so much as inherit from the ice. Bonners Ferry is the natural crossing point because the valley pinches here, where the river narrows between two ridges of glacial debris. Geography made Bonner's business possible, and the same geography made the railroad engineers choose this crossing fifty years later.

The Kootenai River we've been following since the Montana border is one of the continent's more improbable drainage paths. It rises in the Canadian Rockies, flows south into Montana, bends west, crosses into Idaho here at Bonners Ferry, then loops back north into British Columbia before finally joining the Columbia at Castlegar. It crosses the international border twice. That loop — the Kootenai anomaly — is a relic of the ice ages: glacial damming and rerouting reshaped drainage patterns across the entire northern Rockies, forcing rivers into new paths they've kept ever since. We're riding the floor of a valley that water remade in the last heartbeat of geological time.

Naples: unincorporated, small, sitting eleven miles south of Bonners Ferry on US 2 and 95. The name is a curiosity out here — Italian-American settlers, or more likely a railroad or postal clerk who reached for something, anything, that sounded established and European. The geology underfoot here is mapped as man-made land: highway fills, railroad rights-of-way, bridge abutments, small levees. Holocene in age — meaning the last 11,700 years, but mostly the last century. We're riding on our own infrastructure here, the fill that carries the tracks across the soft, wet valley floor.

Look at the valley now and then look at the ridges on either side. The flat bottom is recent alluvium — the river's own gift, built up over millennia from glacier meltwater carrying gravel and sand downstream and dropping it when the current slowed. We've touched on alluvium at various points on this journey; here it's doing something specific: building a trough, a wide agricultural floor between mountain walls. The Pleistocene till on the surrounding slopes — the coarse, poorly sorted gravel left directly by glacier ice, different from the water-sorted alluvium below — records an older, colder moment. Both landscapes visible at once: what the ice left, and what the river patiently reworked after. In northern Idaho this distinction is everywhere. The flat land grows hay and canola. The rocky slopes above it grow nothing a farmer can use.

Elmira: another unincorporated community, barely a dot on the county map. We're entering Bonner County now — a county named for the same ferry operator as the town we just left, partitioned from Kootenai County in 1907. Population jumps: Bonner County has nearly 48,000 people against Boundary County's 12,000. Sandpoint is ahead, and Sandpoint is the kind of place that's grown — a resort economy on Lake Pend Oreille, a different economic animal from the timber and farming communities we've been passing through. The Panhandle of Idaho narrows here, squeezed between Montana and Washington, and the landscape is about to shift again — out of the deep Kootenai canyon country and onto something wider, wetter, and colder in winter, warmer in summer, shaped less by a single river than by a lake so large it practically makes its own weather.

The water out the left window is Lake Pend Oreille — one of the deepest lakes in the country, over 1,100 feet at its plunge. We're riding the old Great Northern right-of-way here, and James J. Hill's surveyors picked this corridor in the 1880s precisely because the lake's drainage carved a natural ramp through the Selkirks. Beneath the train, Pleistocene glaciers did the excavating — we're rolling on their leavings, coarse till and outwash, gravel and clay pressed into the valley floor during the last glacial maximum when the Cordilleran ice sheet pushed down from Canada. The glaciers shaped the lake; the lake shaped the route; the route shaped everything else.

The bedrock under us just now is ancient — Mesoproterozoic sedimentary stone, roughly 1.2 to 1.6 billion years old, among the oldest surface rock we'll see on this whole leg. But it's buried under those Pleistocene glacial deposits, invisible. That's the pattern through northern Idaho: unimaginable deep time underneath, and a relatively thin, geologically recent blanket on top — till, outwash, flood gravel — courtesy of ice that was still here as recently as 15,000 years ago. We left forest behind a while back. The shrub and mixed cover around us now is the Northern Rockies inland maritime foothills — drier than it looks, sitting in the rain shadow of the Selkirks.

If you look up and to the right, that long ridgeline with the ski runs cut into it is Schweitzer Mountain — opened in 1963, expanded into one of the larger ski resorts in the Pacific Northwest. The ski mountain and the town below it are a matched pair: Schweitzer draws winter visitors; Sandpoint's economy lives on that traffic, plus the summer lake trade. It's a pattern as old as the railroad — Hill's Great Northern made this valley accessible, and accessibility determined what kind of economy could take root. The Selkirks up there top out near 7,000 feet. We're at roughly 2,100. The difference is what made the pass possible.

Bonner County was carved out of Kootenai County in 1907 and named for Edwin Bonner, who ran a ferry across the Pend Oreille River in the 1860s before the railroad arrived. Ferry operators were the original infrastructure of this country — they held the crossings that mattered before bridges, before rails. Bonner got a county named for him. Most ferry operators got nothing. The Kalispel people — sometimes called the Pend d'Oreilles by French traders — had been on this water for centuries before any of that. Their name is still on the lake. Their presence is not much else in what we see out the window: that erasure is the older story here, layered under the county-seat story and the ski-resort story alike.

Sandpoint is our station stop — if you're stretching legs, this is the moment. The city sits right where the Pend Oreille River narrows out of the lake's north end, a natural crossing point. The Great Northern arrived in 1881, the Northern Pacific a year later, and the town grew up at the junction like a knot in a rope. By 1898 it had incorporated; by the early 1900s it was shipping timber and lead-silver ore from the Coeur d'Alene Mining District to the south. Today the population is under 10,000 — it's a town that stabilized rather than boomed, which in northern Idaho is its own kind of success. The lake is the real asset: 148 square miles of cold, clear water. Nothing about Sandpoint makes sense without it.

As we pull out of Sandpoint heading south, we're beginning a long, gentle descent toward the Columbia Basin. The land falls roughly 480 feet over the next 150 miles — nearly imperceptible on any individual mile, but cumulative. We're still in the Pacific watershed; the water running off these hills eventually reaches the Columbia. That's been true since we crossed from the Missouri drainage hours back, and it will be true all the way to the coast. The watershed divide is invisible, but it's the hinge on which everything tilts — rain, drainage, ecology, and in the railroad era, the logic of freight movement.

Here the glacial cover thins and the deep rock shows through — Mesoproterozoic sedimentary, laid down somewhere between 1.2 and 1.6 billion years ago in a shallow sea that no longer exists on any map. These are Belt Supergroup rocks, the same formation that makes Glacier National Park's striped cliffs so vivid, though here they're less dramatic, more broken. The fossils found near this stretch are Middle Cambrian marine creatures — trilobites from around 506 million years ago, Elrathia and Albertella — animals that crawled through mud on a seafloor that is now Idaho at 2,000 feet. Deep time has a way of making "Idaho" feel like a very recent administrative decision.

The Pacific Northwest timber economy was one of the great economic engines of the late 19th century — from around 1850 to 1930, it rivaled anything the Great Plains produced. Northern Idaho was part of that: white pine and western larch coming down off the Selkirks and Cabinet Mountains, milled at Sandpoint and Coeur d'Alene, shipped east on the rails that had only just made it possible. The same trains that brought settlers out brought lumber back. It was a one-way metabolism: the forests gave; the economy took. By the 1930s, the easily accessible old-growth was largely gone, and the towns that had organized around it had to find other reasons to exist. Some did. Many didn't. The ghost towns along this leg aren't only from mining booms — some are logged-out mill towns that just stopped.

Straight ahead, Cocolalla sits on the south shore of Cocolalla Lake — unincorporated, quiet, still holding a post office. That post office is the bureaucratic minimum for community survival: a ZIP code, a named place, a reason the mail still comes. Cocolalla has never been much more than a stop on U.S. 95. Before the highway, it was a stop on the rail line. Before the rail line, it was nothing that showed up in American records — though the Kalispel people knew this lake and valley in ways that didn't require records. The name Cocolalla is likely Salish in origin. The place itself belongs, in the official American sense, to Bonner County. In any older sense, it belongs to this valley.

The geology shifts again here — we're back on Quaternary deposits, the younger stuff: continental glacial till, glaciofluvial gravels, modern alluvium. The Pleistocene glaciers that carved Lake Pend Oreille also left this fill behind as they retreated. But the big story coming up is the Missoula Floods — we'll start seeing their deposits more clearly around mile 1840 and south. Those were not ordinary floods. Between roughly 15,000 and 13,000 years ago, a glacial ice dam in Montana failed repeatedly — dozens of times — releasing Lake Missoula catastrophically each time. The floodwater moved at perhaps 65 miles per hour, carrying icebergs, scouring bedrock, depositing gravel bars the size of hills. Some of that gravel is what we're about to roll through.

Out the left window: Bayview, on the southwest arm of Lake Pend Oreille — a small community with a specific Cold War history most people don't know about. The U.S. Navy operates an acoustic research detachment here. Pend Oreille was chosen after World War II because its extraordinary depth — over 1,100 feet — and cold, stratified water provide near-ideal conditions for testing submarine acoustics. Torpedo and sonar systems have been tested in that lake for decades. The Navy in landlocked Idaho, 400 miles from salt water. The logic of strategic geography doesn't always follow the obvious lines.

We're crossing from Bonner County into Kootenai County now — and the demographics shift measurably. Kootenai's median income is about $10,000 higher than Bonner's; its population is nearly four times larger; Coeur d'Alene is one of the fastest-growing small metros in the country. This whole corridor — Sandpoint to Coeur d'Alene — has been drawing people from California, from the Pacific Coast cities, for the past twenty years. Remote work accelerated it. The landscape looks wild; the real estate market is not. That tension — between the appearance of frontier and the reality of a booming amenity economy — is a recurring Western pattern. The open country gets sold as escape; enough people buy in and it's no longer open.

Athol, population 709, part of the Coeur d'Alene metro statistical area in the technical sense, though it feels nothing like a metro. Its main external identity is Silverwood, a theme park a few miles north — the largest in the Pacific Northwest, which is a geographic category generous enough to accommodate some surprises. The town itself incorporated in the late 19th century and has stayed small ever since. The glaciofluvial deposits under and around it — the outburst flood gravels — make for well-drained soil. Hay, wheat, a little canola in Kootenai County. The ground here remembers catastrophic water; the farms don't.

Those glaciofluvial deposits deserve a moment. The Missoula Floods left some of their clearest evidence across the Columbia Plateau to the southwest — the Channeled Scablands that Washington State geologist J Harlen Bretz spent decades trying to explain, against fierce scientific resistance, before being vindicated. But the upstream signature of those floods is here too, in the gravel bars and sorted sediments filling this valley. Bretz first proposed catastrophic flooding in 1923. The geological establishment rejected it for forty years. The evidence was too large — too violent — to fit the uniformitarian model that assumed landscapes changed only slowly. He was right; the landscape had been shaped in hours. In 1979, at age 96, Bretz received the Penrose Medal, geology's highest honor. He reportedly said: "All my enemies are dead, so I have no one to gloat over."

Rathdrum sits in the Rathdrum Prairie — a broad, flat outwash plain that stretches between the Selkirks and the Coeur d'Alene Mountains. That flat is flood-made: Missoula Flood deposits, sorted and spread, creating farmable ground. The Great Northern came through and the town organized around the railroad, as towns here did. It's a Kootenai County community now in the gravitational pull of Coeur d'Alene's growth. The prairie it sits on was once covered by a glacial lake — Lake Rathdrum — formed when ice dams backed up meltwater. The lake drained when the ice gave way. What's left is the flat, the gravel, and a town that doesn't advertise its origins in a catastrophic vanished lake.

Ahead of us over the next couple of hours: the Columbia Plateau, the great volcanic table that covers eastern Washington and Oregon — basalt laid down in successive flows between 17 and 6 million years ago, some flows reaching all the way to the coast. We're still in the outwash plains and glacial deposits of northern Idaho for now, but the bedrock character is about to change. The shrub cover will thin; the terrain will open; the sky will get bigger in the way it does when you move from mountain valleys onto plateau country. The Columbia River is the destination — the great trunk stream that drains this entire region. We've been in its watershed for hundreds of miles. We'll meet the river itself in Washington. For now, we're still descending, still reading the glacier's handwriting in the ground under the wheels.

The deposits under us here are Pleistocene flood gravels — sorted cobbles and sand laid down by the Missoula Flood pulses, or possibly by earlier outburst events. This is the last of the clearly glacial material before the geology transitions to the younger Quaternary sediments of the plateau. The Selkirks are behind us now; the ridgelines to east and west are lower, the valleys wider. The train is reading the landscape the way a geologist reads a core sample — layer by layer, older to younger as we move through space. What took tens of thousands of years to deposit, we cross in an afternoon.

The ground beneath us right now is flood debris — not slow river silt, but the catastrophic wreckage of ice-age lakes that failed all at once. Twelve thousand years ago, glacial Lake Missoula held five hundred cubic miles of water behind an ice dam in Montana. The dam collapsed. Water roared southwest at highway speeds, hundreds of feet deep, stripping the land bare. We're riding on what it left: sand and gravel sorted by a wall of water taller than a ten-story building. The border between Idaho and Washington passes beneath our wheels right here, but the flood didn't notice it.

The country on both sides is that particular western mix — subdivisions edging up against sagebrush, the highway alongside us, chain retail at the exits. Easy to overlook. But look at the hills: they're smooth, rounded, draped. That's the flood's signature. Beneath the gravel wash, buried but present, is basalt — lava flows stacked like pages in a book, poured out millions of years before the ice came. We haven't seen it yet, but it's coming. The whole Columbia Plateau is paved in it, and we're almost there.

Off to our left, Liberty Lake — the lake itself, and the young city built around it. The city incorporated only in 2001, carved from unincorporated Spokane County by residents who wanted their own government. But the name is older than the suburb. The lake was a Spokane tribal gathering place long before white settlement, and the word "Spokane" comes from the Salish for "children of the sun" — a name that has outlasted every political boundary drawn since. The suburb is newest of all the layers here. The lake predates them all.

The Great Northern Railway came through this valley in 1892, James J. Hill's ambition made steel. Hill had watched the Northern Pacific struggle — too many mountain grades, too much bonded debt — and he decided to build his own road to the Pacific, without a land grant, on the sheer conviction that traffic would follow. He was right, mostly. The route through Spokane Valley wasn't just convenient; it was a declaration that the Inland Northwest was worth connecting. Towns along the right-of-way didn't precede the railroad — they were, in most cases, the railroad's own invention, platted and named by the company's surveyors, lots sold before the first spike was driven. That's a recurring pattern we've been watching since Chicago: iron comes first, then people, then the fiction that it was always going to be this way.

Spokane Valley is the largest suburb of Spokane — 102,000 people — though it didn't incorporate as a city until 2003. Before incorporation it was just "the valley," an elastic piece of Spokane County that grew by accretion as the city sprawled east. The name carries the same Salish root as the county and the city and the river: Spokane, the people of the sun. The valley the name belongs to was shaped by those Missoula floods, by volcanic basalt underneath, by the Spokane River running through it. All of that predates the city by an embarrassing margin. Three years old and the third-largest city in Washington. The West builds fast when it builds.

Watch the ground change. Right around here, the Pleistocene flood gravel gives way to something older and harder: the Columbia River Basalts, Neogene lavas, erupted between twenty-three and three million years ago from fissures in the earth's crust — not dramatic volcanic peaks, but long cracks in the ground that bled lava across an area larger than the state of Oregon. The flows stacked, cooling and cracking into the columnar joints you'll see clearly later in the gorge. What we're crossing onto now is the Columbia Plateau — a volcanic plain that makes the canyon country of the Southwest look young by comparison.

The plateau isn't a mountain range; it's a filled basin. Lava after lava, each flow sometimes hundreds of feet thick, buried whatever landscape came before it. Then the Missoula floods tore across the top, stripping and sculpting. Then the Snake River and Columbia cut down through it all, exposing the stacked basalt in canyon walls. We're on the surface of all that now — a high, flat, semi-arid grassland, the driest part of Washington state, where precipitation averages twelve to fifteen inches a year. Wheat grows here, dry-farmed without irrigation, the same way it grew in 1900.

We're pulling into Spokane — population 230,000, second city of Washington, the undisputed capital of the Inland Northwest. The city's founding is almost comically railroad-dependent: a sawmill in 1871, then the Northern Pacific arrived in 1881, and Spokane Falls — as it was still called — exploded. By 1890 the population had grown from a few hundred to thirty-six thousand in a single decade. The city's original fortune came from silver and lead mines in the Coeur d'Alene district to our east, back in Idaho. The ore came out of the mountains; the trains carried it here; Spokane's banks and merchants financed the next round of extraction. That cycle — mine, rail, market town — built the Pacific Northwest's interior economy, and Spokane was its hinge.

The Spokane station we just stopped at opened in 1902, built by the Northern Pacific and Great Northern together — two competing railroads sharing a single elegant depot, which tells you something about the economics of the time. Both roads needed Spokane; Spokane needed both roads. The building went up in Flemish Renaissance revival style, red brick and terra cotta, the kind of architecture that says permanence and civic confidence to any passenger arriving from the east. Spokane was making the same argument every interior western city made in the 1880s and 90s: we are not a way-station. We are a destination. Some of them were right.

Spokane County organized in 1858 — two years before Washington Territory even had the population to become a state. The county is named for the river, which is named for the people. But there's a watershed story here too: the Spokane River drains into the Columbia, which reaches the Pacific. Everything we've crossed since leaving the Missouri's basin has been draining toward this ocean. We entered the Columbia watershed somewhere back in the mountains; from here to the coast, every creek finds the Columbia. That river is our silent companion now. We won't see it for another hundred miles, but we're already in its world.

Off to our right, Spokane International — the airport that was once Felts Field's successor, built on Army Air Corps land that goes back to 1927. The irony of train travel: we pass airports that displaced us. The jet age didn't kill Amtrak entirely, but it remapped the nation's imagination of distance. Before 1960, Spokane was a rail city — you arrived by train, you left by train. The Empire Builder made this run daily. Now the airport handles three million passengers a year, and the train carries a few hundred on a good day. What the train gives back is the land itself. You can't see the basalt columns from 35,000 feet.

We're descending now onto the Columbia Plateau proper — the full expression of it. This is one of the world's great flood-basalt provinces, a place where the earth's interior pushed through the crust not as a single volcano but as a diffuse hemorrhage. The Wanapum Basalt, which will be visible in road cuts as we continue west, erupted roughly thirteen and a half million years ago during the Middle Miocene. Think about that date: it's the same era that produced the dragonfly fossil recorded near here — Epophthalmia biordinata — preserved in the lake sediments that accumulated between lava flows, in brief intervals of geological peace between catastrophes.

The fossils tell us the lavas didn't come all at once. There were pauses — decades, centuries, perhaps longer — when lakes formed in the low spots between flows, when insects and plants colonized the cooled rock, when things lived and died and were buried. Then the next flow came and sealed them. The geological record here is a series of extinctions followed by fresh starts. Which is also, if you squint, the human record.

Ahead of us, Cheney — a college town built on the railroad's certainty about itself. The Northern Pacific platted it in 1880 and named it for Benjamin Cheney, a Northern Pacific director. The town incorporated in 1883. Eastern Washington University sits there now, serving thirteen thousand students, which makes the college effectively the town's economy. But in 1881, Cheney was briefly the county seat — until Spokane's growth made it obvious who was actually winning. The county seat moved to Spokane in 1886. Cheney adapted, became an education town rather than a government town. That pivot — finding a second identity when the first one fails — is how the ones that survived did it.

The wheat fields we're passing now are dry-farmed — no irrigation, just winter rain and snowmelt on deep Palouse soils. The Palouse Hills, the gentle rolling farmland east of here, are made of loess — windblown silt deposited over glacial and post-glacial periods, sometimes a hundred feet deep, remarkably fertile. Farmers discovered in the 1880s that winter wheat thrived here without the rivers and canals that agriculture required in drier parts of the West. That discovery made the Inland Northwest one of the most productive grain regions on the continent. The railroad arrived, conveniently, just as the wheat economy needed a way out. Hill's Great Northern wasn't charitable; it charged what the traffic would bear. But it did, in fact, connect this dry plateau to the Pacific coast ports — and from there, to the world.

The Columbia River eventually carries that grain connection to the sea in a different way: barges run the river system from eastern Washington's interior all the way to Portland. The river does what the train started. We're approaching a landscape where water and rail and grain have been in an interdependent economy for a hundred and forty years, and the relationships have barely changed.

Tyler is an unincorporated community — barely a community at all now, a crossroads on State Route 904 and not much more. But it has a ghost-town quality that the platted railroad towns often get when the line through them stops mattering. These small inland Washington settlements followed a common arc: platted when wheat was moving at volume, given a grain elevator and a post office, named for someone now forgotten, then slowly thinned as the elevator closed or the local branch line stopped running or the nearest town got a paved highway and absorbed the trade. Tyler persists on the map. On the ground, it's thin.

The geology underfoot right now is the Wanapum Basalt's Priest Rapids Member — erupted about thirteen and a half million years ago, a single flow event that covered thousands of square miles. When you see road cuts west of here, you'll see the columnar jointing clearly: hexagonal columns formed as the cooling lava contracted, cracking in the most efficient geometric pattern possible. A physicist would say the columns minimize internal stress. A geologist says it's the same physics that cracks drying mud. The scale is just different — columns forty or fifty feet tall, densely packed, looking almost carved.

The woolly mammoth fossil found near this stretch — Mammuthus primigenius — was contemporary with the last of the Missoula floods: both the animal and the final catastrophic outburst are dated to roughly the same late Pleistocene window. The mammoth walked on flood-sorted gravel. It drank from temporary lakes that filled the scablands between basalt ridges. The floods didn't kill it directly — mammoths survived the floods — but the eventual warming that ended the ice age dried out the grasslands it needed. The basalt outlasted the mammoth by twelve million years and counting. We're riding on the basalt. We pass through in an afternoon.

The soil out here is loess — wind-blown silt, pale and fine, settled over the basalt flood plain in layers ten, twenty, thirty feet deep. Under our wheels, basalt that poured out in sheets fifteen million years ago, some of the most voluminous eruptions in Earth's history. The loess came later, when the ice-age floods stripped the upstream highlands bare and the winds carried the rock flour east and let it fall. What grew in it: wheat. What powered the towns that grew from the wheat: the Northern Pacific. Both are still here. Both are thinning.

Lincoln County was carved off Whitman County in 1883, and named for the president who had been dead eighteen years. That naming impulse matters — 1883 was boom time out here, and new counties needed gravity, legitimacy, a flag to plant. The Northern Pacific had just completed its transcontinental link, and every politician and land speculator wanted their grid square to sound like it belonged to the permanent republic.

It did not always last. What came to Lincoln County was a wheat economy that worked beautifully in wet years and collapsed in dry ones. Median income today sits at sixty-eight thousand dollars — modest but holding. Twenty percent fewer people than the state median can buy into, and the county's industries lean hard on education, health, and the land itself. That combination — thin population, agriculture, a county seat that punches above its weight — is the Columbia Plateau's signature right now. We've been watching it build for fifty miles.

The town of Sprague is just ahead, off to our left. Its lake comes first.

Sprague Lake sits right on the county line, Adams to our left, Lincoln to our right, straddling the border the way so many things out here straddle borders — of watershed, of county, of economic survival. It drains south through Cow Creek into the Palouse River, and from there into the Snake, and from there into the Columbia. Every drop of water that falls on this plateau finds its way eventually to the Columbia, which we'll be riding into before this leg is done. The lake was originally called Lake Colville, for the same fur-trade geography that names the river to our north. Someone changed it. The old name points to what was here before wheat.

Sprague itself was once a division point on the Northern Pacific — one of those towns that existed primarily because a railroad needed a place to swap out crews and engines on a long run. In 1883, when the line was new, Sprague was briefly the seat of Spokane County. Briefly. Within two years, Spokane had annexed that role, and Sprague settled into the supporting role it still plays: a small city of a few hundred people, a grain elevator, a main street that remembers more prosperity than it currently holds.

The ghost towns begin now. We've passed dozens of them on this leg — places platted in the 1880s and 1890s on the assumption that the wheat would always move, the railroad would always stop, the rains would come. Some of the assumptions were right about two out of three.

Keystone — named for Pennsylvania, the Keystone State, by a postmaster who was homesick for the East and wanted to carry some of it with him. It sat sixteen miles northeast of Ritzville on the Northern Pacific line, a rail-era creature, dependent entirely on train traffic. When the traffic thinned, Keystone went quiet. Nothing dramatic. No fire, no flood, no single catastrophe. The railroad just stopped stopping here, and the people followed the railroad's logic. What's left is a name on a map and a few foundations you'd have to know where to look for.

The geology shifts here around mile 1930, from the Neogene flood basalts into a slightly older Miocene mafic volcanic sequence — still the same volcanic province, still the same Columbia River Basalt Group event that buried half of eastern Washington under lava, but a different pulse of it. You wouldn't notice it from the window. The land doesn't show the seams the way the Grand Canyon does. Out here the rock is under wheat and loess and the patient work of grass roots. Only a road cut or a creek bank exposes it — dark gray, columnar-jointed, tight-grained basalt, basalt all the way down.

Those fossils the paleontologists find in this region — Sorex meltoni, a shrew; Hypolagus, a small rabbit-relative — lived here around 4.7 million years ago, when the lava had already cooled and the land was beginning to look something like what it looks like now: dry, grassy, open. The shrew weighed maybe eight grams. It went about its life on ground that would later be buried under loess, under plowed fields, under roads built by a railroad empire's surveyors, who were themselves following the logic of a plateau that the basalt had already laid flat for them.

Tokio, Washington. A ghost town in the Palouse, in Adams County, northeast of Ritzville. The name offers no obvious explanation in the historical record — no Japanese settlers platted it, no treaty was signed here. It's simply one of those place names that drifted west with settlers who liked the sound of something exotic. The community is gone now, leaving behind the name and the coordinates and the category: ghost town. We've been tallying them all leg long. Here's another one.

Ritzville ahead, and it's worth a moment's preparation. In the 1880s, this stretch of the Northern Pacific was the artery the whole wheat economy pumped through. The railroad didn't just carry grain out — it carried people in, carried lumber for houses and coal for stoves, carried newspapers and seed catalogs and the entire apparatus of settlement. Towns spaced themselves along the line at intervals a horse could manage between stations, and the station itself was the center of civic gravity: the post office, the telegraph, the weekly shipment of reality from the outside world.

When the automobile arrived, and then the highway, and then Interstate 90 — which runs beside us now — the calculation changed. Towns that had train service but not highway access faded. Towns that had both survived, scaled back. Ritzville survived. It sits right on I-90, it's the county seat of Adams County, and it has managed to hold on at just under eighteen hundred people. That is not nothing, out here.

The brick buildings on Ritzville's main street went up when hard red wheat was selling and the Northern Pacific was paying dividends. Some of that brick was shipped in on the same railroad that carried the wheat out — a closed loop of capital that built solid, handsome commercial blocks in a town of a few thousand people on a dry plateau. The county courthouse still stands. The grain elevators, the tallest structures for miles, still define the skyline from a distance — the same role a cathedral played in a medieval town, the building that told travelers how far they still had to go.

Adams County today: twenty thousand people, median income sixty-three thousand, poverty rate nearly twenty-one percent. That poverty gap — seven points above Lincoln County just to the west — reflects something real about what happened when the wheat economy mechanized, fewer hands needed, and the surplus people had nowhere obvious to go.

We're sliding south of due west now, dropping elevation almost imperceptibly. The plateau isn't flat — it tilts, and the rivers have cut into it, and where they've cut you get the first real exposure of those flood basalts we've been riding over for a hundred miles. The Columbia Plateau drains to the Columbia, and the Columbia drains to the Pacific, and we are now deep in that basin. Every creek we cross — and we cross several, invisible from here but running in their little valleys below the wheat horizon — is moving toward the same destination.

The land cover is shifting. Lincoln County was grassland. Adams County is split: a third grassland, a third shrub. The bunchgrass gives way in the drier pockets to sage and rabbitbrush, gray-green and aromatic. We haven't left the volcanic plateau, but we're getting drier as we move southwest, and the plant communities know it before we do.

Paha. A populated place, the records say — not quite a ghost town in the official classification, but not quite a town either. A name that's held on past whatever community it once named. Out here, that's more common than the ghost town designation itself: places that never quite died, never quite lived, existing in an administrative limbo of census designations and rural route addresses. Someone's farm. Someone's mailbox. The railroad passed close enough to name it, not close enough to sustain it.

Around mile 1970, the geology changes again — Quaternary sedimentary, the youngest rock we'll see on this stretch, less than 2.6 million years old. What that means in practice: flood deposits, ice-age outwash, the layered evidence of the Missoula Floods that carved the Channeled Scablands to our north. The floods didn't just scour channels; they dropped material too, and where the water slowed, it left bars of gravel and sand and silt that eventually became the flat benches and low terraces visible along creek drainages.

We've been on volcanic country since eastern Montana. The plateau itself is basalt — the same basalt, more or less — and the Quaternary sediments are a thin late-arriving skin over it, the most recent chapter of a very long book. Ice-age floods. Then loess. Then wheat. The sequence repeats itself across this entire plateau, one geological and agricultural stratigraphy laid over the volcanic foundation.

Off to our right — Servia, Washington. A ghost town in Adams County, classified now only as a populated place, which is the census bureau's polite way of saying: there was something here. Named, presumably, by settlers with Serbian roots or Serbian sympathies or simply a liking for the sound of it. The European immigrant towns of the Columbia Plateau carried their old countries with them in their names — Tokio, Servia, Keystone from Pennsylvania — a whole displaced geography written across a dry plateau in the names of places most of them never returned to see.

The fourth ghost town we've passed in Adams County alone. We counted them differently in the boom years.

The basalt resurfaces under us around mile 1980 — back to the Neogene flood basalts, the bedrock that underlies almost everything on this plateau. We've moved through a thin lens of Quaternary sediment and come back to the foundation. That oscillation between the ancient volcanic base and the younger surface deposits has been the geological story of this whole segment: deep time covered by recent time, the Miocene buried under the Holocene, the lava buried under the loess, the loess plowed into wheat fields, the wheat fields feeding a civilization that arrived a century and a half ago and is still figuring out how to hold on.

Ahead the land continues to open. We're losing elevation slowly and the shrub is gaining on the grass. The Columbia Basin is pulling us toward it, the same gravitational logic that pulled the ice-age floodwaters south and west, carving their channels, filling their valleys, leaving this plateau scoured and planted and strung with the names of places that tried to last.

The cluster of buildings coming up ahead — that's Hatton. Seventy-nine people at the last count. It sits out here on the Columbia Plateau exactly where the railroad needed a water stop, a grain elevator, a name on a timetable. The Great Northern built through these flats in the 1890s, and towns like Hatton blinked into existence wherever the line required one. They weren't founded so much as installed. Some thrived into small cities. Hatton stayed at seventy-nine. The elevator is still the tallest thing for miles.

We're riding across the surface of something enormous right now — the Columbia River Basalt Group, one of the largest flood-basalt provinces on Earth. Between roughly 17 and 6 million years ago, magma cracked through fissures in what is now eastern Washington and Oregon and simply poured across the landscape. Not volcanoes in the traditional sense — no cone, no explosion — just curtains of lava bleeding from the earth, stacking layer on layer until the plateau sat hundreds of feet thick in basalt. The rock beneath us is Neogene, 23 to 2.6 million years old. It doesn't announce itself out here — the land is flat, the soil covers it — but it's there, a dark foundation under everything: the wheat fields, the roads, the towns. We left the Northern Rockies behind some miles back. Now we're on the plateau the lava built.

Off to our left, Connell — a working agricultural city of about five thousand. Franklin County begins near here, and Connell is its northern anchor. It grew as a railroad service town, then held on as the surrounding farmland intensified — center-pivot irrigation systems pulled water from the Columbia Basin Project aquifers and turned scabland into potato and hay ground. The county now has nearly a hundred thousand people, most of them down near the Tri-Cities. Up here, it thins fast. Connell is one of the places that persisted — not glamorously, but genuinely. That's its own kind of story.

Watch for a subtle change in the ground out both windows. Around milepost 1990, the bedrock description shifts from the old Neogene basalt to Quaternary alluvium — sand and gravel, geologically speaking, nearly yesterday. That transition marks us moving off the lava plateau and into the drainage zone of something catastrophic. Roughly fifteen thousand years ago, a glacial lake the size of Lake Erie — Lake Missoula, dammed by an ice lobe in present-day Idaho — burst its ice dam. The flood that followed was among the largest in the planet's known history: perhaps ten times the combined discharge of all Earth's modern rivers, roaring southwest across exactly this ground at perhaps eighty miles per hour. It happened not once but dozens of times as the ice dam reformed and failed again and again over two thousand years. The scabland channels, the coulees, the gravel bars fifty feet tall — all of it carved in days, not millennia. The sand and gravel under us right now are Missoula flood deposits. The land looks quiet. It was anything but.

We're well into Franklin County now. The land cover here runs sixty percent shrub — big sagebrush mostly, bitterbrush, rabbitbrush — with grassland filling the gaps. It's the Columbia Plateau's signature palette: silver-green sage against pale sky. The underlying geology has shifted again to younger glacial drift, Pleistocene fine and coarse alluvium, the sorted outwash of ice sheets and the great floods. Wheat and hay still grow where irrigation reaches. Where it doesn't, the shrub-steppe holds. This is the ecoregion's honest face — not farmland pretending to be something it isn't, but dryland country tolerating the presence of people rather than welcoming it.

Near this stretch of the plateau, paleontologists found the bones of three animals that lived here roughly 4.7 million years ago — early Pliocene, when the basalt floods had finished and the land was settling into something like grassland and open woodland. One was Hypolagus ringoldensis, an extinct rabbit, smaller than today's jackrabbit. Another was Nekrolagus progressus, a close relative, similarly small and fast. The third was Paenemarmota sawrockensis — an ancient marmot, something like a ground squirrel crossed with a prairie dog. All three were prey animals, quick and alert, living in the interstices of a landscape that was already drying as the Cascades rose to the west and began intercepting Pacific moisture. Their world wasn't so different from ours out this window: open ground, sparse cover, big sky. They are gone. The sagebrush is still here.

Right here — this flat, level ground — is one of the cleaner windows we'll get onto the Missoula flood geology. The deposits under us are formally named: Missoula glacial lake deposits, Pleistocene outburst flood sediments, sand and silt. Geologists can read the layers where they're exposed in cutbanks: rhythmic laminations, each one a separate flood surge, sometimes dozens of them stacked. The floods sorted the sediment by velocity — boulders dropped first, gravel next, then sand, then the finest silt settling last in slack water. That silt, the Palouse loess, blew east afterward and buried the scabland in some of Washington's most fertile soil. The violence made the farmland. That chain — flood to silt to wheat — is one of the more improbable agricultural stories in North America.

The rail line we're on descends a broad, gentle grade toward the Columbia River, which we'll meet within the next few miles. The Great Northern — James J. Hill's road, the one they called the "Empire Builder," which is also the name of this train — chose this exact corridor through eastern Washington because it offered the lowest, most practical crossing of the land between the mountains and the river. Hill was famously methodical about grades. He refused the steep climbs his competitors accepted; he sent surveyors out for years to find the gentlest possible paths. The result was a railroad that could move grain cheaply enough to undercut competitors and make the Columbia Basin farmland economically viable. The towns strung along this line — Hatton, Connell, Sagemoor ahead, Pasco just beyond — exist because Hill's engineers found a way through. The railway didn't follow settlement here. Settlement followed the railway.

Sagemoor, coming up — a named place on the map, a handful of residents, the kind of settlement that exists mostly as a postal designation and a memory of the optimism that once attached to every wide spot on a railroad line. The name is apt enough: sage and open ground, the plateau doing what it does.

To our right, West Pasco — the residential and commercial fringe that spreads west from Pasco proper. The census-designated place had 3,700 people in 2010 and 1,747 by 2020. That drop of nearly two thousand people in a decade is striking; it reflects the shifting geography of growth within the Tri-Cities metro, where Kennewick and Richland have expanded while West Pasco consolidated. But Pasco itself — the county seat, the Amtrak stop — has grown dramatically, driven by one of the fastest-growing Hispanic communities in Washington state. The city's food-processing industry drew workers; families stayed; a city changed its character in a generation. That's the Columbia Basin story in compressed form: land and labor remaking a place faster than the maps can keep up.

We're pulling into Pasco — a scheduled stop. This is where the Snake River meets the Columbia, one of the great confluences of the interior Northwest, and it made Pasco a transportation node long before the railroad arrived. The Lewis and Clark Expedition camped near this confluence in October 1805, noting the salmon runs and the Indigenous trade networks that converged here. The railroad came through in 1883 — the same year railroads imposed standard time zones on the country, rationalizing the continent into four neat bands so train schedules could be printed and trusted. Pasco became a division point: locomotives serviced, crews changed, ice loaded for the refrigerator cars moving Columbia Basin produce east. The work has changed. The junction hasn't.

As we pull out of Pasco and swing south and west, we're crossing one of the leg's great watershed thresholds. The Columbia River, which we'll be following closely now, is the fourth-largest river in North America by discharge. It drains 258,000 square miles, from the Canadian Rockies through Idaho, Oregon, Washington — a basin that encompasses six states and two countries. Everything that falls as rain or snow across that enormous reach eventually moves through the channel we're approaching. The Snake River — which we'll see joining from our left — is its largest tributary, itself running 1,080 miles from Yellowstone country. Two of the West's great arteries converging. We've been in the Columbia's watershed for much of this leg, but now we're at the river itself. The water divide that sent us here rather than toward the Missouri or the Fraser — that invisible topographic line — lies somewhere back in those basalt flats we crossed an hour ago.

There it is — to our left, the Snake River coming in from the southeast, darkly green and wide. It has traveled roughly a thousand miles to get here: born in the Yellowstone highlands, cutting the deepest canyon in North America through Idaho, forming the Oregon-Washington border for a long stretch before bending north. The Snake carries snowmelt, agricultural runoff, the water history of half the interior West. Where it meets the Columbia — just ahead — the colors sometimes differ for a short distance, the two currents holding their identities briefly before merging. Four dams step the lower Snake up in a series of slack pools; the river we're seeing here is managed, measured, contested. Salmon still try to pass. The argument about whether they can is one of the defining environmental debates of the Pacific Northwest.

Past the confluence, on our left, Finley — a community of six thousand southeast of Kennewick, on the Columbia's south bank. It sits in Benton County now, which the Columbia River demarcates along its north, south, and east boundaries — the river as county line, the oldest of administrative conventions in river country. Finley is quiet, residential, bounded by orchards and the big river. The bedrock here has shifted to open water in the geological record — we're on floodplain and river corridor, the Columbia widening behind Mcnary Dam downstream. The plateau has given way to the river's own geography. We've arrived, essentially, at the Columbia.

The shift in the land out both windows now — from the flat shrub-steppe plateau to the broader, moister river corridor — reflects a change we've been building toward across the whole segment. Back at milepost 1980 we were on Neogene basalt, the old lava surface, dry and wind-worked. By 2040 we're in open water and floodplain sediments, geologically contemporary, reshaped season by season by the river. The elevation has been falling — we've dropped several hundred feet since the plateau. The shrub is still out there, but the cottonwoods and willows have joined it along the banks, marking the water's reach. Benton County's land cover runs thirty-six percent shrub, but twenty-seven percent water — the Columbia makes that possible. The Iron Spine thesis holds here too: the railroad that brought us is following the river now, as railroads always did when a river offered the grade. Water and iron, dictating the route across the continent. We'll follow the Columbia for a good while yet.

The water beneath us right now is the Columbia. Not a river anymore, exactly — this stretch has been stilled by dams into something more like an inland sea, flat and gray-green, wide enough that the far shore barely registers. We're crossing the boundary between two counties, two kinds of country. Behind us, shrubland. The water itself is where we've been living geologically — the packet calls this section "land mostly water," and that's accurate. What we're riding over is basalt country, flooded. The same volcanic plateau that built this whole region, drowned by its own river.

The Columbia Plateau doesn't announce itself with peaks or cliffs. It arrives as a horizontal fact — a vast flood basalt province that covers roughly a hundred thousand square miles across Washington, Oregon, and Idaho. For most of its life, between about seventeen and six million years ago, the earth here kept splitting open in long fissure eruptions, not explosive volcanoes but slow, enormous lava floods that poured out layer after layer, each flow sometimes fifty feet thick, hardening into the columnar basalt you'll see cut in road and riverbank exposures from here to the Cascades. The result is a plateau built by accumulation, not by drama — geology's long patience made visible as flat-topped horizon.

Look ahead along the water. The plateau's edge is doing something subtle — it's not a cliff, it's a terrace, a step system carved where the Columbia has been cutting laterally for millions of years. The basalt we're about to ride across dates to the Miocene, roughly twelve million years old. That's younger than the fossils this region has given up: a small mole — Scapanus proceridens — and a chipmunk-like Neotamias, ground squirrels, a rabbit, all recovered from approximately nine and a half million years ago, from silts that had accumulated between lava flows. A whole warm, wooded world preserved in the intervals between eruptions.

We are, all through this stretch, in the Columbia's drainage. Every creek, every draw, every irrigation ditch is moving toward this river. It is the Pacific watershed's main trunk west of the Rockies, draining a basin the size of France. The water we've been riding beside since eastern Washington is heading the same direction we are — west — and like us, it's constrained by the topography the basalt built. The river carved this valley; the railroad found the valley and followed it; we're following the railroad. The chain is that simple, and that old.

The bedrock shifts here. What's underfoot now is the Frenchman Springs Member of the Wanapum Basalt — Miocene, right around twelve million years old. If you see any cut banks or exposed bluffs along the left side, look for the regular vertical jointing, the hexagonal columns where the lava cooled slowly and contracted. Basalt is democratic rock. It doesn't care whether it's Oregon or Washington; it poured across both without consulting the surveyors. The state line is an abstraction layered on top of continuous geology.

The Frenchman Springs lava belongs to the Columbia River Basalt Group, the most voluminous continental flood basalt province in the world for its age. But here's the layering that makes this country complicated: after the lava, came the water. Between roughly fifteen thousand and twelve thousand years ago, a glacial ice dam in what is now Montana failed repeatedly — dozens of times, possibly hundreds — releasing a lake called Glacial Lake Missoula in catastrophic pulses. Each outburst flood was, by volume, ten times the combined flow of every river on earth today. The floods raced down the Columbia drainage at speeds exceeding sixty miles an hour, stripping soil, carving coulees, depositing enormous gravel bars. The evidence is everywhere on this plateau — and we're about to roll over a deposit of it.

Right here, around milepost 2060, the geology changes to Pleistocene outburst flood deposits — gravel, boulders, silts, all scrambled together by water moving faster than a hurricane. Umatilla, Oregon sits just across the river to our left: a small city of about seven thousand, one of the oldest continuously occupied sites in the Pacific Northwest. People were living near here when the last of the Missoula floods came through. The floods would not have been survivable at ground level — but the evidence suggests human presence on the Columbia Plateau extending back at least fourteen thousand years. Some of the oldest North American archaeological sites are in this drainage. The floods erased much. Not everything.

Umatilla was platted in 1851, which puts its American founding squarely in the middle of a remarkable decade: the California Gold Rush was still burning through its peak years, the Fort Laramie Treaty had just been signed — the first formal US acknowledgment of tribal territories across the northern plains — and the Oregon Trail was at its highest traffic. Umatilla was a provisioning point for travelers moving inland. The river made it necessary; the river made it possible. The city also tells a more recent story: its population includes roughly two thousand inmates at the Two Rivers Correctional Institution, a detail that appears quietly in census data and says something unremarkable and uncomfortable about where we build things and who ends up in them.

Irrigon, across the water on the Oregon side — population just over two thousand. The name is a compound: irrigation plus Oregon, coined when the town was formally incorporated in 1957. The naming logic is honest; the whole lower Columbia basin in Oregon owes its agricultural productivity to water drawn off the river and spread across land that would otherwise support little more than sagebrush and bunch-grass. The irrigation infrastructure that made these towns viable came largely through federal projects after World War II. The name says what the town is for.

The railroad we're riding was built as part of the Great Northern system, one of James J. Hill's lines pushing northwest toward the Pacific. Hill's approach was different from most of the land-grant railroads: he built without federal land subsidies, which meant he had to build where he could actually generate traffic — through farming country, through river valleys, threading the most practical grades. The Columbia River corridor gave him what he needed: a water-level route to the coast. No summit, no spectacular pass, just the river's own patient grade-work over millions of years, handed to the engineers as a ready-made right-of-way. The stations that opened along this line in 1893 — one of the recurring threads of this whole leg — were strung like beads on the river's logic, not the railroad's ambition.

Whitcomb Island ahead in the river — a low, gravel-and-willow island the Columbia has been rearranging since the last Missoula flood pulse left raw material here. The Columbia at this stage is a managed river, but the islands still shift. River islands are negotiable geography; the political boundary here — Oregon to our left, Washington to our right — runs through water that moves. The survey lines were drawn when the river was lower, or higher, or different. The island belongs to Benton County, Washington, by the paperwork, but the river tends to disagree with paperwork on its own schedule.

Benton County, where we've been traveling since shortly past milepost 2028, has a population pushing two hundred thousand — the largest county by population along this stretch of the Columbia. Kennewick is its biggest city; Prosser is the county seat. The county's economy runs on education, health services, professional work. Wheat. Potatoes. Vegetables where the irrigation reaches. What the numbers don't show easily is the degree to which this county and the ones adjacent to it were transformed by a single federal project: the Hanford Site, just north of here, was where the plutonium for the Trinity test and the Fat Man bomb was produced. The towns of the Tri-Cities area — Kennewick, Richland, Pasco — grew overnight in the 1940s to house the workers. Richland's high school athletic teams are still called the Bombers. The mushroom cloud is still on the gym floor.

The airport visible to our left, just back from the Oregon bank, is Boardman Airport — built in 1942, which is to say built for the war. It was an Army Air Forces field, one of hundreds of strips that went up across the West as the military needed training and staging grounds clear of the crowded, foggy coasts. The remote Columbia basin was ideal: flat approaches, reliable summer weather, sparse population, and no enemy within range. The wartime infrastructure that still underlies much of the rural West is often invisible — old runways now serving crop dusters, bunkers converted to storage, roads built for convoys now carrying grain trucks. Boardman is one of the more intact examples, still functioning as a public airport, its military origins legible in the geometry.

We're approaching the edge of Benton County, about to cross into Klickitat County. The population drops sharply — from two hundred thousand to under twenty-three thousand. The land cover shifts too: from the shrub and water of Benton's lakelike Columbia reaches toward the grassland that dominates Klickitat. Named after the Klickitat people, a Sahaptin-speaking nation whose territory extended across much of south-central Washington and into Oregon, the county includes part of the Yakama Indian Reservation. The Klickitat name is one of the places where the erasure is partial — the name survived even as the political and territorial claims it encoded did not. That's a pattern on this whole leg. The word persists; the sovereignty doesn't.

Willow Creek comes in from the left — from the Oregon side, draining out of the Blue Mountains seventy-nine miles to the southeast. It's a small creek at this end, but it carries the story of the land it drains: wheat country in Morrow and Gilliam counties, dry hills, the back edge of the Columbia Plateau where elevation and distance from the river mean sparser precipitation and harder farming. The Blue Mountains themselves are ahead of us in a loose sense — we won't see them directly, but Willow Creek is their messenger, carrying Blue Mountain snowmelt down through the shrublands to the Columbia. One more tributary closing in on the main stem. One more thread of water finding the same answer: west, and down, and here.

Below us, Willow Creek slips into the Columbia from the Oregon side — a creek that's walked 79 miles out of the Blue Mountains to get here, draining 880 square miles of high desert before it quits. You'll see it as a seam of greener willows meeting the brown water. It doesn't announce itself. Neither do most of these tributaries. But each one is a drain for its own watershed, its own piece of continent, feeding the main artery we've been riding beside. The rock under our wheels right now is still Quaternary landslide debris — the plateau breaking and slumping toward the river, the same geology we've been crossing.

The basalt that built this plateau didn't flow out of a single volcano. It seeped — over millions of years, through cracks in the crust, flood after flood, each lava sheet cooling and cracking into the vertical columns you can see wherever a canyon cuts through. We're riding through the result: a landscape thickened by its own past eruptions, the river cutting downward through them, exposing the stack. The Miocene is just ahead — roughly thirteen to twenty-three million years ago, when this part of the Pacific Northwest was still being remade by fire from below.

On the right, that's Roosevelt — population 152 in the last census. Small even by these standards. What makes Roosevelt regionally notable isn't its history but its future: the Roosevelt Regional Landfill sits just outside of town, one of the largest in the country, accepting waste shipped in by rail from Seattle, Portland, Los Angeles. The trains that once carried settlers now carry garbage. The Columbia Plateau absorbs what the coast can't keep. There's a particular kind of erasure in that — a place remembered mainly for what it receives.

Across the river, low on the Oregon side — Arlington. Platted in 1885, it's a Columbia River town that's managed to persist where others haven't: port-listed, county-seat-for-a-while, now a city of 628. The Columbia is a working river, and Arlington has always been a working town, not a scenic stop. It watches the water and waits.

Around mile 2110, the bedrock shifts under us from Quaternary landslide material to Miocene volcanic rock — mafic, meaning iron-rich, dark, dense. The mafic lavas that built this part of the plateau came from the same general pulse of activity that would eventually, in episode after episode, stack basalt thousands of feet deep across the region. We're now moving through rock that solidified somewhere between five and twenty-three million years ago. The landscape doesn't look dramatically different from above, but beneath the thin soil and shrub, the bones of the land are older and more settled. The river knew this rock long before anyone named it.

The formation under us now has a name worth knowing: the Frenchman Springs Member of the Wanapum Basalt. It formed in a narrow window — roughly 13.4 to 13.1 million years ago — a single chapter in the Columbia River Basalt Group's long eruptive history. These were flood basalts: not explosive volcanoes but slow outpourings that spread across hundreds of miles. If you look at the canyon walls where the terrain breaks, you'll catch the layering — each darker band a separate flow, each one cooled and colonized and then buried by the next. Twelve million years of stacking, now read like a book cut open by the river.

The fossils from this general era — about 9.4 million years ago — are small things. A mole, Scapanus proceridens. A rabbit ancestor, Hypolagus oregonensis. A ground squirrel, Citellus shotwelli. Not the dramatic megafauna people expect from the prehistoric West. But small mammals are honest witnesses: they tell us the Miocene here was open, semi-arid, grassy — already beginning to look, in its ecology, like the shrub and grassland we're crossing now. The land remembers its own old self.

Goodnoe — ahead of us, another Klickitat County populated place that appears on maps and little else. These small concentrations of buildings along the Columbia corridor are what's left after the railroad sorted the winners and the rest. Where tracks ran and water was accessible, something stayed. Where neither favored a location, nothing did.

The Klickitat — the county, and before it the people — are woven all through this ground. The Klickitat tribe ranged widely across the Cascades and the Columbia drainage, trading as far as the coast and as far east as the Plateau. They gave their name to a river, a county, and a landscape they understood and managed for centuries before Washington Territory was organized in 1853. That organization — and the Yakama Treaty of 1855, which created the Yakama Indian Reservation that extends into this county — remade the map in a decade. What took millennia to establish was legally redrawn in a few months of treaty negotiations at the Walla Walla Council. Parts of those agreements are still being contested and honored today.

Look left — the John Day River coming in from Oregon. Two hundred and eighty-four miles long, undammed along its entire length, which makes it rare in the American West. The Cayuse people called it the Mah-Hah River. It drains the John Day Fossil Beds country to the southeast — one of the richest fossil records in North America, a place where Eocene through Pliocene mammals are stacked in the sediments. The river carried their bones in solution for millions of years before it gave up and joined the Columbia. Every tributary we pass is a story arriving from somewhere else.

We've been following the Columbia since well before this segment, and it's worth pausing on what that means for the water under us. This river gathers everything — the Snake, the Willamette, the Yakima, the John Day, the Klickitat. It drains roughly 258,000 square miles of the interior Northwest, more than any other river reaching the Pacific. The watershed is the organizing principle of the entire region: where you live, what you grow, how the railroad routed itself, what towns survived. We've been inside that drainage for hours, tracing the artery from tributary to tributary, each one adding its basin's story to the current.

Below us on the Oregon bank, Rufus — named for Rufus Carrol Wallis, an early settler, population 268 today. What Rufus is bordered by matters more than its name: the John Day Dam is right there, completed in 1971, one of four main-stem Columbia dams in this stretch. The dams are the New Deal's longest shadow. The CCC and Bureau of Reclamation were already reshaping this river in the 1930s; the main-stem dams came later but follow the same logic — tame the river, generate power, enable navigation, pay for the project with electricity rates for decades. The water we're looking at is impounded. The river that Rufus Wallis knew, and the Klickitat knew before him, ran free.

The site coming up — Wishram and Celilo — is the hardest erasure on this stretch of river, and one of the most significant on the entire journey.

Celilo Falls was not simply a waterfall. For at least 11,000 years, indigenous people — Yakama, Warm Springs, Umatilla, Nez Perce, and others — came to Celilo to fish for salmon. The falls were a natural fish trap: chinook salmon traveling upstream would mass below the drop, and fishers on wooden scaffolds above would dip-net them by the thousands. In a good year, hundreds of thousands of pounds of fish. Celilo was the oldest continuously inhabited site in North America by some measures, and arguably the most important Native American trading center west of the Rockies. Dried salmon from Celilo moved as currency across the entire plateau trade network.

The Dalles Dam was completed in March 1957. On March 10th of that year, the reservoir behind it began rising. By the morning of March 11th, Celilo Falls was gone — drowned under sixty feet of water in less than a day. Thousands of tribal members came to watch. Some wept on the banks. The fishing rights guaranteed by treaty in 1855 — the right to fish "at usual and accustomed stations" — had just had their station erased. The federal government paid restitution: $26.8 million, split among the tribes. The falls had sustained communities for longer than any civilization that had a dollar sign to put on it.

We're coming into Wishram — station stop, Klickitat County, 366 people, Columbia River. The town exists because of the railroad: Wishram was a division point for the Great Northern, later Burlington Northern, the place where crews changed and locomotives were serviced. It's one of the old railway stations opened in the 1890s, when this line was still being pushed through the gorge. The station building still stands. The town is quiet now, but the tracks through it are still very much in use — we're on them.

Just ahead of Wishram, on the Oregon side, is the site of Celilo Falls — or rather, the water where Celilo Falls used to be. There is no visible break in the river surface now. The Columbia runs flat and wide over the place where the falls roared for thousands of years. If you look and see nothing remarkable, that's exactly the point. The absence is the monument. In 2019, a study modeled what Celilo would look like if the Dalles Dam were removed: the falls would re-emerge within weeks. The rock is still there. It's just under sixty feet of reservoir. Some of the tribes have never stopped asking.

We're back in Frenchman Springs basalt as we leave Wishram behind — the same formation that carried us around mile 2120, now reappearing in the gorge walls. The Columbia River Gorge itself is a Cascade Range water gap: the river established its course before the Cascades rose, and as the mountains lifted, the river kept cutting, staying at grade. It's one of the most dramatic examples on the continent of a river that simply refused to be rerouted. The gorge is the river's insistence, written in basalt. Over the next hour or so, the terrain will gradually drop — a modest two hundred feet over a hundred and fifty miles — but the walls around us will tell a story of uplift and erosion that dwarfs any human account we've been carrying. The gorge is how the Columbia answers a mountain range. We follow it west.

Across the river to our left — that cluster of white grain elevators and low rooftops is The Dalles, Oregon. The name comes from the French voyageurs who called the narrows of the Columbia *dalles* — flat flagstones, for the basalt ledges that once choked the river here before the dams drowned them. This was the end of the Oregon Trail. Emigrants who had walked two thousand miles from Missouri arrived at this particular bend and had to decide: raft the river or haul overland. The town that grew up to service that decision was platted in 1849 — the very year California gold sent a second wave of desperate people through, and The Dalles became an inland port almost by accident.

The rock under our wheels right now is the Frenchman Springs Member of the Wanapum Basalt — a mouthful for something that poured out of the earth as a thin, fast sheet about thirteen and a half million years ago. Picture a flood of magma, not from a single volcano but from long fissures cracked open across what is now eastern Washington, spilling westward in successive waves. This particular flow traveled hundreds of miles before cooling into the dark, columnar ledges we've been reading in the canyon walls all morning.
