The Columbia River has been cutting down through those layers ever since — a river older than the gorge it carved, slowly out-pacing the rock that tried to bury it.

Now watch the canyon. The walls are pulling closer, and the basalt is giving way to something older and more irregular — Miocene volcanic mafic rock, the catch-all term geologists use for the darker, iron-rich lavas that don't fit neatly into a named flow series. We're crossing a seam in the record, though from the window it looks like one continuous wall of dark cliff.

Lyle, right window — five hundred people, a gas station, a grain elevator beside the tracks. It sits at the mouth of the Klickitat River, one of the Columbia's tributaries, and the Klickitat people for whom the county is named used these fishing grounds for thousands of years before any town existed here. The railroad arrived and a small depot went up; the depot is long gone and the town barely registered in the 2020 census. One more settlement that the iron road called into being and then mostly forgot.

We're still in Klickitat County — named after the tribe, who were themselves part of the broader Plateau culture that traded across the Cascade passes long before Lewis and Clark came through in 1805. The Columbia here is the boundary and the highway both, and for ten thousand years it was the most reliable road in the Pacific Northwest. Salmon ran this far inland in numbers the early accounts read as almost mythological — explorers describing the river surface broken by fish for miles. The Yakama Reservation begins not far to our north, and the treaty rights that reserved Columbia River fishing for the tribes are still litigated today, which tells you something about how much the fish still matter and how contested the history remains.

As we approach Bingen, notice the canyon beginning to deepen. We're sliding into the Columbia River Gorge proper — the place where the river punched through the rising Cascades rather than going around them. That's the key geological fact of everything we're about to see: the Columbia was here first. The Cascades lifted around it over millions of years, and the river just kept cutting, maintaining its grade while the mountains grew on either side. The result is the only sea-level passage through the entire Cascade Range — which is exactly why the railroad came this way, and why the Oregon Trail emigrants argued about this stretch, and why the gorge is now a National Scenic Area.

Bingen — our station stop here, right bank of the Columbia. The town sits across from Hood River, Oregon, and they share an economy now built largely on the gorge's wind. This is one of the premier windsurfing and kiteboarding destinations in North America; the geography that funnels Columbia Plateau air through the mountain gap creates a near-permanent westerly that draws athletes from around the world. But Bingen was a railroad town first — the Great Northern came through here in 1893, the same year the national economy collapsed in the Panic, which meant the line was built and then immediately starved of freight. Towns like this spent their first decade waiting for the economy to catch up to the infrastructure.

Leaving Bingen, we cross the line between Klickitat and Skamania County, and almost immediately the character of the land shifts. Klickitat was forty percent grassland — wheat and hay country, ranches running cattle on open benchlands, the dry-side economy. Skamania is sixty percent forest. We haven't crossed a state line; we've crossed a moisture divide. West of here the Cascades wring rain out of Pacific storms, and the Douglas fir and western red cedar take over. The county seat is Stevenson, a few miles ahead; the population of the whole county is barely twelve thousand people spread across a landscape of steep forested ridges and river-cut canyons.

Around mile 2190 the bedrock record takes an interesting turn — we pass over a seam of Holocene fill, which in geological terms means almost yesterday: less than twelve thousand years old, the blink since the last ice age ended. We've touched Holocene rock before on this trip, but here it has a specific story. The Missoula Floods — those catastrophic ice-dam failures in Montana that sent walls of water racing down the Columbia drainage repeatedly between fifteen and thirteen thousand years ago — deposited sediment along this corridor in quantities that still shape the valley floor. What reads as "artificial fill and modified land" on the geological survey is partly natural flood sediment and partly a century of human regrading for the highway and railroad.

Look left. This is the gorge at full scale. The walls run to four thousand feet above the river; we're threading the bottom of a canyon that cuts clean through a mountain range. The legal boundary of the Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area runs along both banks here, protecting eighty miles of this corridor — the Oregon Trail came through it, Lewis and Clark canoed it, the first transcontinental highway followed it, and now two railroads and an interstate run its length. All of that layered use in one narrow slot because there is no other sea-level way through the Cascades. Geography concentrated everything into one corridor and it's been that way since the first people walked south from the Plateau following the salmon runs.

The railroad we're riding follows the north bank; the Union Pacific's line runs the south bank through Oregon. For most of the gorge's railroad history these were competing routes — Great Northern and Northern Pacific jockeying for freight on the Washington side, Union Pacific and Southern Pacific working Oregon. The competition kept rates lower and built redundant infrastructure that served the region well enough that both lines still operate. It's one of the few places in the American West where you can watch a freight train on the opposite shore while riding a passenger train, the river between you, and understand the whole logic of the gorge in one glance.

Stevenson — county seat, right window, a city of about fifteen hundred people strung along the riverbank. The Columbia River Gorge Interpretive Center is here, and it holds what may be the largest collection of fish wheels ever assembled in a museum. Fish wheels were mechanical scoops mounted on the river that rotated with the current, dipping and lifting salmon continuously — some harvested forty tons in a day. They were banned in Washington in 1934 and Oregon in 1926, after they had helped reduce salmon runs by an order of magnitude in less than fifty years. What took ten thousand years of indigenous harvest to sustain, industrial mechanization compressed into a single generation.

The andesite flows of Stevenson Ridge run along our right — these are Miocene volcanic rocks, the same broad era as the basalt we've been riding through all segment, but andesite is slightly different in composition, higher in silica, associated with the stratovolcanoes of the Cascade arc rather than the fissure floods of the plateau. We're at the geological transition where the Columbia Plateau's flat flood basalts give way to the Cascades' more explosive volcanic architecture. That transition is why the gorge exists at all: the plateau lavas built up a relatively flat surface to the east, the Cascades rose to the west, and the river between them maintained its course by cutting down as fast as the mountains rose.

The Quaternary alluvium that lines the valley floor here — sand and gravel laid down by the river over the last two and a half million years — is some of the deepest in the gorge. Every Missoula Flood deposit, every seasonal high-water episode, every bank slump from the steep forested walls above has contributed to the material our train runs on.

Across the river to our left: Bonneville Dam, completed in 1938. The first federal dam on the Columbia, built by the Army Corps of Engineers during the Depression, it drowned the Celilo Falls — the great fishing ground where the Plateau people had gathered for salmon for at least ten thousand years. Celilo was one of the oldest continuously inhabited sites in North America. It disappeared under the reservoir in 1957 when The Dalles Dam filled. The Bonneville fish ladders are a famous engineering compromise: a way of acknowledging that the salmon runs mattered while not actually stopping the dams. The runs declined anyway. That particular negotiation between industrial ambition and ecological reality is still ongoing, right here on this river.

The last miles of our segment run through mass-wasting terrain — the geological survey calls it landslide deposits, Quaternary age, meaning the steep canyon walls have been periodically failing and slumping into the valley floor for the last two and a half million years. The gorge is geologically young and geologically unstable; the same steepness that makes it spectacular makes it prone to collapse. In 2016 the Eagle Creek fire burned a hundred thousand acres on the Oregon side; the destabilized slopes have been sliding ever since, periodically closing the Historic Columbia River Highway and requiring engineering work to keep the railroad running.

We're about to cross into Skamania County's deepest forest. The Eastern Cascades Slopes and Foothills ecoregion — which we entered around mile 2170 — is giving way now to the wetter, western side of the range, where the precipitation doubles and the forest closes in. Ahead, over the next stretch, the gorge will narrow further and the walls will go dark with Douglas fir and hemlock. The Columbia Plateau's open grassland, the shrublands we left behind us this morning, feel like a different country now. The watershed we're following empties into the Pacific, and the Pacific is pulling us toward it.

The basalt cliff rising ahead of us — Cape Horn, named by settlers who clearly felt they'd earned something — drops nearly eight hundred feet straight to the river. We're still in the Western Cascades here, landslide country. The rock under us is Quaternary mass-wasting: slopes that let go, slabs that fell, entire hillsides that gave up and slid down to the Columbia. The cliff face itself is Columbia River Basalt, lava that flooded out of fissures in eastern Washington fifteen to six million years ago and pooled here, cooling into the columnar forms you can see from the water. Geologically it's young. Humanly it's dramatic. The gorge carved it into spectacle.

We've been riding the Columbia since eastern Washington — one of the longest uninterrupted river corridors on this continent's rail network. The Columbia Gorge is the only sea-level cut through the Cascade Range, which is why the river is here, why Lewis and Clark came this way, and why the railroad followed. There's no pass to climb. The mountain range simply couldn't stop a river that had been here longer than the mountains themselves — the Columbia was flowing before the Cascades rose, and it kept cutting as the land heaved up around it. That's an antecedent river. The Cascades grew; the river stayed. We followed both.

The landscape softens here. The mass-wasting deposits give way to river alluvium — sand and gravel laid down by the Columbia in its quieter moods, the same Quaternary age, but this material was carried not fallen. Flat ground, willows at the margins, the smell of mud and open water. We're dropping toward the floodplain that separates the gorge from the cities.

Clark County, Washington, takes its name from William Clark of the Corps of Discovery — the same expedition that floated down the Columbia in 1805 and described this confluence country as rich beyond anything they'd seen in the interior. The county was organized in 1845, originally called Vancouver County, and renamed within months, which gives you a sense of how fast American administrative ambition moved through here. By the 1840s, the Hudson's Bay Company's Fort Vancouver — just across the river from where we're heading — had been the economic center of the Pacific Northwest for two decades. The British fur trade, then the American settlers, then the railroad. Each layer erased or absorbed the one before. The Chinook and Cowlitz peoples who had lived along this reach for thousands of years traded at Fort Vancouver too, briefly, before smallpox and displacement did what they always did.

The long concrete span to our left carries Interstate 205 — the freeway that bypasses Portland's downtown. Segmental bridge, finished in 1982, named for a former Oregon Transportation Commission chairman who spent his career building roads. It's the youngest major crossing of the Columbia in this corridor. We'll cross the river ourselves in a few minutes on something older and more particular to us: a railroad bridge built for trains, not cars. Worth noting the layering here — river crossing by canoe, by ferry, by rail, by bridge, by freeway — each technology superimposed on the same geography, the same constraint the Columbia imposed on anyone trying to move between Washington and Oregon.

We're crossing the Columbia now — the last crossing of this river that defined the entire western half of our journey. We entered the Columbia watershed far to the east, at the Continental Divide, and we've been inside it since. The river drains 258,000 square miles: British Columbia, Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Oregon, Washington. Everything that falls as rain or snow in that immense basin eventually finds its way here, and then to the Pacific. On the other side of this crossing, we're in Oregon. The watershed doesn't change — we're still in the Columbia's grip — but the state line matters to the humans who drew it, and in a moment we'll have crossed it.

Vancouver, Washington. One of the oldest continuously occupied sites in the Pacific Northwest — Fort Vancouver, the Hudson's Bay Company post established here in 1825, was the first significant European settlement west of the Rockies. The British ran it as a supply depot and fur trade center for twenty years before the Oregon Treaty of 1846 drew the international border at the 49th parallel and handed the region to the United States. The fort's chief factor, John McLoughlin, is called the Father of Oregon by some and a traitor by the HBC. He gave aid and supplies to American settlers who arrived destitute on the Oregon Trail. He was repaid by being stripped of his land rights. He became an American citizen and died in Oregon City in 1857. The city named for the man who mapped this coast sits just across the river, and we're about to pull into the station named for the territory he helped lose.

The Oregon Slough Railroad Bridge ahead of us — BNSF calls it Bridge 8.8 — has been swinging open for river traffic since 1908. Swing-span, through-truss design: the center section pivots on a pier to let tall vessels pass. It's older than the Interstate bridges, older than most of the infrastructure you can see from this window, and it's still the working spine of rail freight into Portland. Built the same year the Great White Fleet sailed around the world under Theodore Roosevelt. Railroads and federal ambition were both at their zenith, and this bridge was part of it — a prosaic piece of engineering that has outlasted a dozen political moments by simply doing its job.

A word for what's on the other side of this station — not geography, but ecology. We're about to enter the Willamette Valley, and it's worth knowing what that means before we leave Portland behind. The valley runs roughly 150 miles south from here, between the Coast Range on the west and the Cascades on the east. It's one of the most fertile agricultural landscapes in North America: deep alluvial soils, mild rainy winters, dry summers — a Mediterranean rhythm that produces grass seed, wine grapes, hazelnuts, hops. The Kalapuya people managed it with fire for millennia, burning the valley floor each fall to maintain the open prairie that fed the camas they harvested. Euro-American settlers arrived in the 1840s on the Oregon Trail looking exactly for this — the promised land after the desert crossing. They plowed it, drained it, planted it. The Kalapuya were removed to the Coast Reservation by 1856. The valley today is the heart of Oregon's population and agriculture both. We'll be moving through it for the next several hours, and the flatness you'll see — the extraordinary flatness — is the work of the Missoula Floods: catastrophic ice-dam releases from glacial Lake Missoula that scoured eastern Washington and deposited silt a hundred feet deep across this valley, again and again, between fifteen thousand and thirteen thousand years ago. The flatness is a flood signature. The fertility is the flood's gift.

The clock tower ahead — terracotta and brick, the hands showing the right time — has been Portland's railroad landmark since 1896. Union Station opened the year after Frederick Weyerhaeuser began buying Pacific Northwest timberland. The year the first Ford was still a decade away. This station was built in the era when the train was the only way in or out. It's still standing, still running, still ours. Notice the "Go by Train" sign on the tower as we come in. Somebody put that up with conviction and nobody has seen fit to take it down.

3.text: The train moves. Watch the platform slide away — that tangle of track fanning out behind Union Station is one of the densest rail junctions on Earth, twenty-two tracks converging where the Chicago River bends. This station opened in 1925, the same decade the automobile was already starting to eat the railroad's passenger business. But the Southwest Chief's ancestor — the Santa Fe's Super Chief — ran from this building beginning in 1936, and it ran because the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe had spent fifty years building the corridor we're about to follow all the way to Los Angeles. We're threading into that corridor now.

Cook County, Illinois — 5.2 million people, more than forty percent of the entire state — presses in on both sides as we clear the city. The bedrock under us right now is Silurian dolostone and limestone, laid down between 445 and 424 million years ago when this latitude sat near the equator and a warm, shallow tropical sea covered the interior of the continent. The fossil record from that sea is specific and strange: trilobites — Calymene celebra, Sphaerexochus romingeri — crawling the seafloor where Chicago's Loop now stands. Dolomite is limestone that's had its calcium partly replaced by magnesium, a chemical swap that happens slowly in pore water, and it's tougher than ordinary limestone — which is why the Silurian bedrock here held up under the weight of glacial ice that came later, much later, and shaped everything we're looking at above ground.

Cicero ahead — named, improbably, after the Roman orator. Founded 1867, a farming township that got absorbed into Chicago's westward sprawl. But Cicero has a second history. In 1951, when the Clarks, a Black family, moved into an apartment here, a white mob of 4,000 people rioted for four days. The Illinois governor called the National Guard. That event isn't marked anywhere you can see from this window. The brick bungalows and two-flats we're passing look like any Chicago suburb. The landscape rarely announces its deepest stories.

We're moving through what geographers call the Central Corn Belt Plains — flat, rich, terribly drained before European settlement. The flatness isn't original landscape; it's glacial legacy. The Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated from this region roughly 14,000 years ago, and in its retreat it left behind an almost featureless till plain, lake-bed silts, and meltwater channels that became today's rivers. The soil that built up afterward — dark, organic, deep — is some of the most productive agricultural land in the world. The irony is that right now, leaving Chicago, the land cover is almost entirely developed: pavement, rooftops, warehouses. The corn is coming. But here the city has buried the prairie floor under two hundred years of infrastructure.

Hinsdale approaching — one of the wealthiest villages in Illinois, founded 1873. The houses behind the manicured tree line run to several million dollars each. The Silurian rock underneath them is the same rock under the working-class neighborhoods fifteen miles east.

The gap between Hinsdale and Chicago's west side is about nine miles and, in terms of median household income, something like $50,000. Suburbs like this one were built, in part, by the railroad — the commuter rail line that runs these same tracks gave 19th-century professionals a way to live at distance from the industrial city. Every pleasant village we pass for the next twenty miles is a product of that same logic: rail enables distance, distance enables exclusion.

The land opens slightly as we push southwest. DuPage County — the collar county west of Cook — has a median household income of $107,000, the second-highest of any Illinois county. But the corridor itself is older than the suburbs. The Santa Fe Trail — the overland trade route from Independence, Missouri, to Santa Fe, New Mexico — ran its eastern branch through this general latitude, and by the 1820s and 1830s the towns along it were platting themselves onto a grid that the railroads would later follow almost exactly. Commerce likes to follow already-broken ground. The AT&SF railroad was doing the same thing in iron that ox-cart traders had done in mud forty years before.

Naperville out the left window — named for Joseph Naper, who platted the town in 1831, the same year Cook County was organized. Population today: 149,000, fourth-largest city in Illinois. DuPage River runs through it. In 1831, when Naper arrived, the land was tall-grass prairie and burr oak savanna; the Potawatomi had been pushed west only a year earlier under Andrew Jackson's Indian Removal Act. The town grew fast because it sat at a natural crossing of the river, which is exactly what towns always needed before the railroad — a ford, a bridge, a reason to stop. The railroad arrived in the 1860s, and after that the river mattered less than the track.

The geology is about to shift under us. We've been riding Silurian rock since Chicago — that tropical-sea dolostone, 430-odd million years old. Around milepost 50 the bedrock changes to the broader Paleozoic category, older and differently constituted, though the glacial drift above it continues to mask it completely. You'd have to drill to see any of this. The landscape you're looking at — the flat fields, the drainage ditches, the grain elevators on the horizon — is an entirely manufactured surface layered over geology that has almost nothing to do with the present economic uses of the land. A farmer in Kane County does not think much about the Silurian sea. But the soil fertility that makes farming here possible traces back, indirectly, through that glacial weathering of that same marine limestone.

Aurora — 180,000 people, second-largest city in Illinois after Chicago. Founded 1834, incorporated 1836. The Fox River runs through it. Aurora was one of the first American cities to use electric streetlights, in 1881, which is why it called itself "the City of Lights" before Las Vegas had any claim on that phrase. It's a manufacturing city, Kane County's economic anchor, and it sits right on the line where Chicago's metro sprawl starts to thin. Past Aurora the suburbs loosen, the fields widen, and we begin to see something that more closely resembles the agricultural Illinois this land was organized around.

Here is the chain worth tracing slowly: the Fox River valley attracted settlement in the 1830s because the river provided water power for mills. Mills attracted farmers. Farmers grew corn. Corn needed to get to market, so the railroads came — the Aurora Branch Railroad in 1850, eventually absorbed into the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy, which the AT&SF partnered with to reach Chicago. So the corridor we're riding was shaped by Fox River water power in 1834, corn economics in 1850, and railroad land grants in the 1860s. Every layer of motive deposited the next one.

Kendall County opens to our south — corn and soybeans in rotation, median income $106,000, poverty under five percent. This is prosperous agricultural Illinois. The fields look effortless. They are not. Each acre requires precision drainage, GPS-guided planting, commodity futures hedging, and federal crop insurance. The pioneer mythology of the self-sufficient farmer is not entirely wrong, but it describes about 1% of what actually happens on these fields.

Yorkville to the left — county seat of Kendall County, founded 1833 on the Fox River. Population 23,000 today, a bedroom community more than a market town. It was platted in 1836, the year the Potawatomi ceded their last Illinois lands by treaty. The timing is not coincidental — the same federal machinery that removed one people created the legal framework that allowed another to buy and register land within months.

Plano on the right — and here is a specific story. In the late 19th century the Plano Harvester Company manufactured farm implements here: reapers, binders, the machinery that made large-scale grain farming of the prairie possible. Cyrus McCormick's reaper revolution spread through companies like this one. What McCormick's reaper did for Illinois corn, John Deere's steel plow had done for Illinois soil — the native prairie sod was so dense and fibrous that cast-iron plows clogged and failed; Deere's self-scouring steel plow, invented in Grand Detour, Illinois in 1837, opened the prairie to the grain economy in a single decade. Plano was part of that machinery ecosystem. The town was platted in 1872, after the railroad arrived.

Around milepost 50 the bedrock shifts — Paleozoic sedimentary rock in the general sense gives way, and by milepost 60 we'll be over Early Ordovician sedimentary layers, 485 to 470 million years old. Ordovician means a sea even older than the Silurian one we've been riding over since Chicago — a deeper, colder past. These seas came and went in pulses over hundreds of millions of years, each one leaving carbonate sediment that compressed into rock, and the whole sequence is buried under glacial till so thoroughly that the surface tells you nothing about it. But it's there, and if you could core down through the black topsoil and the gray glacial clay and the gravel lenses, you'd hit marine limestone that remembers an ocean this continent hasn't seen in half a billion years.

The fossil record here includes Ectopistes migratorius — the passenger pigeon — dated to the Holocene, the present epoch, 11,700 years ago to now. The passenger pigeon flew these skies in flocks of billions. The last one, a female named Martha, died in the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. What the prairie and the passenger pigeon had in common was abundance beyond imagining, and what they shared was a common fate: the 1860s and 1870s, the railroad decades, were the decades that ended both.

Sandwich, Illinois — named not for the English town but almost certainly for the Earl of Sandwich, whose name had already attached to the food item by the time this town was platted in 1859. Population 7,200, split between DeKalb and Kendall counties. 1859 — the year of Pike's Peak gold rush, the year John Brown raided Harper's Ferry. While prospectors were flooding into Colorado Territory and the country was lurching toward civil war, someone was laying out town lots on the Illinois prairie and naming them after a British aristocrat's lunch.

DeKalb County ahead — and the numbers shift meaningfully. Median income drops to $68,000, poverty rises to fifteen percent. A large part of that is Northern Illinois University in DeKalb, which skews the student population into lower-income brackets. But DeKalb County is also where the prairie economy shows its seams: corn and soybeans are the crops, but the processing, the value-added work, the management — that happens in Chicago, 60 miles behind us. The collar counties closest to the city captured the wealth; the agricultural counties beyond them grew the food.

DeKalb itself has one sharp claim on American history: it is where Joseph Glidden invented barbed wire in 1874. Barbed wire ended the open range. It fenced the prairie into private parcels, made the cowboy's world impossible, and — more than any other single technology — physically realized the idea of private property on the grasslands. The great cattle drives, the Chisholm Trail, the open-range ranching economy: all of it collapsed within a decade of Glidden's patent. We'll be crossing the country those cattle trails crossed. Remember where barbed wire was born.

The fields out every window are running at their flattest now — black soil, no rise or fall, the land grid-ruled by section roads into perfect squares. Below us, the Early Ordovician seafloor we've been riding since Chicago. That layer is still here, 485 to 470 million years old, shallow tropical marine limestone, buried deep under glacial till. The glaciers ground it smooth and buried it. We're riding on the ceiling of a drowned equatorial sea. What changes now, quietly, is what the rock below us is about to become.

This part of Illinois settled in a single burst between roughly 1830 and 1860 — the same thirty years that saw the Santa Fe Trail open trade to Mexico, the Mexican-American War redraw North America's map, and the California Gold Rush pull a hundred thousand people west. The Illinois prairie filled in from the east, one county at a time, because the railroad was coming. Federal land grants financed the track-laying by selling alternating sections to settlers — a template copied across the continent for fifty years. Every small town we pass through on this leg was, in some sense, invented by that formula: platted beside the rail, named by a promoter, sold by a brochure. The corridor is older than any single town on it.

Leland appears — a water tower, a grain elevator, the flat geometry of a prairie village platted in 1857. Population under a thousand now. Founded the same year the Supreme Court handed down Dred Scott, the same year the financial Panic of 1857 collapsed land speculation across the Midwest. Timing matters in settlement history: the towns that survived were the ones that secured their railroad connection before the panic hit, before the Civil War, before the next wave passed them by. Leland got its connection. Barely.

The fossils in these fields tell a story of vanished abundance. In the till and gravel pits of LaSalle County, paleontologists have recovered Megalonyx jeffersonii — Jefferson's ground sloth — and Cervalces scotti, the stag-moose, a creature the size of a draft horse with antlers spreading wider than a car. Both about 129,000 years old, from an interglacial warm spell. Castor canadensis, the beaver, was here too, gnawing streams that no longer exist on a landscape that looked nothing like these corn rows. Jefferson himself named the ground sloth, from a cave in Virginia in 1796. He believed it might still be alive somewhere to the west and partially tasked Lewis and Clark with watching for it. They didn't find it. Its bones are here, under the corn.

Earlville, founded 1844 — pre-railroad, unusual for this stretch. It started as a stagecoach stop on a plank road before steel rail arrived. Population 1,613 at the last count, down from 1,701 a decade earlier. Small, slow contraction — the arithmetic of a farm economy that needs fewer hands each generation. LaSalle County is still two-thirds developed land, one-third cropland, but the balance keeps tipping.

One fossil in these fields earns a longer look: Bassleroceras lasallense. An orthoconic nautiloid — a straight-shelled cephalopod, maybe a foot long, jet-propelled through warm shallow water hunting trilobites — about 483 million years old. Named directly for this county. The name lasallense anchors it here, to LaSalle County, Illinois, which is a small specific thing to know about a field of soybeans. But science names things where they're found. This was found here. Its closest living relatives are the nautilus shells people collect. The animal itself is gone. Extinct before there were trees on land, before there were insects, before vertebrates had legs.

Around mile 70, the bedrock makes its first quiet shift — from Early Ordovician into the broader Paleozoic sequence. The glacial till buries it completely. But the rock matters for what's coming: over the next thirty miles, the formations below will step forward in time into something stranger and more specific — the coal-measure rocks of the Pennsylvanian Period. Illinois was once a tropical swamp. The proof is under our wheels.

Mendota — our station stop. Population seven thousand, which makes it substantial for north-central Illinois. Founded 1855, at the peak of the land-grant railroad boom. The name is Dakota Sioux — "junction" or "meeting of waters" — borrowed for its sound by settlers who were nowhere near Dakota country. That habit was common: reaching the prairie's edge, settlers lifted Indigenous place-names and planted them in the corn, reaching for the gravity of deep time. The actual deep time, of course, was already right below them.

The Santa Fe Trail — the great trading road between Missouri and Santa Fe — was the commercial artery of this corridor for sixty years before the railroad arrived. Opened in 1821, the year Mexico gained independence from Spain and welcomed American trade. The trail ran far to our southwest, through Kansas and the Raton Pass. But the economic logic it established — prairie corridor, Southwest destination, goods and people flowing west — is the same logic that built this railroad and later built Route 66. The corridor is older than any single technology. It's a geographic fact: the flat, well-watered middle of the continent funnels movement southwest. We're riding that funnel now, as every generation has.

Meanwhile, below us, the Paleozoic sequence continues its quiet rotation. Approaching milepost ninety-six, the rock shifts into something entirely new: the Carbondale Formation, Moscovian in age, roughly 310 to 307 million years old. Moscovian — named for the region around Moscow, where European geologists first precisely dated these rock boundaries in the nineteenth century. It's a stage within the Pennsylvanian Period, the Coal Age. When this rock formed, North America sat near the equator. Think Louisiana bayou, scaled to a continent. Tree ferns forty feet tall. Clubmosses. Horsetails. A steaming delta that persisted for millions of years. The Carbondale Formation is its compressed remains: shale, sandstone, limestone, and coal seams up to 350 feet thick in southern Illinois. Illinois has been burning that carbon for two centuries. The industrial Midwest was built on a tropical swamp that died 310 million years ago.

Dover off the right window — population 135. Founded 1833, one of the earliest settlements in this county. A river landing on the Illinois River, a few miles to our south. The Illinois was the original highway here: French voyageurs, then American flatboatmen, then steamboats carrying grain downstream to the Mississippi and south to New Orleans. Dover didn't fully make the transition from river to rail. The towns that did are still here. Dover is 135 people and a county road running through without ceremony.

Around mile 100, the bedrock steps back in time — to the Bashkirian Stage, 323 to 315 million years old, the opening chapter of the Pennsylvanian. Sandstone, shale, coal again. Older than the Carbondale Formation, but the same basic world: tropical delta, rising and falling sea level, swamp forest and marine incursion, over and over. What's interesting is that we're reading these layers in reverse: as the train moves west, the surface rock gets slightly older, because of the gentle westward tilt of the Illinois Basin's flank. We're not drilling down through time — we're riding across its tilted edge, like running a finger along the spine of a tilted stack of papers. The coal is always nearby. The swamp is always underfoot.

Princeton — county seat of Bureau County, our second station stop. Founded 1833, the same year as Dover. Population around 7,200. Princeton has something the other towns on this stretch mostly lack: it was an active station on the Underground Railroad in the 1840s and 1850s. Owen Lovejoy, abolitionist congressman, sheltered freedom seekers here — in a home that still stands. His brother Elijah had been murdered by a pro-slavery mob in Alton in 1837, for publishing an abolitionist newspaper. Owen made his life's work the response. Princeton sits unremarkably on the corn plain. The moral geography of the antebellum United States runs right through it.

The passenger pigeon — Ectopistes migratorius — is in the fossil record of these Illinois fields. A species that, as recently as the 1870s, darkened the sky in flocks of a billion birds. John James Audubon wrote that one flock took three days to pass overhead. They nested in the old-growth forests of the eastern half of the continent. By 1900 essentially gone from the wild. The last individual died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. Industrial-scale market hunting — shotguns, railroad delivery to Chicago's markets — combined with the clearing of the forest they depended on. The same railroad corridor we're riding now carried their carcasses east to market. The species survived the glaciers, survived twelve thousand years of the current epoch, and didn't survive the railroad economy. There is nothing out the window to mark the fact.

Buda, ahead — 482 people, Bureau County. Founded 1854, the same year Congress passed the Kansas-Nebraska Act, which reopened the question of slavery's extension into western territories and lit the fuse for the Civil War. Named for Budapest — a common habit of immigrant settlers who planted their home cities' names in Illinois corn and called it home. Bureau County's land-cover data shows 100 percent cropland. No forest, no scrub, no wetland. Pure agriculture, edge to edge.

The rock beneath us shifts one more time before we leave this segment. The Shelburn and Patoka Formations — Kasimovian in age, 307 to 305 million years old — are the closing chapter of our brief catalog of Pennsylvanian coal measures. Shale, limestone, sandstone, coal again. The Kasimovian sits just above the Moscovian in the sequence. After it comes the Permian, when the great coal swamps dried as Pangea assembled and the equatorial belt shifted. The rain stopped. The swamps died. What had been a tropical delta became desert interior. That long drying is the deeper story of the corridor we're riding — it's the reason the land out west gets harder and drier mile by mile. We're not there yet. But the coal seams below us are its prelude: the last green world before the drying began.

The elevation holds nearly flat for another 150 miles. The corn persists. The grid roads continue. But somewhere past the Mississippi, the land starts to change its mind. The rivers get shallower. The rainfall drops — not dramatically at first, just a few inches per year. The trees thin along the creek bottoms. The grass shortens. We're still in the wet heart of the continent. We're heading for its edge.

The village ahead — Neponset, population 427 — was platted in 1855, the very decade the railroads were carving their grid across northern Illinois and land speculators were naming clusters of grain elevators as if they were cities. Most of those clusters stayed small. Neponset is one of the ones that simply persisted: same corn, different combines. The Santa Fe line we're riding was the artery that gave these villages life, and we'll trace that corridor all the way to the Pacific — but right now, it's just an elevator, a water tower, and a sky that goes flat in every direction.

The AT&SF — the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe — was one of the great land-grant railroads, and it built this line across northern Illinois in the 1880s as the eastern terminus of its ambitions toward New Mexico and California. But the deeper story of this corridor predates the iron rails by sixty years.

The Santa Fe Trail opened in 1821, the year Mexico won independence from Spain and threw open its northern trade frontier. Missouri merchants immediately pushed mule trains southwest toward Santa Fe, carrying cloth, hardware, tools — the manufactured goods a remote province couldn't make — and returning with silver, furs, and mules. The trail ran roughly southwest from Independence, Missouri, and for sixty years it was one of the most consequential commercial arteries in North America. Then the railroad arrived, and in 1880 the AT&SF laid track into Santa Fe itself. Overnight, the ox-cart economy became a ghost. The trail that had taken months now took days. Towns that lived off the wagon trade withered; towns on the rail line boomed.

We're on that line now. The corridor didn't change — only the technology riding it did.

Off to our left, Kewanee — the name is Winnebago for "greater prairie-chicken," the big grouse that once boomed across these prairies in the tens of millions. The city was founded in 1854, the same decade Illinois' prairie was being turned under by the tens of thousands of steel plows John Deere had been selling since his 1837 invention in nearby Grand Detour. The prairie-chickens needed the native grass. The native grass needed the deep-rooted prairie sod. The plow broke that sod in a decade, and the birds that gave this city its name were gone from most of Illinois within a generation of its founding. Population today: 12,500. There's a certain elegiac compression in that name, if you know to listen for it.

The bedrock shifts under us right now, though you'd never guess it from the flat fields. Around mile 140 we cross from the Kasimovian formations into older Bashkirian rock — about 323 to 315 million years old — sandstone, shale, and coal laid down when this part of the continent sat near the equator, covered by shallow tropical seas and periodic coastal swamps.

Think about what that means. Every coal seam in central Illinois — and there are many, some hundreds of feet thick — is a compressed library of Pennsylvanian swamp forest. The trees that became Illinois coal were related to nothing alive today. Tree-ferns sixty feet tall. Club mosses the size of sequoias. Dragonflies with two-foot wingspans. The oxygen content of the atmosphere was higher than now, which let insects grow large, which let the forests burn easily, which created charcoal layers sometimes found between the coal seams. All of it pressed flat under the weight of the ice sheets and the rock above it, over three hundred million years.

The coal made Illinois. The coal made the railroads profitable. And the railroads made these towns.

Galva ahead — named for Gävle, Sweden, because the founders were Swedish immigrants who arrived in the 1850s. There's a quiet history here worth pausing on. Just a few miles north sits Bishop Hill, founded in 1846 by Erik Jansson's utopian commune — one of the more dramatic religious experiments in American history. Jansson believed himself a prophet; his followers sold everything in Sweden and crossed the Atlantic. Bishop Hill thrived briefly, then Jansson was shot dead in a courthouse in 1850 by a disgruntled colonist, and the commune dissolved. The survivors spread out, some to Galva, some to the farms we're passing right now. By the time the railroad came through in the 1850s, this stretch was Swedish-American country, growing the same corn and soybeans that fill these fields today. Stone outlasts everything; Bishop Hill is a state historic site now.

Here's the chain that built every town we're passing through, and the chain that left so many of them at 400 or 2,000 people instead of the 20,000 their founders imagined: the railroad land grants.

Between 1850 and 1871, Congress gave the railroads roughly 170 million acres of federal land — an area larger than Texas — on the condition that they build track. The railroads didn't just lay rail; they became the West's greatest real estate promoters. They platted towns every eight to twelve miles along the line, sold lots, published pamphlets in Swedish and German and Czech, sent agents to European ports. Settlement wasn't spontaneous. It was marketed.

The catch was that not every platted town could become a city. Population, commerce, and growth clustered at rail junctions, county seats, places with water power or coal. The rest got one elevator, one church, one saloon, and a slowly declining census. The railroad made and killed towns with the same hand. We've been watching that sorting ever since we left Chicago.

Altona, 463 people, Knox County. It exists because a farmer needed to be within a day's wagon-haul of a depot in 1870, and it persists because leaving is harder than staying when your family has been here four generations. That's the real geography of these small towns — not economic logic but inertia and attachment. The grain still moves through the elevator. The school consolidated with the next town over some years back.

Knox County, which we're moving through now, had active coal mining through the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The Bashkirian coal seams at mile 140 and the Carbondale Formation coming up near mile 160 — coal-bearing Pennsylvanian sequences, both of them — were worked by miners who were mostly Welsh and Italian and Eastern European, brought over by the same railroad promotional apparatus that brought the Swedish farmers to Galva. Different pamphlet, different language, same pitch: come west, there is work.

Galesburg ahead is the biggest city between Chicago and Kansas City on this line, and it earns that size from a specific historical moment. In 1858, Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas held one of their seven famous debates on the Knox College campus here. Douglas was defending popular sovereignty — let territories vote on slavery. Lincoln was arguing the nation could not endure half slave and half free. Ten thousand people came to listen, which was larger than Galesburg's entire population at the time. They came from fifty miles in wagons, on the same road network this railroad would replace.

Carl Sandburg was born in Galesburg in 1878, the son of a Swedish immigrant blacksmith. He grew up watching the rail workers and the labor organizers and the slow compression of prairie into cropland. The house still stands on Berrien Street, a small white cottage two blocks from the tracks.

In 2004 Maytag closed its refrigerator plant here after forty years, moving production to Mexico. Sixteen hundred jobs, gone in a year. The railroad had already consolidated its yards elsewhere over decades of mergers. Galesburg is now part of the BNSF system — Burlington Northern Santa Fe, the AT&SF's descendant. The corridor that the Lincoln-Douglas debate was partly about, the corridor that the railroad then built, the corridor that brought the factory and then took it away — it's the same corridor. All the big American arguments run forward in time until you can see where they landed.

We're slowing for Galesburg. The station here is part of the old AT&SF infrastructure — the railroad built to impress at every division point, the depot meant to say: we are staying, we are substantial, we are the future. The future reorganized and merged and consolidated. But the train still stops. Watch the platform — a few passengers will step off, a few will board carrying the particular luggage of people who've said their goodbyes.

West of Galesburg we're crossing into a new ecoregion — quietly, without announcement, but the land is beginning to tell you. The Interior River Valleys and Hills replaces the Central Corn Belt Plains we've been crossing since Chicago. The distinction: the glaciers didn't smooth this western section as completely. Rivers have had time to carve down through the till, exposing the Pennsylvanian bedrock in creek cuts and bluffs. The terrain acquires a faint roll. Woodlots follow the stream corridors. The occasional farm sits in a slight valley rather than exposed flat on the open ground.

The Interior River Valleys and Hills is a transition zone — not the tabletop-flat corn plain behind us, not the real hills ahead, but a country of gentle dissection where the glacial plain begins to drain itself into the Illinois and Mississippi systems. The watershed is still the Upper Mississippi's. But the land is beginning to articulate itself, to show some relief, to hint at the more varied country that comes once we cross the river.

That crossing is still ahead. But the gradient has already begun.

Cold Brook Township, on our right — 467 people, Warren County, established 1853. The name is the creek, Cold Brook, draining southeast toward the Illinois River. One of those invisible watershed seams runs through here. The water that fell on Galesburg an hour ago drains north and east to the Illinois and on to the Mississippi. Water falling just west of here takes longer routes, sorted into different tributaries. The watershed is not yet the Missouri's, but we're in the zone where the drainage network is sorting itself out for the long pull west. Water always knows where it's going. We're following it.

Warren County is named for Joseph Warren, the patriot-doctor killed at Bunker Hill in 1775 — which tells you that people naming these places in 1825 were still anchored emotionally to the Revolution even as they moved into a continent the Revolution had barely touched. The county seat is Monmouth, a few miles south of us, which in 1848 produced Wyatt Earp. His father Nicholas moved the family west repeatedly, chasing opportunity: Illinois to Missouri to California to Iowa and back, the classic mid-19th-century American restlessness. Wyatt ended up in Kansas, then Tombstone, then the Yukon and Alaska and finally Los Angeles, where he died in 1929. The corridor we're riding fed that westward motion for seventy years. Earp's life traced the whole arc of it, stop by stop.

There's also this, in the creek sediments and the old pond deposits of this part of Illinois: fossils of Megalonyx jeffersonii — Jefferson's ground sloth — dating to roughly 129,000 years ago. An animal the size of a large ox, with claws like curved daggers. Thomas Jefferson described the first specimens in 1797 and initially thought the claws belonged to a giant lion. He named it partly in hope it might still be alive in the unmapped interior. Lewis and Clark were partly instructed to look for one. They didn't find any. The last ground sloths in North America died roughly 10,000 years ago. Under the corn: the bones of a world entirely gone.

The fields stretching left — 100% cropland, every acre — are Warren County's essential character: corn, soybeans, hay, the same rotation running west toward the Missouri border and beyond. The county's population has held roughly flat for over a century. Agricultural productivity keeps rising — fewer farmers, more acres, larger machines — while the population drifts. The towns thin. The elevators remain. The corridor persists.

The bedrock at our feet is Morrowan now, the oldest Pennsylvanian sequence in this segment — 323 to 312 million years old — still buried, still coal-bearing, still the foundation under the agrarian surface. The Mississippi is twenty-five miles ahead. Missouri beyond that. The prairie will continue, but the river crossing changes something. It always has. Every traveler on every iteration of this corridor — the wagon freighters of the Santa Fe Trail, the AT&SF engineers, the Route 66 motorists, and now us — felt the Mississippi as a threshold. The West, in some felt sense, begins there.

The black soil out both windows is Morrowan rock in disguise — 315-million-year-old sandstone and shale and coal seams, buried under glacial till and then plowed into corn. Warren County grows nearly everything on the same few dozen feet of topsoil, beneath which the Carboniferous lies like a book nobody opens anymore. Population 16,000, spread thin across a county the size of a small city. The economics are familiar now: education, health, manufacturing filling the gaps that farming used to cover alone.

This stretch of western Illinois sits on what 19th-century Americans called the Military Tract — six million acres carved up after the War of 1812 and handed as bounties to veterans who mostly sold their claims to speculators within months of receiving them. The men who actually settled it came a decade later, Irish and German immigrants who'd watched the Erie Canal open the interior and decided to walk further west. They found a landscape that wanted to be farmed. It wanted nothing else. No timber worth cutting, no minerals near the surface, no river close enough to float goods. Just the grass, the sky, and the dark loam underneath. They stayed.

Around mile 190, the bedrock under us changes without any ceremony — the Morrowan coal measures give way to something older and stranger. We've crossed into Givetian rock, formations laid down roughly 380 million years ago, during the Middle Devonian period. That number is worth sitting with: 380 million years ago, there were no trees. The tallest plants on land were waist-high. Insects had not yet evolved wings. And here, where Illinois's western counties now grow soybeans, a shallow tropical sea spread across the continent, leaving behind what would become the New Albany Shale, the Saverton Shale, the Louisiana Limestone — formations that geologists name with the precision of archivists tracking the dead.

The New Albany Shale in particular runs deep through this region, up to 460 feet thick in southern Illinois. It's a black, organic-rich rock that would matter enormously in the 20th century: the same shales that marine organisms slowly compressed into here became, much later, the source beds for oil and natural gas. The Devonian sea built an energy economy it would never live to see.

Media, Illinois: population 121. The name alone is a kind of joke now. It was platted in the 1850s when this corridor seemed destined for something larger. It didn't grow. It didn't exactly die either — just stopped at a number it's been near ever since. There are hundreds of Medias across the Midwest, towns that named themselves hopefully and then waited for a railroad spur that arrived late or not at all.

The Tournaisian rock under us now — from around mile 200 — is Early Mississippian, laid down about 355 million years ago, just after the great Devonian extinction event that killed something like 70 percent of all marine species. The sea that deposited it was shallower and clearer than the Devonian one. Coral reefs built up. Crinoids — sea lilies, their stems jointed like stacked coins — proliferated in staggering numbers. We'll see their descendants in the rock around mile 230.

Meanwhile, above the bedrock, the human story is running its own extinction sequence. This stretch of Henderson County lost nearly a third of its population over the last 40 years. The farms got larger, the machinery got more capable, and fewer families were needed to work the same acres. The schools consolidated first, then the hardware stores, then the grain elevators. What's left is a landscape that looks productive — and is — but that sustains far fewer lives than it did in 1950.

Henderson County on our right — named for Richard Henderson, the North Carolina land speculator who tried to buy Kentucky from the Cherokee in 1775 and got Daniel Boone to blaze the Wilderness Road. Henderson's Transylvania Company was one of the earliest private attempts to commodify the American interior, and though it failed legally, the impulse stuck. The county bearing his name is small, 6,400 people, and has been shrinking since mid-century. Its seat is Oquawka, down on the Mississippi. The river made these towns; the river's commerce fading unmade them.

We're approaching the Mississippi, and the river's approach changes everything — the light, the topography, the history's density. This river was the artery. Not a metaphor: the actual circulatory system of the interior continent. Keelboats and flatboats began moving downriver commercially around 1790. The first steamboats reached St. Louis in 1817. By 1830 the river was carrying more freight than any transportation corridor in the world. The towns that sit along it — Fort Madison ahead, Nauvoo just across — grew up in that era, before the railroads arrived and made the river into something secondary.

The Santa Fe Trail, which is the through-line of this entire leg, began in 1821 at Franklin, Missouri, not far south of here. Traders loaded wagons with American manufactured goods, crossed Missouri, and returned with Mexican silver and furs. For sixty years, that trail was one of the great commercial routes of North America. What we're riding now — the Southwest Chief's rail corridor — largely parallels the logic of that same passage west, the same pull toward Santa Fe and the Pacific trade, reshaped by steel and steam.

Henderson County's pasture — that 33% that isn't cropland — begins to appear in the rougher ground near the bluffs. These are the dissected lands, ravines and hollows where the plow couldn't follow, where cattle graze on grass that looks almost unchanged from the pre-settlement prairie.

Lomax: 404 people, down from 454 in 2010. The village sits just back from the Mississippi bluffs, a place that was once part of the river-trade world and is now simply a place where people live close to something they can no longer use for commerce the way their great-grandparents could. These bluff-edge towns along the upper Mississippi are among the oldest continuously inhabited sites in Illinois — but inhabited by different peoples for almost entirely different reasons across time.

The geology under Fort Madison is catalogued simply as Paleozoic sedimentary — the broader label the maps apply when the formations are mixed and difficult to distinguish at this resolution. But what that means is: we're riding over hundreds of millions of years of accumulated sea bottom, the compressed record of oceans that existed before the Atlantic, before the Appalachians as they now stand, before anything we'd recognize as North American geography. The Mississippi itself, cutting down through all of it, has exposed those layers in the bluffs to our left. Those bluffs are a stratigraphic column you can read at highway speed.

Fort Madison on our right — the train rolls through at river level, and through the window you may catch the Mississippi itself, wide and brown and moving with a silence that belies how much freight it still carries. Fort Madison is one of the oldest American settlements in Iowa, the site of a U.S. Army fort built in 1808, just five years after the Louisiana Purchase. The fort was besieged by Sauk warriors during the War of 1812, and the American garrison burned it and escaped downriver under cover of darkness. The town built on the ruins became an important stopping point on what would become, a decade later, the main westward corridor. Population now: 10,270. Lee County below us is the only county in Iowa with two county seats — Fort Madison and Keokuk, split by enough political rivalry in the 1830s that neither would yield to the other.

We're crossing the Mississippi now, or just have crossed it, and something subtle but real has shifted. We've moved from the Illinois till plain into Iowa — and though the landscape looks the same on both sides of the river, we've entered a different watershed. The streams ahead drain to the Missouri rather than directly to the Mississippi. That's the first hint of the great reorganization coming over the next several hundred miles, where drainage basins and rainfall patterns and the very character of the land will shift us from the humid Midwest toward the arid West. Not here. Not yet. But the river behind us was the boundary.

On our left, across the river in Illinois: the bluffs above Nauvoo. This is one of the most charged pieces of American religious geography — Nauvoo, where Joseph Smith led the Latter-day Saints after expulsion from Missouri in 1838 and 1839, building a city that briefly rivaled Chicago in population. At its peak in the mid-1840s, Nauvoo had perhaps 12,000 residents. Joseph Smith was killed by a mob in 1844. The community fractured. Brigham Young led the main body west across Iowa in the winter of 1846, eventually walking to the Great Salt Lake. The city they left behind was burned. The township's population is now 963. The temple has been rebuilt, white limestone on the bluff, visible from the river. History returned to itself.

The Mexican-American War began in 1846 — the same year the Mormon exodus crossed these bluffs heading west. Two great westward movements, one voluntary, one coerced by conquest, in the same year. The continent was being reorganized at speed.

Lee County, Iowa, where Fort Madison sits, was named in 1836 — the year Clark County, Missouri, just ahead, was also organized. Both named in a two-year burst of frontier administration in the mid-1830s, as American settlement began moving across the Mississippi in earnest. Clark County, Missouri is named for William Clark himself — of Lewis and Clark — who served as Governor of Missouri Territory after the expedition, and spent his later years in St. Louis managing Indian affairs for the young republic. He died in 1838. The counties were being organized in his name while he was still alive to see it.

That expedition had crossed just north of here in 1804, heading up the Missouri. When they came back in 1806, the journey that had seemed impossibly long going west seemed almost routine returning east. Jefferson's purchase had given the country a map. The maps made the settlement feel inevitable. Whether it was inevitable is a different question — one the ghost towns along this corridor keep raising.

The bedrock changes again around here, and this one is worth noting. We've entered the Augusta Group — Burlington, Keokuk, and Warsaw formations, Osagean age, 345 to 343 million years old. Early Mississippian. The rock is limestone, dolomite, and it is extraordinarily fossiliferous — packed with the remains of crinoids, those colonial filter-feeders that carpeted the Mississippian sea floor in such abundance that entire formations are made almost entirely of their stem segments. The fossil Macrocrinus mundulus comes from exactly this age and this region. If you found a piece of this limestone on a streambank, you'd likely see the cross-sections of crinoid stems — round, with a star-shaped hollow through the center — pressed into the gray rock like coins.

The Mississippian sea that produced this rock was warm, shallow, clear — a tropical carbonate platform not unlike the Bahamas today, but stretched across the interior of North America from what is now the Gulf coast all the way up to Canada. Three hundred and forty-five million years ago, this exact spot was somewhere around the equator.

We're entering Clark County, Missouri — named for William Clark, the explorer whose route through this country helped define the idea that the West was reachable. The county organized December 16, 1836. Population now: 6,600, smaller than it's been in 150 years. The land cover shifts here — two-thirds cropland still, but a third forest creeping back in the rougher ground. The Paleozoic bedrock below continues, anonymous and vast, the compressed sea floor of ages so remote that naming them seems almost impertinent.

Ahead of us, the corridor continues southwest — toward Quincy, toward Missouri, toward the old Santa Fe Trail's eastern terminus. The land will look like this for a while longer: the flat-to-rolling Midwestern template, the big sky, the grain. But the gradients are in motion. The elevation is barely changing. The rainfall is about to start declining, almost imperceptibly, mile by mile. That's the story that will define everything we see over the next hundred miles and beyond.

Sixty-seven percent of Clark County is under crop — soybeans, corn, hay — and the fields here have been turned since the 1840s. The county was organized in December 1836 and named for William Clark, who paddled the Missouri River just south of here in 1804. By the time the county was organized Clark had been dead three years, but his name on the landscape carries the whole logic of this corridor: he came through, he mapped it, people followed. The bedrock below these fields is Paleozoic sedimentary rock, compressed seafloor from a time between 251 and 541 million years ago. The land above it has been producing grain for a century and a half.

The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway. We should introduce it properly, because we'll be riding its bones all the way to Los Angeles. The AT&SF was chartered in 1859 with an aspirational name: Atchison, Kansas to Topeka, Kansas to Santa Fe, New Mexico — three towns connected by ambition and not yet by rails. It took until 1880 to reach Santa Fe, and by then the company had already pushed on toward Albuquerque and California. What it built was the longest railroad under single management in the world at its peak — Chicago to Los Angeles, the same corridor we're traveling. The route through northeastern Missouri was assembled from earlier regional lines the AT&SF absorbed in the 1870s and 1880s. The name arrived late. The tracks were already here. And the corridor those tracks follow was already old when the railroad engineers found it: the same valleys and drainage divides that the Santa Fe Trail wagon masters had worked out in the 1820s and 1830s. The land itself defines the path. The technology changes; the line on the map barely moves.

Just ahead — a small trestle over Wade Branch, a tributary of the Fox River, bound eventually for the Des Moines and then the Mississippi. We're still firmly in the Upper Mississippi watershed. That shifts around milepost 300 — a drainage divide where the streams start running toward the Missouri River instead. It's a quiet seam, invisible from the window, but worth watching for.

The AT&SF platted towns at regular intervals along its right-of-way through the 1880s. The logic was purely practical: a farmer hauling grain to a rail elevator couldn't travel more than about six miles with a horse and wagon in a reasonable day. So the railroad spaced depots roughly every six to ten miles, and around each depot a town formed — a grain elevator, a general store, a church, a school, a blacksmith. The towns were the railroad's product. When trucks and hard-surfaced roads arrived in the twentieth century and farmers could drive twenty or thirty miles to a county seat, the intermediate depots lost their purpose. The towns stayed, but hollowed. What we're passing through is the aftermath of that arithmetic.

Left window — Medill. Population 82 at the last census. There would have been a post office once, probably a depot, a feed store. The number 82 isn't a collapse; it's a kind of stasis, the handful of families who stayed when the economic rationale for the place expired. The land here is still working — 67% of Clark County is cropland — but one operator with a modern combine works acreage that would have required a dozen families in 1900. The town shrank. The farms grew. That arithmetic plays out in every cluster of houses we'll pass for the next fifty miles.

The Santa Fe Railway understood early that it was not just in the transportation business. It was in the settlement business, and the settlement business was a form of marketing. The railroad received federal land grants — alternate sections of government land on either side of the right-of-way — for every mile of track it built. It then sold those sections to settlers, at prices that looked cheap against eastern land and the cost of getting there. The railroad dispatched agents to Germany, Scandinavia, and the American upland South. It printed brochures. It ran excursion trains for prospective buyers. Towns like Medill and Baring and Gibbs were its inventory — places manufactured to generate the freight traffic that would pay back the capital the railroad had borrowed to build the line. The genius and the ruthlessness were identical: if a town failed to produce enough business, the railroad simply passed it by. The town kept the name. The railroad moved on.

Just ahead — Railroad Lake, a reservoir in Clark County. The name is perfectly honest. Steam locomotives consumed enormous quantities of water, and the AT&SF had to supply it every thirty to forty miles along the line. Reservoirs like this one were industrial infrastructure first — the railroad's own water supply — and became fishing holes and local landmarks only after diesel locomotives made the water stops obsolete. The railroad's need for water shaped this land as surely as the farmers' need for grain.

In the limestone and shale layers under the fields we're crossing, paleontologists have found Stethacanthus — a small Devonian shark, about the size of a large salmon, with an extraordinary structure on its back: a flat platform covered in tooth-like denticles, shaped like an anvil or a shaving brush, whose purpose is still debated. It lived here around 358 million years ago, in a shallow tropical sea that covered the entire interior of North America. Laevipinna subspatulata, a brachiopod filter-feeder built like a small ribbed clam, shared the same water. Both are common in Missouri's Paleozoic exposures. That sea retreated as the continents drifted. Its floor compressed into limestone and shale. The limestone formed the gentle upland ridges; the shale eroded into the creek valleys. The valleys channeled the streams. The streams guided the wagon masters. The wagon masters established the routes. The railroad followed the routes. The highway followed the railroad. Stethacanthus is why this line runs where it runs. That is not metaphor. That is the actual chain.

Fabius — unincorporated, Knox County. The name probably comes from Quintus Fabius Maximus, the Roman general who wore Hannibal down by refusing pitched battles. Whether whoever named this village in northeast Missouri knew that history, or just liked the sound of it — can't say. Knox County itself was organized in February 1845, named for Henry Knox, Washington's Secretary of War. The Founders arrived in Missouri county names about fifty years after they died.

The land cover is shifting, slightly. Clark County was two-thirds cropland, one-third forest. Knox County is similar, but watch the tree lines along the creek bottoms. We're at roughly 750 to 800 feet elevation, and annual rainfall here is still enough — around 38 to 40 inches — to sustain corn and soybeans without irrigation. Over the next two hundred miles those numbers will fall steadily. By the time we cross into Kansas tonight, rainfall will be in the low thirties. By western Kansas, mid-twenties. By the Colorado line, under fifteen. The trees will thin to ribbons of cottonwood along the creek banks; the center-pivot irrigators will start appearing in the fields; the crops will change. The gradient is barely visible now. It won't be by morning.

Baring — population 125, Knox County. Technically incorporated, which in Missouri means it can levy a tax and maintain a fire district. Founded in the railroad era — 1886 or 1887 — which is the same founding window as nearly every community along this stretch of the AT&SF. Knox County had over 15,000 residents in 1900. It had 3,744 at the last census. The land produces more food than it ever has. It just doesn't require as many people to do it. Baring is what a town looks like when it has found the equilibrium between those two facts.

Gibbs, just ahead, was founded in 1886. That specific year keeps appearing in the records of these small Missouri towns, and it's worth understanding why. Eighteen-eighty-six was the year Geronimo surrendered to General Miles in Skeleton Canyon, Arizona, ending the Apache Wars — the last organized armed resistance to American expansion in the Southwest. The following year, 1887, three things happened in rapid succession. The Dawes Act broke tribal land holdings into individual allotments, opening the surplus for white settlement. The Interstate Commerce Act established the first federal regulation of railroad rates, born from farmers' fury at the pricing power the AT&SF and its competitors had wielded without restraint. And railroad land grants continued platting towns across the West, printing towns onto the landscape faster than settlers could fill them. Three laws, two years: one dismantling Indigenous land tenure, one regulating the railroads that were eating the profits of the farmers who depended on them, one enabling the very settlement those farmers represented. Gibbs was founded in the middle of all of it, a village of 70 people now, full of expectation then. The year a town is born tells you what kind of country it was born into.

Kenwood — unincorporated, Knox County. A cluster of farms with a shared name. The kind of place that appears on maps because someone filed the paperwork once, decades ago, and the cartographers never had reason to remove it.

Around milepost 290, the bedrock shifts. We'll roll off the ancient Paleozoic seafloor we've been crossing since we entered Missouri and onto the Cherokee Group — the Cabaniss and Krebs subgroups — Pennsylvanian rock, about 306 to 312 million years old. This matters: the Pennsylvanian is the coal age. Named for the coal-rich rock of Pennsylvania, but the formation runs through Missouri and Kansas and into Oklahoma in the same characteristic pattern — cyclic deposits of sandstone, shale, limestone, and coal. Sandstone when a river was there. Shale and coal when a tropical swamp returned. Limestone when the sea briefly flooded back in. Then the cycle repeating. The Pennsylvanian equatorial interior looked something like the modern Everglades — low, vast, hot, covered in tree ferns and giant club mosses that grew eighty feet tall and fell into the swamp and were buried. The Cherokee Group contains several workable coal seams. Not thick enough here to build a company town around, but the same rock type that would, farther south and west, fuel the Colorado Fuel and Iron empire and the company towns of Colfax County. We're touching the edge of that world.

Gibbs. Seventy people. Founded 1886 — that year again. The timing is structural, not coincidental. These small Missouri towns were incorporated into the settlement wave at the exact moment the last legal and military barriers to continental expansion were being cleared. The energy of that moment — the conviction that land was available and prices were going up and the railroad would carry your grain forever — crystallized into hundreds of places like this. Some grew into county seats. Most found a modest equilibrium and then began, slowly, to thin.

The station we're approaching at La Plata was built in 1887 as a passenger and freight depot, opened in 1888. By 1945 it had been standing for nearly sixty years and the AT&SF replaced it with what still stands — Art Deco, clean horizontal lines, the streamlined moderne that the railroad loved because it suggested speed and efficiency and the coming future. Nineteen forty-five was actually the railroads' peak for passenger traffic — the war was ending, the cars were coming back, and for one brief moment the train was still the primary way a family traveled across the country. The new station was built at the exact apex of that era and the beginning of its decline. The AT&SF understood, even then, that architecture was advertisement. Fred Harvey's hotels and restaurants along the line were famous; the stations were the same impulse. A small-town depot in Missouri got a considered design because the design was a promise about the journey ahead.

Ahead — La Plata station. Nineteen forty-five Art Deco, built by the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe to replace an 1887 original. The Southwest Chief still stops here. It was restored in the 1990s and again in 2022. Forty-five miles of small towns hollowing out behind us — Medill at 82, Baring at 125, Gibbs at 70 — and here is a building built in 1945 that still does exactly what it was built to do. The corridor absorbs the ghost towns and keeps moving. That persistence is the thing.

Just past La Plata we cross the drainage divide — the hydrological line where the streams stop running toward the Mississippi watershed and start running toward the Missouri. It's invisible from the window. The land looks exactly the same on both sides: hayfields, fence lines, a red barn. But the water is already committed to a different river system. The Missouri gathers drainage from the Rockies and the High Plains and carries it south and east to meet the Mississippi at St. Louis — it drains a far larger and drier territory than the tributaries we've been crossing all morning. In the subtlest geographic sense, we have just entered the West. Two hundred miles from now, you'll see it clearly. Right now it's only the water that knows.

The fescue out there — the grass on both sides of the right-of-way — is not native. It came from Europe in pasture-seed mixes, replacing the big bluestem and indiangrass that ran wall-to-wall across this country before the plow arrived. We're in Macon County now, organized in January 1837 and named for Nathaniel Macon, a North Carolina senator and Revolutionary War figure. Sixty-seven percent of this land is pasture. The reason is underground: the bedrock here is the Marmaton Group, Pennsylvanian limestone and shale laid down in a tropical sea three hundred and ten million years ago, laced with coal seams the surveys call "workable." That last word contains an entire economic history.

The coal and the railroad arrived at roughly the same moment in northern Missouri — the 1880s — and together they did something the Santa Fe Trail's ox-cart era never managed: they fixed the settlement pattern in place. The Trail ran from 1821 to 1880, and it moved goods and people across the continent, but it didn't anchor towns. A trail can shift a mile in a wet season. The locomotive drove iron stakes into the geography and declared: here. Every eight or ten miles — a day-trip distance for a farmer hauling grain — the Santa Fe platted a siding, a water tower, a grain platform, and called it a town.

The coal added a second draw. The Marmaton seams were thin and discontinuous — the geological surveys hedged with phrases like "some workable" — but in the promotional literature of the 1880s, that ambiguity disappeared. Mining companies sank shafts. Miners moved their families in. Boarding houses and company stores appeared. For one generation, these small Missouri towns had a double economy: farm trade and mine. Then the beds played out, one after another, through the 1890s and into the early 1900s. The farms stayed. The miners left. What remained was a town built for a population it no longer had.

Elmer: fifty-one people, down from eighty a decade ago. The grain elevator, a handful of houses, the right-of-way. It never grew into anything the railroad hadn't already assigned it — a service stop, a platform, a name on a schedule. It persists. It just persists smaller every census, each count trimming a little more off the original promise.

The pasture on both sides is not laziness. Macon County sits on tight Pennsylvanian claypan — the same impermeable shale that underlies the limestone — and in wet years the water sits on the surface rather than draining.
