The fossils shift with the rock: hadrosaur trackways are found in these strata, the broad three-toed prints of duck-billed dinosaurs walking the coastal margins of the Cretaceous sea. Also shark teeth — Squalicorax falcatus, a crow shark, not a giant but a persistent, opportunistic predator. The sea was full of them.

But let's talk about what the Santa Fe Railway did with this landscape once it arrived. By the 1880s, the AT&SF had a problem: it had land grants to sell, towns to fill, and a West that prospective settlers found threatening rather than welcoming. The solution was Fred Harvey and a deliberate, systematic act of image-making. Harvey Houses — restaurants, hotels, hospitality — went up at regular intervals along the line, including through New Mexico. They were impeccably clean, staffed by "Harvey Girls," the company's famously recruited and trained waitresses, and they served real food on real china at standardized prices. The message was: the frontier is civilized now. You can bring your family here. It's safe to come. This was marketing operating as infrastructure. The railroad didn't just move people west — it manufactured a version of the West that was easier to move toward.

Valmora — founded 1916, still technically on the map. It began as a tuberculosis sanatorium: the high, dry New Mexico air was prescribed for respiratory patients in the early twentieth century, and several sanatoria opened in this region during that era. Patients came from the humid East and Midwest, hoping the altitude and aridity would heal their lungs. The AT&SF ran advertisements explicitly promoting New Mexico air as medicine. They weren't wrong, exactly — the altitude and low humidity genuinely helped, in the era before antibiotics. The railroad sold the landscape as a health product. Some of those patients stayed after they recovered. A few of those who couldn't leave became the founders of small New Mexico communities, which is an unusual way to settle a place.

The land cover shift since Wagon Mound has been real and visible: less grass, more shrub — four-wing saltbush, snakeweed, the occasional juniper gaining ground on the higher slopes. This is the Upper Canadian Plateau tipping gradually toward the plant community that will dominate in the piñon-juniper woodland of the Southern Rockies ecoregion, which we'll enter around milepost 1250. The shrubs aren't a sign of degraded land. They're the native flora. Grass is the anomaly here, possible only where enough moisture falls or where the soil holds water between rains.

Watrous, population 99. Small now, but historically a genuine crossroads. The Santa Fe Trail forked, and the two branches — the Mountain Branch through Raton Pass, which we've been following, and the Cimarron Cutoff, the faster but waterless shortcut — rejoined here at Watrous, at the confluence of the Mora and Sapello rivers. Samuel Watrous arrived in 1849, built a trading post, and for two decades supplied the wagon trains and the nearby Fort Union garrison. Fort Union, a few miles east, was the largest military fort in the Southwest, the supply depot for the entire New Mexico Territory. The army built it in 1851; it was abandoned in 1891. The fort made Watrous; the railroad made Fort Union unnecessary; and Watrous became 99 people and a post office. The corridor moved on; the infrastructure that served the corridor didn't survive the move.

Fort Union's ruins are just out of sight to our east as we pass Watrous — the largest ruins of a nineteenth-century American military fort in the Southwest, three successive forts on the same ground, the last one closed in 1891. It was built here because the Trail was here. It was abandoned here because the railroad made it unnecessary. The army no longer needed a massive depot to supply overland wagon supply chains once those supply chains could move by rail, faster, in greater volume, in all weathers. Fort Union is what supporting infrastructure looks like when the thing it supported has been superseded. The adobe walls dissolved slowly back into the earth once maintenance stopped, and the prairie began to reclaim them.

We're climbing now — gradually, not steeply, but the grade is real. The summit near milepost 1200 tops out around 6,700 feet, and on the other side of it the bedrock shifts to Triassic sedimentary rock — 200 to 252 million years old, laid down before the dinosaurs reached their full diversity, in the early chapters of the age of reptiles. And the water that falls on the far side of that low rise will no longer find its way to the Arkansas and the Mississippi and the Gulf. It will find the Rio Grande instead, and run south through the heart of New Mexico, past Albuquerque and El Paso and into the Chihuahuan Desert, making it to the Gulf of Mexico — or not, depending on the drought.

We're about to cross a continental divide — not the famous one in Colorado, but a quiet, real one. The watershed beneath us is about to change.

We've just crested it — 6,703 feet, the high point of this stretch — and the train begins its long lean downhill. You won't feel it so much as see it: the sagebrush thickening at the shoulders of the right-of-way, the grass shortening, the soil paling. We've been riding the Southwestern Tablelands since well back, that high dry tableland of shortgrass and pasture. Now the land shifts its register. Over the next ninety miles we'll shed nearly 1,800 feet, and the land will spend every one of them getting drier, scrubbing away the grass until shrub dominates. Water is doing the accounting.

The Santa Fe Trail crossed this same ridge. Wagon freighters in the 1840s read this break in the terrain the way the railroad's surveyors did thirty years later — it's the lowest negotiable gap for hundreds of miles in either direction. Topography doesn't care whether the wheels are iron-rimmed or steel-flanged. The route was always here, waiting.

Off to our left, a small airstrip — Las Vegas Municipal Airport, five miles northeast of town. Worth a glance because it illustrates what every new transport technology does out here: it lands right beside the old one. The trail came first, then the rail, then the highway, then the airfield, each generation of corridor stacking on top of the geography that forced them all to the same gap. The strip is quiet most days. The train is not.

Las Vegas, New Mexico is not the Las Vegas anyone's thinking of. It predates Nevada's city by about a century, founded as a Spanish colonial plaza in 1835, and by the time the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe laid tracks through in 1879 it was already a going town — which made it unusual. The railroad usually made the towns; here the town was already made. What the AT&SF added was the machine that would sell it. The Fred Harvey Company set up its first New Mexico operation right here, importing uniformed waitresses — the "Harvey Girls" — to serve meals on white linen to passengers who twenty minutes earlier had been breathing cinders on the train. It was a calculated act of civilization-manufacture, and it worked: the railroad wasn't just moving freight, it was selling an experience, a story, a West that was romantic and manageable and safe enough for a family from Chicago.

Watch ahead and to the left as we pull into Las Vegas — the long Moorish-Mission facade, the red tile roof, the covered portal: the Castañeda Hotel, built 1898–1899 by the AT&SF and operated by Fred Harvey until 1948. It's one of the great set pieces of the Harvey system. President Theodore Roosevelt spoke from its platform on a whistle-stop tour. For decades it was the physical proof of the railroad's argument: that the raw West had been domesticated, that you could step off the train into a gracious hotel and eat a proper meal and feel the distance collapse. Then the automobile arrived, Route 66 pulled the traffic away, and the Castañeda went dark for half a century. It reopened as a hotel again in 2019. The building outlasted two transportation eras; it may outlast a third.

Las Vegas station is one of the more intact AT&SF depots left in New Mexico — brick, solid, still in use by Amtrak three times a week in each direction. The town around it has the particular texture of a place that had one very good era and has been managing the memory ever since. Victorian storefronts on the plaza, a state university, and a poverty rate running above twenty-three percent. The railroad built it; the highway era quietly redirected the energy elsewhere.

The bedrock underneath us has just switched character — the Triassic red beds give way to Early Cretaceous sedimentary rock, about 145 to 100 million years old. In the Cretaceous, a shallow inland sea — the Western Interior Seaway — covered much of what is now the middle of North America, lapping across the lowlands from the Gulf to the Arctic. These layers are the seafloor of that vanished ocean. We're riding over marine mud, compressed. The sea is long gone; the aridity gradient we're descending is, in a way, its permanent ghost.

The Cretaceous sea matters to the corridor story more than it might seem. When the seaway retreated and the Rockies began pushing up to the west — the Laramide orogeny, roughly 70 to 50 million years ago — the drainage patterns that formed became the channels that humans would follow. Rivers run off young mountains; trails follow rivers; railroads follow trails. The geographic logic goes all the way back to that Cretaceous seafloor tilting up and shedding water eastward.

The community of Romero slips past — a handful of structures, a name on the map. There are dozens of these along the old AT&SF right-of-way. Some were section-house communities — railroad workers' housing at regular intervals, spaced by how far a maintenance crew could walk to a breakdown. When the railroad mechanized its track maintenance in the mid-twentieth century, the section houses emptied. The names stayed.

Here's the chain the land keeps repeating: geology sets the terms — water, or the lack of it, soil depth, elevation; those terms determine what you can grow or graze; what you can grow or graze determines whether a settlement survives or fades; and then one more variable, always: whether the railroad wanted to stop. The AT&SF had enormous power over which communities lived. A depot meant a grain elevator, a general store, eventually a school. No depot meant slow strangulation. The railroad land grants gave the company every other section of land along its right-of-way — it was literally in the corporation's interest to build towns, fill them with customers, and keep them alive as markets. When a town stopped being profitable, the railroad found reasons to pass it by. The Santa Fe Trail had done the same thing a generation earlier, simply by the route its freighters chose. The corridor chooses the survivors.

The rock under the wheels has shifted again, and this one deserves a moment. We're now on the San Andres Formation — limestone and dolostone, with some shale, laid down roughly 275 to 273 million years ago in the Artinskian stage of the early Permian. This is the first time we've hit Artinskian rock on our journey. Artinskian is a name for a precise slice of geologic time, when shallow tropical seas covered this part of North America — warm, clear, teeming with marine invertebrates. The limestone you see in outcrops along these cuts is their compressed remains: shells, reef debris, the calcareous mud of a seafloor that sat at roughly the latitude of the modern Bahamas. We were a very different planet. The Appalachians were higher than the Alps. The supercontinent Pangea was just beginning to assemble. And here we are on its ancient seafloor, heading west.

Limestone matters to the water story in a specific way: it dissolves. Rainwater, slightly acidic, eats through calcium carbonate over geological time and opens caves, sinkholes, and underground channels — karst terrain. The Permian limestone belt of eastern New Mexico is riddled with it; Carlsbad Caverns, a few hundred miles south, is carved from a slightly different Permian reef formation. Up here the karst is subtler, more likely to show up as a dry arroyo that vanishes into the ground than as a spectacular cave. Water in karst country is never quite where you expect it. Early settlers on this terrain learned that lesson at cost.

Chapelle — another dot on the map, ahead and passing. In the 1880s and 1890s, these small communities along the railroad were platted fast, populated with optimism, sometimes dying within a decade. The ones that survived usually had a water source the others lacked, or a family with enough capital to hold through the dry years, or the luck of being on the right side of a county seat decision.

Bernal — named for Eric Bernal of Las Cruces, an unincorporated community that has been here long enough to accumulate a name and little more. This is Hispanic New Mexico at its oldest and thinnest: land-grant families who preceded the railroad by two or three generations, whose farms and ranchos were already in place when the AT&SF surveyors came through in the 1870s. The railroad didn't create these communities; it arrived among them. Sometimes that meant prosperity; often it meant displacement as the Anglo commercial economy moved in alongside.

The Pecos River is beginning to orient the landscape to our south and west. Ribera, ahead, sits at its bank. The Pecos drains a long arc of the southern Rockies and the Sangre de Cristo range — it's the water system that made the Pueblo cultures viable in this otherwise arid country, and later made Spanish colonial ranching possible, and later still anchored Anglo cattle operations. Every corridor eventually leads to water. The Santa Fe Trail used springs and creek crossings the way a climber uses handholds. The railroad had to have water too — steam locomotives consumed thousands of gallons per day — so the AT&SF sited water tanks at regular intervals, and the water-tank stops often became towns.

Below the Artinskian limestone we've just passed, the rock shifts again to Pennsylvanian formations — sandstone, limestone, dolostone laid down 315 to 300 million years ago. We encountered Pennsylvanian rock earlier on this leg, back around milepost 600; it re-emerges from under the younger Permian cover here. The fossils collected from these outcrops include foraminifera — single-celled marine creatures called Ivanovia and Bradyina — their tiny calcite shells smaller than a grain of rice, preserved in the limestone through 315 million years. They traveled with the rock from sea bottom to mesa top and they are still there, if you know how to slice and polish the stone thin enough to see them.

Ribera — at the foot of Rowe Mesa, along the Pecos River. The mesa face is visible to our west: flat-topped, that resistant caprock holding up a platform while softer rock erodes beneath it. The Pecos below is modest in June by most measures, but in this country modest is enough. We're at the threshold of the Southern Rockies ecoregion now, the land gathering itself. The vegetation has been shifting for the last twenty miles — the open sagebrush of the tableland giving way to scattered juniper, the first real trees in a while, drawing their livelihood from slightly more moisture caught against the foothills.

The Pecos Valley attracted a particular kind of attention in the 1880s and 1890s from the AT&SF. The railroad marketed this landscape as health country. Dry air, high altitude, abundant sunshine — the prescription, according to late-Victorian medicine, for tuberculosis, which they called consumption. The Santa Fe Railway ran advertisements in eastern newspapers promising cure-seekers a land of healing air.

It wasn't fraudulent, exactly. Dry altitude does reduce the bacterial load in damp, crowded lungs. Thousands came. Some recovered; many didn't. But the influx of health-seekers, artists, and writers who arrived in New Mexico on AT&SF trains in the 1880s through 1910s became the seed of what we now think of as Southwestern culture as an exported commodity — adobe architecture, Navajo rugs, Pueblo pottery, all of it filtered through the aesthetic sensibility of people who came by train from Philadelphia and stayed. The Harvey Company commissioned murals. The railroad ran excursions to Pueblo villages. The West was not just being settled; it was being curated.

Ilfeld — named for Charles Ilfeld, a German-born merchant who arrived in New Mexico in 1865 and built one of the most extensive wholesale trading networks in the region. Ilfeld's company, headquartered in Las Vegas, supplied dry goods, hardware, and food to ranchers, miners, and settlers across northeastern New Mexico for decades. He was exactly the figure the railroad depended on: a commercial distributor who took the freight off the train and moved it into the interior by wagon. The community bearing his name sits along Interstate 25's frontage road today — the highway layered over the wagon road layered over the trail.

The Southern Rockies ecoregion begins somewhere in the next few miles. The boundary is ecological rather than geological, defined by vegetation and climate bands rather than a line on a rock map. But you can feel the change coming. The shrubland is breaking toward juniper-piñon woodland. The horizon ahead is more vertical. The mesas are giving way to the first long ridges of the foothills, and behind those ridges the Sangre de Cristo Mountains — the southernmost chain of the Rockies — are rising toward twelve and thirteen thousand feet.

Sangre de Cristo. Blood of Christ. The Spanish named these peaks for the red light that settles on them at dusk — the same alpenglow that turns the granite pink at sunset on every high range in the West. The naming happened in the early colonial period, when missionaries and soldiers were moving north out of Mexico City's viceroyalty into country no European had mapped. They were following the Rio Grande north, just as we have been following the trace of the Santa Fe Trail. The same corridor, two centuries apart.

Rowe — a small census-designated place on our right, 304 residents as of 2020. The Pecos River is close; Rowe Mesa rises to the south. This is exactly the topography — flat-topped mesa, river drainage below, a small community at the junction — that repeats itself through San Miguel County like a theme with variations. Each version of the pattern has a different name, a different founding family, a different moment when the train stopped or didn't stop and made the difference between growth and stagnation.

The Glorieta Pass is just ahead — and it is the reason the Southwest Chief exists, why the Santa Fe Trail went where it did, why this town or that one got a depot and another didn't. Glorieta is the lowest negotiable crossing of the Sangre de Cristo range, the seam in the mountains that allowed a through route from the plains to the Rio Grande valley. In March 1862, during the Civil War, a Confederate force driving up from Texas toward the Colorado goldfields was turned back here in three days of fighting. Control of the pass meant control of the corridor; losing the pass meant the Confederacy's western campaign collapsed. The AT&SF surveyors who came through in the 1870s were following the same logic the armies had: there was simply no other way through. We are about to go where everyone who needed to cross these mountains has always gone.

The rock under our wheels right now was mud at the bottom of a shallow inland sea — Pennsylvanian, then Permian — two hundred and seventy million years old, give or take. Sandstone, limestone, dolostone, and chert all mixed together in the same beds. You can see it in the cuts: that pale, buff-colored banding on the cliff faces to either side. We're still high, just over seven thousand feet, and the canyon is narrowing as we climb toward Glorieta Pass. This is the hinge of the whole journey west. Every mode of transport that ever crossed New Mexico used some version of this gap.

Glorieta Pass sits at around 7,500 feet — not dramatic by Colorado standards, but it was the key that unlocked the Southwest. The Santa Fe Trail wagons ground through here in the 1820s, the first American commercial caravans to reach New Mexico after Mexico opened its borders to trade. Then the U.S. Army in 1846, Kearny's Army of the West, marching this exact route to claim New Mexico in the Mexican-American War without firing a significant shot. Then Confederate troops in 1862, trying to seize the West for the South, and the Union forces who stopped them right here at what some called the Gettysburg of the West — a two-day engagement in this narrow canyon that ended Confederate dreams of reaching Colorado's gold. And then the railroad itself, the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe, threading through in 1880 along almost the same grades the wagons had worn. One corridor, one mountain notch, six decades of history compressed into a few miles of canyon.

The small cluster of buildings to our right — that's Glorieta, population just over five hundred. A quiet place now, a scattering of homes in the piñon and juniper. But stand on the hillsides east of here and you're walking the ground where, in late March 1862, Federal troops from Colorado surprised a Confederate supply train and burned eighty wagons of ammunition, food, and medicine. Without supplies, the Confederate force had to retreat all the way back to Texas. The Southwest stayed in Union hands. Today's Glorieta has no particular marker you'd see from the train — just the canyon, the trees, the same geography that made it matter.

Watch what happens to the vegetation as we come down off the pass. We're dropping — not fast, but steadily — and as we lose elevation, the moisture thins. Up high, you had ponderosa pine, Douglas fir tucked into the north-facing slopes. Now it's piñon and juniper doing the work. These two species are the signature of the Colorado Plateau's lower flanks: drought-tolerant, slow-growing, adapted to places where ten or twelve inches of rain a year is a good year. Piñon nuts were a staple food for Pueblo people for millennia. Both trees smell extraordinary in the rain — but rain here is a negotiation, not a given. The land cover data tells the story bluntly: eighty-six percent of Santa Fe County is shrub. That's the aridity speaking.

Cañada de los Alamos — the canyon of the cottonwoods. A census-designated place of about four hundred and twenty people tucked into a draw to the right. The cottonwoods it's named for would follow a seasonal stream: in the arid Southwest, cottonwood groves are water indicators, the way a green smear on a topo map tells you where to dig. Spanish settlers reading this landscape four centuries ago named what they saw with precision. A cañada is a small canyon or drainage. The alamos are the trees that proved water was there.

Here is the story of Lamy, which is coming up at milepost 1274, and it's one of the purest examples of how the railroad made and unmade the Southwest's towns. Santa Fe was the destination — had been the destination since the 1820s, the end of the trail, the seat of New Mexico's government, a city of genuine antiquity. But when the AT&SF surveyed its route in 1879 and 1880, the grades into Santa Fe itself were too steep for practical operations. The engineers solved the problem by not going there. They laid the main line through a flat valley eighteen miles southeast of the city, created a junction depot, named it after the Archbishop of Santa Fe — Jean-Baptiste Lamy, a French-born prelate who had spent decades building Catholic institutions across New Mexico — and that was it. If you wanted to reach the capital, you took a branch-line spur. The railroad didn't bend to the city. The city bent to the railroad.

The Fred Harvey Company opened a hotel at Lamy — the El Ortiz, small but elegant — because Harvey understood that every junction was a meal stop, and every meal stop was a revenue opportunity and a civilizing gesture. Harvey Houses were famous for linen tablecloths, china, trained waitresses in a landscape where the alternative was cold beans in a tin plate. They were also, deliberately, a marketing device: the Santa Fe Railway and Fred Harvey together were selling not just passage but an experience. The romantic Southwest, the ancient culture, the sun-drenched difference from the industrial East. El Ortiz closed in 1938. The depot still stands.

We're at Lamy — our scheduled stop here. The depot to your right is Mission Revival: adobe-colored stucco, tile roof, arched windows. It's a design choice, not an accident. The railway's architects were deliberately invoking Spanish colonial New Mexico, making the built environment match the romance they were selling to Eastern passengers. The Harvey Company understood that the package — the food, the hotels, the curio shops, the Pueblo pottery and Navajo rugs on display — had to feel coherent. They hired ethnographers. They commissioned murals. They curated the Southwest for consumption by people who would otherwise never come here. Santa Fe is eighteen miles to the northwest. The branch line connects them. Most passengers today still can't go there by train.

The bedrock is changing under us now — the formations shift around milepost 1270 from those ancient Pennsylvanian and Permian rocks into Triassic sedimentary layers. The Triassic opened about 252 million years ago, right after the largest mass extinction in Earth's history — the end-Permian event that killed perhaps ninety percent of marine species. The fossils the record flags for near this stretch include Brachyphyllum comancheanum — a conifer, a Triassic tree — and two cone-bearing plants, Masculostrobus and Alostrobus, from about 237 million years ago. That's what was growing in a humid river floodplain where New Mexico now stands, before the land dried, before the Rockies rose, before any of the human history we've been tracing had a planet to happen on.

Off to the left: Galisteo, population two hundred and fifty. Named after the Galisteo Pueblo, a Towa-speaking community that was here long before the Spanish arrived — a large pueblo, perhaps two thousand people at its peak, abandoned in the early eighteenth century after a series of raids and epidemics. The modern census-designated place carries the name forward. It's one of dozens of cases in New Mexico where you're standing on or near a ruin of something that preceded the European encounter by centuries, and the current settlement is a ghost of a ghost. The Santa Fe Trail passed through here. Spanish missionaries built a church. The pueblo is now an archaeological site. The village holds on at a few hundred residents.

Around milepost 1280, we're crossing quietly into a different ecological zone — the Arizona and New Mexico Plateau ecoregion. The Plateau is vast, stretching across most of New Mexico and Arizona at middle elevations, and it's defined above all by aridity and by the way that aridity shapes the biological community. Fewer trees, more open shrubland. Grasses that evolved under low rainfall. The sense of space widens because the vegetation can't get tall enough to close it in. The Rio Grande drainage, which we're working toward, is the organizing fact of life here — not because it's a generous river by eastern standards, but because in this country any permanent water is everything. Settlements cluster on it. Agriculture happens near it. The Rio Grande gave the Pueblo world its spine.

The geology makes another jump here — and this one is a genuine time warp. Sixty-six to thirty-four million years ago: Paleocene, the epoch right after the extinction that killed the non-avian dinosaurs. What we're crossing is the Diamond Tail Formation — yellow, orange, and gray coarse-grained sandstones, crossbedded, layered with purplish-brown and maroon mudstones. These rocks were river and floodplain sediments deposited while the land was reorganizing after the Cretaceous ended, the Rockies rising and shedding material eastward. The fossils from this era found nearby include Hyopsodus powellianus and Homogalax protapirinus — small, early hoofed mammals, close to the base of the lineages that would eventually become horses and tapirs. The world was starting over. Again.

La Bajada — coming up to the right around milepost 1300 — gives its name to a geographical feature that was one of the most significant barriers on the road between Santa Fe and Albuquerque. La Bajada Mesa is an escarpment, a basalt-capped bench that drops sharply to the lower Rio Grande basin. The descent was notoriously difficult for wagons on El Camino Real, the Royal Road that ran from Mexico City to Santa Fe for two and a half centuries before the Santa Fe Trail. Carts had to be lowered by rope in places. The railroad avoided it by taking a longer route around. Route 66 later had to deal with it too. The escarpment is still there: that dark horizontal line on the mesa edge to the southwest is basalt that poured out and froze while early mammals were finding their footing on a post-Cretaceous Earth.

Population twenty-six. The census found twenty-six people living at La Bajada in 2020, at a place whose escarpment was a major logistical obstacle for every transport technology from Spanish colonial ox-carts to mid-century automobiles. The mesa is named for the difficulty of passing it. The bedrock here transitions to Cenozoic sedimentary — Miocene age, roughly twenty-three million years to recent. Miocene is when the Basin and Range province began its stretching and faulting across the Southwest: the land pulling apart, creating the alternating ridges and valleys that give the region its character. The Rio Grande Rift — the great tear in the continent's crust that the river occupies — was actively widening in the Miocene. That's why the valley ahead of us looks the way it does: wide, flat-floored, flanked by fault-block mountains. The river didn't carve the valley. The land opened and the river moved in.

The Rio Grande Rift is one of the continent's active features — not dormant geology but an ongoing event. The crust here is being pulled east and west simultaneously, thinning in the middle, producing volcanism along the rift margins. The Jemez Mountains to the northwest sit over a supervolcanic caldera that last erupted about 1.25 million years ago in a cataclysm that spread ash across a significant fraction of North America. The Valle Grande caldera left a depression twelve miles across. The Pueblo people who built their towns in the Jemez River valley lived on the flanks of a volcano, knew the hot springs, used the obsidian that the volcanic geology produced. Obsidian tools from the Jemez sources have been found at archaeological sites hundreds of miles away. The geology here was not background. It was trade goods, it was medicine, it was sacred geography.

Domingo — a populated place ahead of us in Sandoval County, on the old AT&SF main line. A junction point, named for a nearby pueblo. The railroad created small service communities like this across New Mexico wherever it needed water towers, section gang housing, or freight loading. Many are barely there now, or entirely gone — names on maps that reference a function the railroad no longer performs. The pattern repeats across every mile of this corridor: the railroad draws the line on the map, the town exists because of that line, the traffic changes, and the town recedes toward its original desert emptiness.

Sandoval County — which we're entering now — has a county seat at Bernalillo, on the Rio Grande. Bernalillo is old: Spanish settlers established themselves here in the 1690s, near a cluster of Pueblo communities that had been on the river for centuries before that. When the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 drove the Spanish out of New Mexico — the most successful Indigenous uprising in North American history, killing four hundred colonists and clergy and pushing the rest to El Paso — Bernalillo was abandoned. The Spanish returned under Diego de Vargas, and Bernalillo was resettled. It's one of the oldest continuously occupied European settlements in what's now the United States, and it sits beside one of the oldest continuously occupied Indigenous landscapes on the continent. The river made it possible. The river is why there's a human history here at all.

We're crossing the Rio Grande's floodplain deposits now — Holocene, meaning the last eleven thousand years or so. The geology is as young as geology gets: unconsolidated coarse sand, round pebble gravel, thin lenses of silt and clay. These are the river's own leavings, material it's carrying down from the Rockies and setting aside every time it floods. The Rio Grande here is braided and shifting, bounded by cottonwood and tamarisk on its banks, running olive-green or muddy depending on the upstream snowpack. For everything living on this plateau, it is the whole world.

Albuquerque is close now — a few miles downstream on the Rio Grande, the largest city in New Mexico. The AT&SF reached it in 1880, the same year it came through Glorieta Pass, and the effect was immediate: the old town of Albuquerque, which had stood on the river since 1706, was eclipsed by New Albuquerque, platted next to the depot. The railroad didn't go to the existing town; it created a new one beside itself and let the old one either adapt or fade. The Fred Harvey Company built the Alvarado Hotel right next to the tracks — one of the showpiece Harvey Houses. The Alvarado is gone now, demolished in 1970. The depot still operates. We've been on this corridor for a thousand miles, and the corridor still holds: the same groove that ox-carts cut, that rails formalized, that the highway paved, and that this train still follows.

The Rio Grande is just off our left now — you can't quite see it through the cottonwood breaks, but the trees give it away. That line of dark green is the bosque, the riverside woodland that has drawn people here for ten thousand years. Chical is barely a name on the map ahead, one of dozens of small settlements strung along this valley like beads on a thread. The thread is water. Here in the middle Río Grande corridor, at just over five thousand feet, the river is the only reason there's a town at any of these mileposts — the only reason there's been cultivation, livestock, a road, a rail line.

The ground beneath us right now is young — geologically speaking, almost embarrassingly recent. Holocene floodplain deposits: unconsolidated sand, pebble gravel, silt, clay, laid down in the last twelve thousand years by the Rio Grande and its western tributary, the Rio Puerco. When you look at a geologic map, this corridor glows white — the youngest material on a sheet otherwise stained with tens of millions of years of color.

That youth is deceptive. The valley itself is ancient. The Rio Grande Rift, the great north-south crack in the crust that created this basin, has been pulling apart for roughly thirty million years. The river runs in a trough that tectonics made. And the Santa Fe Trail, which the railroad essentially followed when it came through in 1879, ran in a corridor that Pueblo people, Spanish colonizers, and Anglo traders had been using for centuries before a locomotive ever crossed New Mexico. The technology changes. The corridor persists.

Off to our right, on the mesa above the river valley, the white and tan geometry of Rio Rancho stretches across the high ground — tract homes, shopping centers, the unmistakable signature of mid-twentieth-century land development. Rio Rancho was platted in 1961, not by homesteaders but by AMREP Corporation, a New York land company that bought up fifty thousand acres of mesa and sold lots by mail-order, pitching the New Mexico sunshine to retirees and suburbanites who'd never been west of the Hudson. It worked. From roughly a thousand people in 1970, the city grew to over a hundred thousand by the time the century turned. The third-largest city in New Mexico, made by a direct-mail brochure. Fred Harvey sold the romance of the Southwest from the dining car. AMREP sold the retirement dream from a Manhattan mailroom. Different century, same instinct.

The mesa to our right — the West Mesa — sits above the river at something like a hundred-foot escarpment. The bedrock up there is older than what's under our wheels: Quaternary sedimentary material, volcanic debris from the Jemez Mountains to the northwest, all of it telling the story of what happens when a river system sits inside a rift valley for millions of years. Material shed off the rising flanks accumulates. The Rio Grande carves down. You get terraces — the old floodplains, stranded high and dry.

The aridity of the mesa is startling if you look at it against the bosque. The valley floor, green with cottonwood and tamarisk and irrigated fields. The mesa: gray-brown shrub, almost lunar. Two hundred feet of elevation, and it might as well be a different continent. Water is that precise here.

North Valley is the older face of the metro, the agricultural fringe that got absorbed. As we pass through, you can still read the older landscape in the layout: long, narrow fields running perpendicular to the river, the old Spanish land-grant strips that divided frontage equitably so each family had a share of the water. Those strips — the acequias that ran through them — are a medieval Iberian inheritance, transplanted to this valley in the seventeenth century. Some of the irrigation ditches running through these neighborhoods are still in use. Gravity-fed, hand-maintained, over three hundred years old. The highway and the subdivision came later. The acequia came first.

We're approaching Albuquerque now, the largest city in New Mexico and the reason this leg of the Southwest Chief exists at all. The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe reached Albuquerque in April 1880, and the town's founders immediately faced a problem: the existing town of Albuquerque — the old plaza, the Spanish colonial core founded in 1706 — was a mile and a half east of where the railroad chose to lay its tracks. The railroad didn't bend for the town. The town bent for the railroad.

A new Albuquerque grew up around the depot: New Albuquerque, they called it. Hotels, saloons, merchandise houses, all oriented to the tracks. Within a few years, the two towns had merged and the rail-adjacent grid had become the center. It's a pattern we'll recognize from dozens of stops on this line — Dodge City, La Junta, Raton, Las Vegas, NM. The locomotive didn't just pass through the West. It decided where the West would be.

Albuquerque station. We're at the center of one of the oldest continuously inhabited river valleys in North America. The Pueblo people built towns here along the Río Grande long before 1706. The Spanish came and built over and beside them. The Americans came and built beside the Spanish. And now 700,000 people in Bernalillo County, most of them within a few miles of this station.

If you step off and look west from the platform, the West Mesa horizon is flat as a blade — the edge of the Colorado Plateau, lifting toward Arizona. To the east, the Sandia Mountains climb to over ten thousand feet, hard and pale in this morning light. Their name means watermelon in Spanish, for what the granite does at sunset: the rock goes pink, then red, then blood orange. Geology as spectacle. We'll carry that image southward.

Bernalillo County was organized in 1852, four years after the Mexican–American War transferred New Mexico from Mexican to American administration. The county name is Spanish. The treaty lines are American. The valley is Pueblo. Every place name in this stretch is a palimpsest — a document written over older documents, the ink of one era bleeding through the next.

South of the station we pass through the South Valley, a community of thirty-eight thousand that sits on ground the EPA has flagged as a Superfund site — industrial contamination from decades of manufacturing and rail yard operations. The pastoral illusion of adobe and cottonwood meets the unglamorous reality of what a rail junction actually accumulates over a century and a half. Coal ash. Solvents. The residue of commerce. That's the history the brochures don't mention.

South Valley stretches to our right — dense, working-class, predominantly Hispanic, a community that has absorbed the environmental costs of proximity to industry and infrastructure while the wealthier parts of the metro moved upslope and upwind. It's a geography of consequence: who lives near the rail yard and who lives on the mesa with the views. The patterns here were set in the 1880s and reinforced through the twentieth century. The ground itself carries the record.

South of Albuquerque, the valley begins to open and quiet. The urban density thins. We're re-entering the agricultural fringe, and the bedrock shifts under us, though we can't see it directly: around milepost 1360 we'll cross onto the Upper Santa Fe Group, one of the defining formations of the Rio Grande Rift — conglomerates and coarse sandstones and fine alluvial fans accumulated as the rift pulled apart and the flanking mountains shed debris into the widening basin. Material that was once highland becomes valley fill.

The Santa Fe Group is named for the city we passed days ago, but the rock laid down this chapter of its story right here, in this stretch of the middle valley. It's Miocene to recent: anywhere from fourteen million years old to nearly present. The same tectonic event, expressed in sediment at our feet.

Valencia County begins just ahead — seventy-six thousand people, median income a notch below Bernalillo, poverty at nearly eighteen percent. The metro falls away and the valley reasserts its older character: hay, legumes, small-scale irrigation. The land here has been farmed continuously for centuries. The shrub is the default state of the uplands; the green is always borrowed from the river.

Bosque Farms is off to our left, tucked between the bosque and the irrigation ditches — a small village of four thousand that has maintained its agricultural identity even as the metro crept southward. The name is straightforward: farm in the bosque, in the cottonwood gallery forest. People have been farming this specific ground for centuries. The fields here grow hay and alfalfa, crops that exist only because the acequia system captures the river and delivers it by gravity across the floodplain. Without the ditch, this is desert. With the ditch, it's lush enough to be mistaken, briefly, for somewhere much wetter.

Here is a useful fact about where we are: we are roughly thirty-five miles south of Albuquerque's central plaza, and we are still, technically, in the Albuquerque metropolitan statistical area. The metro has simply elongated itself down the river corridor to absorb Los Lunas and Bosque Farms and everything in between. This is the modern form of the persistent corridor — not a trail or a track but a statistical boundary that annexes communities along the river's axis.

The Rio Grande keeps doing what it has done for millions of years. The administrative geography reorganizes around it every few decades. The river doesn't negotiate.

Los Lunas to our left, county seat of Valencia County, population seventeen thousand. The name comes from the Luna family — prominent New Mexican landowners, the kind of Spanish colonial landed gentry who survived the Mexican period and the American period both by adapting and allying. The village grew on the east bank of the river, where the Santa Fe Trail's branch road passed through, and then grew again when the railroad arrived. The same corridor, again.

The Neogene sedimentary rock begins to appear in the bluffs around here — older than the Quaternary fill under the valley floor, the Neogene strata representing the deeper basin history, deposited through the Miocene and Pliocene as the rift continued its slow opening. I want to say a proper word about Neogene rock, because we'll be seeing more of it as the landscape opens southward.

Neogene: the geologic period running from about twenty-three million years ago to roughly two and a half million years ago, when the Pleistocene ice ages began. It's the second half of the Cenozoic's middle act — the Miocene and the Pliocene packed into one designation. In this part of New Mexico, Neogene sedimentary rock is mostly the product of the Rio Grande Rift: as the crust pulled apart, the flanking ranges rose and the basin dropped, and the eroded material from those rising mountains poured in and accumulated. Gravel, sand, clay, interbedded volcanic ash. The bluffs and cutbanks we see in the valley walls are the rift filling itself in, layer by layer, over millions of years. When the Rio Grande carved down to its current level, it exposed those layers. We read them now like a calendar — the deeper you go, the older the entry.

The fossils in this stretch go both old and young in a strange combination: Acanthoceras amphibolum and Phelopteria gastrodes, marine creatures from the Cretaceous seaway that covered this region a hundred million years ago — clams and ammonites from an inland ocean that is now five thousand feet above sea level. And Glaphyrites millsi, a nautiloid from three hundred million years ago, even older, from the Pennsylvanian sea. Those creatures are not in the bluffs we're passing — they're in the bedrock that the rift exposed in the surrounding ranges. But they're under this valley in some form, beneath the Neogene fill. The whole column is down there. We're riding on top of it.

The land here is one hundred percent shrub, according to the land-cover surveys — a stark number after the eighty percent developed we passed through in Bernalillo County. Valencia County named itself after Valencia, Spain, in 1852, the year it was organized under American administration, a nod to the Spanish colonial heritage that predated American sovereignty by a century and a half. That naming impulse — tethering a new American county to a Spanish city — is itself a kind of palimpsest. The land already had names in Tiwa and Towa and a dozen other Pueblo languages. The Spanish came and renamed. The Americans came and renamed again, often by keeping the Spanish names. The layers accumulate.

Hidden Mountain is a low mesa we're approaching from the north — and on its flank sits one of the stranger artifacts in New Mexico, which is saying something. The Los Lunas Decalogue Stone: a large boulder inscribed with nine lines of text, first reported formally in 1933, purporting to be an ancient Hebrew inscription of the Ten Commandments. The inscription uses a Paleo-Hebrew script; some proponents have argued it was carved by Phoenician sailors or ancient Israelite explorers in pre-Columbian North America.

It is, the scholarly consensus holds, a hoax — probably nineteenth century, though the exact perpetrator remains unknown. But the hoax itself is instructive. Pre-Columbian transoceanic contact theories have circulated in American culture since the early nineteenth century, fueled in part by a deep American discomfort with the idea that the continent's ancient history belongs entirely to indigenous peoples. The Decalogue Stone says more about the desires of its carver than about the ancient Hebrews. It's a ghost on the land of a particular kind: a forgery that haunts the landscape because it tells us what someone desperately wanted to believe.

We're passing Hidden Mountain now, the low mesa to our left where the stone sits. You won't see the inscription from the train — it's partway up the slope, facing away from us. But the mesa is there, gray-brown against the sky, the kind of unremarkable landform that litters this valley. The Quaternary sediments are back under our wheels — the rift basin filling itself in again with younger material. Elevation still around five thousand feet. The river still to our left, still running. Still the reason we are here at all.

Over the next hour and a half, we'll begin the long climb toward the continental divide — Belen ahead, then Socorro, the ground rising almost imperceptibly but steadily as the valley narrows and the rift's walls close in. The Rio Grande will stay our companion for a while yet. It has been running alongside the corridor for longer than anyone who ever traveled it.

The ground under us right now is young — geologically speaking, almost newborn. Quaternary sediments, laid down within the last two and a half million years, washed off surrounding highlands and settled here in the Albuquerque Basin. Look at the shrubland stretching in every direction: cholla, saltbush, the occasional juniper on a rise. No trees unless someone planted them. The Rio Grande is to the east, out of sight, but its influence is what keeps any of this populated at all. We're sitting at just over five thousand feet. Over the next hour and a half, that number climbs steadily — a thousand feet more before we're done.

We're running roughly parallel to a route that has carried human traffic across this basin for centuries. The old Camino Real — the Royal Road from Mexico City north to Santa Fe — came through this valley. Spanish colonial governors, missionaries, soldiers, trade goods, livestock. Then, in the 1820s, the Santa Fe Trail came from the east, American merchants riding wagons down from Missouri. Then the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway laid iron over much of the same corridor in the 1880s. Then Route 66 followed. And now us. Four transportation revolutions, the same underlying geography, the same shortage of water dictating where you can stop and where you cannot. The land doesn't change; the machines carrying people across it just get faster.

Off to the right — the Rio San Jose. Ninety miles long, a tributary of the Rio Puerco, which itself drains into the Rio Grande. In the wet season you'd see real water moving; right now, depending on the time of year, it may look like little more than a sandy wash. That's the signature of an arroyo in the high desert: episodic, fierce, then dry. The Spanish word "arroyo" stuck for a reason — the Anglo settlers didn't have a word for a river that only sometimes is one. The San Jose drainage is also the thread we'll follow westward for the next stretch, up through the volcanic country ahead.

Water in the Southwest isn't just scarce — it's unreliable in a particular way that defeated farmers who arrived from the humid Midwest. They knew rivers. They did not know rivers that ran full in July from a thunderstorm fifty miles away and were bone dry by August. The Pueblo peoples who've lived in this landscape for a thousand years built their agriculture around that variability: check dams, small reservoirs, fields positioned to catch sheet flow off rock. The Anglo homesteaders in the late nineteenth century tried to impose the grid and the plow. Many of them left. The ones who stayed learned to read the land the way the Pueblo already had.

Now something changes underfoot — and you can see it. The pale basin sediments give way to dark rock: basalt and andesite, volcanic lava flows, Middle Pleistocene in age but some of it newer still. This is the Grants volcanic field, and we're entering it. The flows south of here and west toward Grants include some that are Holocene — geologically brand new, erupted within the last ten thousand years, within the span of human memory if humans had been here to watch. The landscape turns darker, rougher. Malpais — the Spanish word, "bad country" — is what the old-timers called this. You can see why. The lava is angular and unweathered, black and broken, not yet softened by erosion. Cattle ranchers avoided it. Even the trains had to find routes around the worst of it. This is volcanic country, and we're in it for the first time today.

The Grants lava flows belong to a chain of volcanic features that runs across this part of New Mexico — cinder cones, lava tubes, frozen lava lakes. El Malpais National Monument protects a big section to the south. Inside those lava tubes, ice persists year-round, even in summer: cold air pools in the tubes and never fully warms. The Acoma Pueblo, whose lands we're approaching, have oral traditions about the lava — the land's formation isn't just geology to them, it's part of a living story of the place. The AT&SF railway engineers in the 1880s had more immediate concerns: the flows made grading impossible in places and drove the route to find the seams of older, smoother ground between them.

A small scatter of houses on the left: Highland Meadows, a census-designated place, fewer than six hundred residents. Not much to see from the train. But it sits right at the edge where the Quaternary basin sediments end and the volcanic rock takes over — you can sometimes see the color change in the soil even from here, from buff to dark gray-brown. One of those unremarkable places on the map that, geologically, happens to sit on a seam.

The Santa Fe Railway ran this route in part because of what lay ahead — Grants, and beyond it, coal and later uranium. The railroad wasn't just moving passengers; it was the industrial spine of the region. Freight revenues from New Mexico's extractive industries kept the line economically viable long after the romantic era of Pullman travel faded. Fred Harvey, who put his restaurants and hotels at railway stations across the Southwest, understood that passengers were the marquee but freight was the engine. His Harvey Houses sold the romance; the boxcars carried the reality.

The geology shifts again, and now it shifts hard. We're rolling onto the Chinle Group — Middle Triassic rock, somewhere between 206 and 238 million years old. Two hundred and thirty million years. When these mudstones and sandstones were laid down, there were no birds, no flowering plants, no mammals worth speaking of. The supercontinent Pangaea was breaking apart. Dinosaurs were just beginning to appear. And this part of the world was a broad, warm floodplain — rivers draining across low terrain, depositing sediment the color of rust and purple and gray. That's what you see in the exposed cuts and washes: banded rock, purples and reds, the mudstone that crumbles at the edges. The Chinle is famous throughout the Colorado Plateau for exactly these colors. It's the same formation that floors much of Petrified Forest National Park, a couple of hours west of here as the crow flies.

The fossils that come out of this general stretch of New Mexico tell the story of a later sea, not Triassic rivers. Near Grants, paleontologists have found sharks: Squalicorax, a Late Cretaceous predator with serrated teeth, and Ptychodus, a crushing-jawed shark that fed on shellfish. Eighty-five million years ago, an interior seaway covered much of what is now the American interior, from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic. New Mexico was seafloor. The Cretaceous Western Interior Seaway — warm, shallow, several hundred miles wide. The creatures fossilized in these beds were swimming above what is now ranch and reservation land. It takes a moment to hold that image alongside the dry scrub and dark lava outside.

The small community of Mesita on our left, and ahead the place called Marmon — both connected to Laguna Pueblo, whose land we're crossing. Laguna Pueblo was founded in 1699, the last of the Rio Grande Pueblos established before the Spanish reconquest fully settled in. By the late nineteenth century, the AT&SF railway came directly through Laguna land. Walter Marmon, a surveyor from Ohio, arrived with the government surveys in the 1870s, married into the Laguna community, and became deeply embedded in tribal affairs. His name stuck to that place ahead. It's one of those quiet facts the landscape holds: the Anglo name on a Pueblo site, layered history compressed into a dot on the map.

The Fred Harvey Company and Laguna Pueblo had an unusual commercial relationship. Harvey built a station at Laguna, and for decades Laguna women sold pottery and woven goods to train passengers on the platform — one of the earliest structured Indigenous arts markets in the Southwest. The Harvey Company recognized that passengers wanted "authenticity," and the Laguna potters produced it, but on their own terms, adapting designs and forms to what sold. Scholars have argued both sides of that exchange: exploitation, or one of the few economic leverage points available to Pueblo communities at a time of extreme federal pressure? The pottery sold at Laguna in 1905 is in museum collections now. The women who made it are remembered by name in some of those records. Laguna men, meanwhile, were laying rail and maintaining track on the same right-of-way. The Harvey Company sold one Southwest to tourists; the Laguna people were building it, simultaneously, with their hands.

We've crossed into Jurassic sedimentary rock — 201 to 145 million years old. Jurassic layers appear here for the first time in our journey and will be part of the story all the way into Arizona. These deposits belong to a world after Pangaea fully split: the climate had dried, and vast erg deserts covered much of the interior West — seas of dunes, hundreds of feet deep, now compressed into sandstone. The Morrison Formation, famous for its dinosaur beds — Stegosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Allosaurus — is Jurassic. You can't see the fossils from the window, but the rock that holds them is right under the shrub. The same Jurassic wind that stacked those dunes is now stone, and we're riding over it.

New Laguna sits directly on the old Route 66 alignment — or rather, Route 66 ran directly through Laguna Pueblo land, as the railroad had before it. "New" Laguna was established in the mid-nineteenth century as a Laguna community closer to the rail corridor. The rail brought access to markets for craft work; Route 66 brought tourists who bought pottery from stands along the highway. The "new" in New Laguna reflects a pragmatic adaptation: the community moved toward the corridor, toward the commerce, rather than watching it pass at a distance. Same corridor, different generation, same calculation.

Route 66 was commissioned in 1926 and officially ran from Chicago to Santa Monica — 2,400 miles — but it was never a single engineered road. It was a designation stitched together from existing state and county roads, some paved, some gravel, some still dirt in wet weather. Through New Mexico and Arizona, large stretches ran beside or directly on the old AT&SF right-of-way. Steinbeck called it the "Mother Road" in The Grapes of Wrath, 1939 — giving it mythological weight from the Dust Bowl migration: hundreds of thousands of displaced families driving west along exactly this corridor, past the Pueblo communities, through the Malpais, toward California. Decommissioned in 1985. Parts of the old alignment are visible from the train window — the faded asphalt, the abandoned motels and gas stations. Ghost infrastructure. The corridor persists; the technology keeps changing; the ghosts accumulate.

To our right, North Acomita Village — population 357, a community of Acoma Pueblo. Acoma's mesa-top village sits about fifteen miles south of our route, one of the most dramatic inhabited sites in North America: a pueblo on a sandstone mesa 357 feet above the surrounding plain, occupied continuously since at least the eleventh century. The people of Acoma have been watching this corridor for a thousand years. The railroad came through in the 1880s. Route 66 followed. The train we're on is the third version of the same passage, and Acoma is still here.

In 1599, a colonial force under Juan de Oñate attacked Acoma Pueblo following the killing of several Spanish soldiers. The battle lasted three days. Oñate's punishment: men over twenty-five had one foot amputated and were enslaved for twenty years; younger men and women were enslaved. The Spanish then built the San Esteban del Rey Mission at the top of the mesa — completed 1641 — its roof timbers hauled by hand from mountains forty miles away. The mission still stands. Acoma never stopped being Acoma. We're riding past the edge of a community that has survived everything the corridor could bring: Spanish conquest, American annexation, the railroad, the highway, the tourist gaze. The thin veneer of modernity here is thinner than most.

The bedrock here is Late Pleistocene alluvium — unconsolidated gravel and sand washed into the valley floors during wetter periods, the same kind of river-laid material we've seen before in this journey but now in a different context: local drainages off the lava fields and sandstone mesas rather than the Rio Grande system. We're higher now, and the washes cutting through the alluvium reflect that — shallower, flashier, the plumbing of the high desert visible in the sandy channels. The elevation has been lifting almost imperceptibly, but we've gained several hundred feet since Albuquerque.

Fred Harvey died in 1901, but the company that bore his name kept building along the AT&SF for decades after. The Harvey Girls — young women, mostly from the Midwest, recruited to work as waitresses in the Harvey Houses — became an unlikely piece of Southwest mythology. They wore black uniforms with white aprons, were trained to exacting standards, and were forbidden from marrying for the first year of their contract. Roughly five thousand of them eventually married local men and stayed in the Southwest anyway, a significant demographic thread in the region's social fabric. A 1946 film starring Judy Garland immortalized them as frontier civilizers. The actual Harvey Girls were mostly working-class women who took the only decent-paying respectable job available to them west of the Mississippi in the 1890s and 1900s. Both the myth and the fact are true. The Santa Fe Railway manufactured one; the other is what actually happened.

Ahead, the small settlement of Anzac — named after the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, the forces at Gallipoli in 1915. Anzac, New Mexico was platted during or just after World War One, when the name carried weight. Towns across rural America bear those wartime names: Verdun, Argonne, Pershing. Most are now small or gone. Anzac, New Mexico persists, barely — a dot on the county map, a name that remembers a battle fought in the Dardanelles on the other side of the planet, here in the shrubland of Cibola County. The place-naming impulse is itself a kind of ghost-making: commemorating the distant while the local fades.

We're nearing the sixty-mile mark of this segment, and the elevation has lifted us close to a thousand feet above where we started. The rock below the train has cycled through a compressed archive of time: Quaternary sediment, Pleistocene lava, Triassic river mud, Jurassic dune sand, Pleistocene alluvium again. Each layer a different world — a tropical floodplain, an inland sea, a desert of dunes — all of it stacked and now visible in roadcuts and washes. Ahead, the terrain steepens. The high point of this run waits beyond Gallup, and on the far side of that divide, the watershed changes: water that falls there runs not toward the Rio Grande but toward the Colorado River and the Gulf of California. We haven't crossed that line yet. But the land is already leaning that direction.

The soil out ahead has a peculiar bleached-out look — pale gray and ochre, the color of desert hardpan. We're sitting on unconsolidated alluvium laid down during the late Pleistocene, sediment scraped off the mountains and spread across the valley floor by rivers that have since mostly given up. The Colorado Plateau presses in from the west here; this is where the grassy short-prairie we rode through hours ago has finally surrendered to shrubland. Less than twelve inches of rain a year now. You can read that on the ground as clearly as a dial.

Grants is just ahead, and the story of how it came to exist is a tidy case study in how the West was sold — literally. The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway pushed its mainline through here in 1881, and the company did not merely build a railroad. It built towns, platted lots, printed promotional brochures in German and Swedish, and dispatched agents to Chicago and Kansas City to tell farmers that the Southwest was a garden waiting to be tended. The Santa Fe Railway owned the land on either side of the tracks — part of the enormous federal land grants that the Pacific Railway Act had bestowed on railroads since 1862. Sell the land, fill the trains. The model was efficient and it was everywhere through here. Every town we pass for the next sixty miles was, in some sense, a railroad product.

Grants is one of those towns that remade itself three times and nearly died each time. It started as a railroad camp — the Grant brothers, Canadian contractors, gave it a name while grading this section in 1881. Then came cattle, then carrots and potatoes, which earned it a brief burst of agricultural optimism in the 1940s. And then uranium. In 1950, a Navajo shepherd named Paddy Martinez found yellow-orange rock near Haystack Mesa, about ten miles north of here. It turned out to be carnotite — uranium ore — and Grants became the Uranium Capital of the World almost overnight. The boom ran until the early 1980s, when the bottom fell out of the market. The mines closed. What you see driving through downtown now is what the aftermath of a resource boom looks like when the resource is gone: empty storefronts, deep poverty rates, and a mining museum that is also, quietly, a memorial.

Look south — the land opens up into a wide, shallow basin bounded by dark mesas. That darkness is important. Around mile 1460 the bedrock beneath us will change: we'll cross from unconsolidated Pleistocene alluvium onto something much younger and stranger. The Zuni-Bandera volcanic field stretches across this country — lava that poured out in some cases only a few thousand years ago, some of it within the last millennium. Black basalt flows that look, from above, like someone poured tar across the desert and let it cool. The Acoma people called the lava field "malpais" — badlands — and it is: impossible to cross on foot, a natural fortress. Water, when it does fall here, vanishes into fractured lava. The aridity isn't just about rain; it's about terrain that refuses to hold it.

Milan, off the right window, was essentially a suburb that the uranium boom assembled and the uranium bust deflated. The village incorporated in 1969, near the peak of the mining years, and it has been quietly declining since. Population under 2,500 now. It's the kind of place that exists because a resource existed — which is to say it's the same story as Grants, condensed. The West is full of these mirrors.

Route 66 runs right alongside us through here — or what's left of it. The old highway is never far from the tracks on this leg, and that's not a coincidence. When the U.S. government laid out Route 66 in 1926, the highway engineers threaded it through the same mountain passes and river gaps the Santa Fe Railway had surveyed in the 1870s, which the railroad surveyors had traced by following the same corridor the Santa Fe Trail wagons had used since 1821. The corridor is more than a route. It's a groove worn into the continent by four hundred years of traffic — Spanish traders, Mexican merchants, American wagon trains, iron locomotives, Ford Model A's, and now us. Every new technology arrives and finds the same path already waiting.

Off the left window, Bluewater Village takes its name from a reservoir a few miles south — Bluewater Lake, impounded in 1927 by an earthen dam built primarily to irrigate crops downvalley. Four hundred and sixty-four people live here now. The water supply is fragile: this is a semi-arid basin where irrigation projects were engineered in an era of optimism about hydrology that the twentieth century did not fully justify. A wet decade in the 1910s convinced settlers that the land was more hospitable than it was. Then the drought returned. Water out here is always a negotiation between aspiration and physics, and physics usually wins eventually.

Around mile 1460 we ride onto a different world. The bedrock has shifted — we're now crossing Middle Pleistocene basalt and andesite, lava flows erupted roughly 780,000 years ago and younger, the leading edge of the Zuni-Bandera volcanic field. In places along this corridor the lava is geologically fresh: the El Malpais flows, south of the tracks, include surface eruptions dated to perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 years ago. The Puebloan people who lived here when those flows crept across the land left accounts in oral tradition — they watched the earth bleed. The National Monument that now protects this landscape covers 114,000 acres of frozen lava, cinder cones, and lava-tube caves where ice accumulates year-round, insulated from the desert heat above. The Triassic sedimentary rock starts around mile 1470 — a hard jump backward in time, from 780,000 years to 251 million. The continent was assembled differently then: this land sat near the equator, tropical, crossed by rivers draining the early Rockies' predecessors into broad basins where Cynepteris ferns and the earliest dinosaur relatives left their traces. Some of those fossils are still here: Lyssoxylon grigsbyi, an early conifer, pressed into Triassic mudstone about 227 million years ago. The land we're crossing is not one land but several, stacked.

Prewitt is barely a crossroads — a cluster of structures at an old Route 66 interchange. A gas station, a truck stop, some residences. The settlement exists because the corridor needed services every twenty miles or so, and Prewitt was at a useful interval. That's really all it ever was. The railroad didn't bother with a depot here. The highway generated a thin economy, and when bypasses and interstates reorganized traffic, communities like Prewitt were left marooned on the old alignment. Ghost towns in slow motion.

The Fred Harvey Company is worth pausing on here, because its influence on everything we've been seeing is enormous and mostly invisible now. Harvey was an English-born businessman who struck a deal with the Santa Fe Railway in 1876: he would run the restaurants and hotels at the stations, and the railroad would give him the exclusive contract. What he built was remarkable. Harvey Houses — clean, well-staffed, with actual silver and linen on the tables — appeared at intervals across the Southwest, staffed by a corps of carefully recruited young women from the East who came to be called Harvey Girls. The company didn't just feed passengers; it shaped the image of the Southwest that easterners carried home. Harvey and the Santa Fe Railway began collecting and marketing Pueblo and Navajo art in the 1890s, staging "Indian Detour" excursions, hiring Indigenous artists to demonstrate their crafts in the depot arcades. They were selling the West as a destination precisely as they were building the infrastructure that made the West accessible. The authenticity was curated, the experience manufactured — and yet the art itself was real, and some of what they preserved might otherwise have been lost. That ambiguity sits here in every piece of turquoise jewelry sold at a gas station in Prewitt.

Thoreau — the community off the right window — is majority Navajo, with a population of around 2,400, most of whom live within or adjacent to the Navajo Nation's eastern boundary, which runs close here. The town's name is pronounced "thuh-ROO" locally, after Henry David, though the connection to the Massachusetts writer is indirect — the post office chose the name in the 1880s, perhaps aspirationally, perhaps arbitrarily, as post offices often did. The Navajo presence through this corridor is not incidental. The Nation's land stretches north from here across a huge swath of the Colorado Plateau — an area the size of West Virginia. What the railroad called "empty land" for its promotional brochures was never empty. It was grazed, farmed, and inhabited. The line between Grants and Gallup cuts through the eastern Navajo homeland, and the history of that intersection — forced relocation, the Long Walk of 1864, land agreements broken and redrawn — runs under every mile of track.

We're climbing now. The grade steepens gradually, almost imperceptibly, but the engine feels it. We're trending toward the Continental Divide — not a single dramatic ridge here but a broad, rolling high-country swale, the land tilting almost gently from one ocean's watershed to another. The Rio Grande drainage, which has carried the water from these slopes east toward Texas, is about to give way. West of the Divide — just a few miles ahead — rain that falls on this plateau eventually finds its way into the Little Colorado River, and from there into the Colorado. Different ocean. Different destiny. The cattle that grazed here in the 1880s, the homesteaders who drilled wells in the 1920s, the Navajo herders who've moved flocks through these passes for centuries — all of them were navigating a landscape where water doesn't stay where you expect it to.

Continental Divide, New Mexico — population 187, elevation around 7,200 feet — is the smallest kind of town that can exist: one that the corridor deposited here and mostly forgot. But it sits on something enormous. The watershed boundary we're crossing is the hydrological spine of North America. Every drop of rain that falls on the east side of this low, unassuming pass eventually reaches the Gulf of Mexico. Every drop west of it will push toward the Gulf of California, or evaporate in the Colorado's lower reaches before it gets that far. We're at roughly 7,200 feet here — the high point of this segment. From this crest, the land will drop about a thousand feet over the next 150 miles as we descend toward the Arizona line. The aridity we've been tracking all day deepens from here: less water, thinner soils, harder rock.

Fort Wingate, coming up on our left at mile 1500, has one of the more layered histories of any installation in the American Southwest — three different locations bearing the same name across forty-four years. The first Fort Wingate opened at Seboyeta in 1849, one year after the Mexican-American War delivered New Mexico to the United States. A second was established at San Rafael in 1862. The third — the one whose ruins we'll see — was built at this location in 1868, the year the Navajo returned from the Long Walk. Four years earlier, in 1864, Kit Carson had forcibly marched roughly 8,000 Navajo people from their homeland to a relocation camp at Bosque Redondo, 350 miles east. The experiment was a catastrophe: crop failures, disease, starvation. By 1868, even the federal government had admitted failure. The Treaty of 1868 allowed the Navajo to return to a portion of their ancestral land — and Fort Wingate was established to oversee that return, the same army that had driven them out now tasked with managing their repatriation. The fort remained active until 1993, a century and a quarter in this one valley. It's on the National Register of Historic Places now. Gallup is just a few miles ahead.

Look left — you can see the footprint of the old fort spreading across the bench above the valley floor. The buildings are a mix of late nineteenth-century stone and early twentieth-century brick; the Army used the site continuously for 125 years, adding structures as missions changed. During World War II, it served as a munitions depot. After 1993, the land was returned in part to the Navajo Nation, and what you see now is a kind of archaeological present tense: a place that held conquest, treaty, two world wars, and reconciliation all in the same acreage. That's the Southwest in a single frame — the layers don't succeed one another cleanly; they pile up, and you can see them all at once if the light is right.

Off to our left, those low adobe and concrete ruins behind the chain-link — that's Fort Wingate, or what's left of it. The Army planted a fort here in 1849, shifted it twice, and by 1868 had settled on this spot for the long haul. For a century and a quarter it served as a munitions depot, storing ordnance through two world wars. The Army walked away in 1993. What you see out there now — crumbling magazines, rusted rail spurs, weedy parade grounds — is the surplus of empire, sitting quiet on Navajo land it was built to control.

The Santa Fe Railway threaded through here in 1881, following a corridor that ox-carts had already worn for sixty years on the Santa Fe Trail — and before that, Pueblo traders and Spanish expeditions had used the same low passes for two centuries. That's the deep logic of this stretch of New Mexico: the geography compels you. The terrain between Albuquerque and the Arizona line funnels every form of travel — foot, hoof, rail, rubber tire — through the same narrow corridor. The fort existed to garrison that corridor. We're still in it.

Down below the surface, the rock underfoot right now is Triassic — the same deep red sedimentary formation we've been riding since eastern New Mexico. About 220 million years old. We'll leave it soon.

Here — right around this mile — the bedrock shifts. We've crossed into the San Rafael Group: Middle Jurassic sandstone, siltstone, and gypsum laid down roughly 168 million years ago, when the interior of North America was a sweeping coastal plain edged by a shallow sea. The Entrada Sandstone is part of this group — the same formation that, a few hundred miles north in Utah, has eroded into the arches and fins of canyon country. Here it's buried under soil and scrub, but it's there. The gypsum in these beds — the Todilto Formation, thin and distinctive — formed in sabkha flats at the sea's edge, salt water evaporating in brutal heat. That gypsum is the mineral that becomes drywall, the mineral that crystals grow in caves. Buried 168 million years. A vanished sea, legible in the cliff face if you catch the right angle.

Gallup is a couple of miles ahead, and before we pull in it's worth knowing what made it. The town was platted in 1881, the year the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad — the line our tracks still follow — pushed through. The railroad paymaster, David Gallup, had his office here; the crews came to collect wages; the place got called Gallup's and the name stuck. Tidy founding story. But the more durable story is what happened after: the Santa Fe Railway, which absorbed the Atlantic and Pacific, realized the Four Corners region was thick with Navajo, Hopi, and Zuni weavers, silversmiths, and potters making extraordinary things. Fred Harvey — the company that ran the railway's hotels and dining cars across the entire Southwest — turned Gallup into a gateway for that trade. Harvey buyers came out here, worked with Native craftspeople, standardized designs for the Anglo market, shipped work east on the very trains we're riding. The arrangement made Harvey rich. It made Gallup the self-styled Indian Capital of the World. What it made for the craftspeople was considerably more complicated.

Gallup. Population just under 22,000, and a substantial share Navajo, Hopi, and Zuni — many from the surrounding reservation land that presses in from three sides. The trading post economy Fred Harvey shaped here still leaves its mark: pawn shops, jewelry dealers, and trading companies line the main drag. The station on our left is a Spanish Colonial Revival building from 1923, one of the original Harvey House stops. Route 66 ran straight through here, and for decades Gallup was one of its anchor towns — the last real stop before the long Arizona desert crossing. The railway made this town. The highway sustained it.
