We are arriving at the eastern pole of this long transect. The landscape ahead is not shaped by water's scarcity. It is shaped by water's power.

If you catch a glimpse of an old iron bridge near Kimmswick — a classic Pratt through truss, the kind of X-brace lattice that defined American bridge engineering — that's the Windsor Harbor Road Bridge. Built in 1874 and 1875 by the Keystone Bridge Company, the same firm that built the Eads Bridge over the Mississippi just a few miles downstream. Keystone was the Carnegie company — Andrew Carnegie made his first real money selling iron bridges, before he made his fortune in steel. This bridge was dismantled from its original site and moved here in 1930. Same steel, different river. The Depression-era habit of recycling infrastructure rather than building new.

1874, the year it was built: barbed wire was patented that same year. Within a decade the open range was fenced. The cattle drives were already beginning their short, brutal era. The Santa Fe Trail was still open for business — it wouldn't close until the railroad fully supplanted it in 1880. This bridge is an artifact of a very particular American moment — iron over water, wire over grass, rail over trail, all happening at once.

There's a recurring thread on this leg — the mail routes, the stagecoach lines, the ephemeral corridors that preceded the railroad. The Butterfield Overland Mail ran from 1858 to 1861, 2,800 miles from St. Louis to San Francisco in about 25 days. Stations every twelve to fifteen miles, relay points every forty or fifty. Most of those stations are gone — foundation stones in desert grass, or nothing at all. The railroad that followed, as so often, erased the very thing it replaced. Towns that existed because of the stage route found themselves bypassed by the rail line, and they simply stopped. The Missouri Pacific Railroad — predecessor to lines that eventually became part of this Amtrak corridor — made and unmade towns across the same geography.

We've left most of that ghost-town country behind. St. Louis, a few miles ahead, is the counter-argument: a city that persisted, that accumulated layers, that survived being superseded. Founded as a French fur-trade post in 1764, it became the gateway city for westward expansion, the outfitting point for Lewis and Clark, the eastern terminus of the Santa Fe Trail, and eventually a railroad junction so dense with competing lines that it required one of the great engineering feats of the 19th century — the Eads Bridge — just to cross the river.

We're crossing Holocene alluvium now — the youngest geology on this segment, essentially the river's own deposit work, clay and silt and sand laid down since the last ice age ended twelve thousand years ago. The Mississippi floodplain machinery is already operating around us: flat land, rich dark soil, the river nearby and not shy about reminding everything of its presence. Flood control infrastructure is part of the landscape here in ways that would have been unimaginable two centuries ago.

The Meramec River meets the Mississippi just south of St. Louis — we've been roughly paralleling the Meramec for some miles. The Meramec is, by Ozark standards, a substantial river: limestone-bedded, clear, cold in its upper reaches, famous for caves. Meramec Caverns, upstream near Sullivan, was used as a hideout by Jesse James — or so the story goes, polished to a high gloss by decades of roadside-attraction marketing. What's true: the Ozarks harbored outlaws and guerrillas during and after the Civil War in ways that left deep marks on the region's culture. Missouri was a border state, with Confederate and Union sympathizers sometimes literally neighbor to neighbor. The James gang was a postwar phenomenon, but the conditions that produced it — displaced Confederate veterans, a culture of resentment, porous terrain — were the direct legacy of the war's particular brutality in Missouri.

The ecoregion we're entering now, around milepost 2430, is called the Interior River Valleys and Hills. Where the Ozark Highlands we've been crossing are older, higher, more forested — that resistant dome of Precambrian and Paleozoic rock — the Interior River Valleys are lower, more dissected, defined by the great rivers cutting through them. The Mississippi and Missouri meet just north of St. Louis. From that confluence, the unified river carries roughly six times the water of the Colorado, south to the Gulf.

The bedrock makes another jump here — Serpukhovian, about 327 million years old, a name from the Carboniferous period. North of Scranton, Pennsylvania, in a different world — but the same age rock underlies very different landscapes. Here it's buried under the city's expansion and the river's alluvium. We're entering St. Louis County, population just over a million, the most populous county in Missouri. The landscape is fully urban now — developed land all the way to the river.

Lemay — unincorporated, about 17,000 people, named for the De LeMay family who farmed here in the early 19th century. Lemay Township is one of the older settled pockets in St. Louis County, downstream from the city proper, a working-class community that grew up around the industries that preferred the riverfront. Sewage treatment plants. Industrial facilities. The unglamorous infrastructure that every city needs and no one downtown wants nearby.

St. Louis was, for most of the 19th century, the largest city west of the Mississippi — or the largest city of the interior, depending on how you counted. It was the place where the eastern United States ended and the western begun. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark departed from just north of here in 1804. The city outfitted them, and outfitted the hundreds of thousands who followed over the next seven decades.

The Eads Bridge, completed in 1874, was an engineering landmark of the first order. James Buchanan Eads had never built a bridge before. He'd salvaged sunken riverboats, building the world's first practical diving bell. He understood the Mississippi — its currents, its scour, the way it stripped foundations. He designed caissons driven to bedrock far below the riverbed, using compressed air to keep water out while workers excavated. Those workers suffered from caisson disease — the bends — killing a dozen men and disabling many more before anyone understood the cause. The bridge that resulted was the longest arch bridge in the world at completion and the first major steel bridge in America. It took seven years to build and it's still carrying traffic.

The same year: barbed wire patented. The Santa Fe Trail still open. The last of the great buffalo herds still being hunted to extermination on the southern Plains.

St. Louis peaked, demographically, in 1950 — 856,000 people. Today the city proper is under 300,000. The metropolitan area grew; the city shrank. It's one of the most dramatic population losses in American urban history, driven by white flight, suburban expansion, highway construction that severed neighborhoods, and the collapse of the manufacturing economy that had made the city's working-class wealth. The city and county separated in 1876 — a decision that looked sensible at the time and has been a structural problem ever since, locking the city into its 1876 boundaries while the county grew around it.

The median household income in the city: $52,000. Poverty rate: 20%. Compare that to St. Louis County just outside: $78,000 median, 9.6% poverty. The same river, the same name, two very different economies separated by a 150-year-old administrative line.

Off to the right — in the Gate District neighborhood — the former Immaculate Conception Church. Built 1874, expanded 1908, placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1977. It's no longer a working parish — the Catholic church that once anchored a working-class neighborhood, now a landmark of a neighborhood that's been through several lives. The Gate District was, at various points, a German immigrant neighborhood, an African American neighborhood after the Great Migration, and a neighborhood that experienced significant disinvestment in the late 20th century. The church persists as architecture even as the community around it transformed.

St. Louis. The Gateway Arch is visible from the train on the right — 630 feet of stainless steel, the tallest monument in the Western Hemisphere, designed by Eero Saarinen and completed in 1965. It sits at the exact spot where Pierre Laclède chose to build his fur-trading post in 1764 — the highest ground near the confluence of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers, close enough to the junction to control both. Laclède understood the geography. Every significant westward expedition for the next century would pass through this city or through the confluence just upstream.

The river we'll cross is the Mississippi — roughly a third of a mile wide here, brown and fast and carrying the suspended soil of half a continent. When Mark Twain piloted steamboats on this river in the 1850s, there were hundreds of boats working the main channel. Now there are barges — enormous, pushed by tugs — moving grain and coal and chemicals in volumes the steamboat captains never imagined.

Crossing the river, we cross a state line — Missouri behind us, Illinois ahead. But we also cross a hydrological moment that the whole leg has been building toward.

Think about where we started this journey: the Sonoran Desert, the Chihuahuan Basin, the dry country. Out there, rivers are intermittent. Creeks run only after rain. Water is fought over, diverted, priced. Settlements built near springs and not a mile farther. The Santa Fe Trail followed water, begged for water, died without water.

Here the river is so large, so powerful, so reliable, that the question was never whether it would flow — the question was whether it could be controlled, crossed, confined. The Army Corps of Engineers has spent two centuries wrestling with the Mississippi, building levees, dredging channels, straightening meanders, trying to make the river behave like a canal. The river keeps insisting it is not a canal. The floods of 1927, 1993, 2011, 2019 — each one a reminder that the scale of the thing exceeds the engineering response to it.

We are, as of this crossing, in Illinois. Illinois is a different country from Missouri — geographically flat, agriculturally dominated by corn and soybeans in ways that Missouri, with its hills and forests, is not. The Illinois side of the river, Metro East they call it, is suburban St. Louis — Granite City, Edwardsville, the sprawl that crosses state lines because it doesn't know states.

The Near North Riverfront on the Missouri side — industrial and transitional, the kind of land that used to move goods and now waits for the next thing. Grain elevators. Rail yards. The infrastructure of the river trade that built St. Louis and persists after the trade has transformed past recognition.

The geology under Illinois is Carboniferous — Visean age, about 333 million years old, the Lower Pope Group, a sequence of limestone and sandstone and shale that was being laid down while vast coal swamps covered much of what's now the eastern interior of North America. Illinois has coal because of those swamps. It has limestone because of those seas. The same Carboniferous period that gives us the coal fields of West Virginia and Pennsylvania gives Illinois its particular bedrock, though erosion and glaciation have covered most of it under thick sheets of till left by the Pleistocene ice.

The Interior River Valleys and Hills ecoregion we've entered is lower and flatter than the Ozarks behind us. Madison County ahead — corn, soybeans, wheat; a third wetland, a third developed, the rest agricultural. Edwardsville is the county seat, a university town, one of the older settlements in Illinois, platted in 1818 — the same year Jefferson County, Missouri was organized, that post-War of 1812 moment when the middle of the continent was being divided and named at a rapid pace.

We're settling into the long flat of the Illinois plain now. The ridge lines are behind us. The rivers ahead are wide and gentle-looking — though they are not gentle. The water line we've been crossing all leg is behind us. We are, fully and finally, in the humid East. The landscape ahead is defined not by the absence of water but by its slow, patient, continental accumulation.

Off the left window, right now — that broad silver band where two rivers meet. The Missouri coming in from the north, the Mississippi just below us. The Missouri is the longest river in the country, longer even than the Mississippi proper, rising in the Bitterroot Range of southwestern Montana and running nearly 2,500 miles to reach this exact point. Everything we've ridden since leaving Texas — the scarcity, the alkaline flats, the thin creeks — has been trending toward this. Here the continent tips eastward and all that drainage gathers. We've crossed the hydrological spine of North America. From here water doesn't evaporate and blow away — it collects, joins, runs to the Gulf.

The confluence we just passed isn't just geography. It's a hinge point in American history that kept recurring. Lewis and Clark paddled up the Missouri from almost exactly this spot in May 1804 — forty-three men in a keelboat and two pirogues, pushing against the current for eighteen months before they'd see the Pacific. The Missouri was their highway into the unknown interior, the same river that drained the beaver country that sustained the fur trade, the same river that guided the Mormons west, the same river the railroads paralleled as they pressed into the northern plains. Every corridor we've traced across this continent — Butterfield's stagecoaches, the mail routes, the cattle trails — was organized around water. The Missouri is the biggest fact in the northern half of the story.

The bedrock under us has shifted quietly. Back at Alton we crossed out of the Visean limestones we've been riding through — those 330-million-year-old shallow-sea floors — and into something younger and darker: the Carbondale Formation. Moscovian age, roughly 310 million years old. The name Moscovian comes from the Moscow Basin in Russia, where these same-age rocks were first described. What it means here, in Illinois, is coal. The Carbondale Formation is the great coal-bearing sequence of the Illinois Basin — shale and sandstone and limestone in repeating cycles, with coal seams threaded between them like dark pages in a book. Each coal seam is a buried swamp, a Pennsylvanian forest that fell, compacted, cooked slowly over 300 million years into fuel.

Alton sits on bluffs above the Mississippi, and it earned its place in history twice over. In 1858 the seventh Lincoln-Douglas debate happened here — Lincoln and Douglas arguing slavery's future on a makeshift platform before ten thousand people in October cold. But Alton is also the place where Elijah Lovejoy ran his abolitionist printing press and was murdered by a pro-slavery mob in 1837, his press thrown into the river. He's considered the first martyr of the American free press. The town knew what was at stake in that 1858 debate because it had already paid for the argument in blood. Twenty years later the debate was settled, and twenty years after that the coal seams now beneath our wheels would be powering the industries of a reunited country.

We're climbing now, almost imperceptibly. The Mississippi valley falls behind us and the land opens into the rolling plains of central Illinois — the great corn-and-soybean plateau that feeds the world's grain markets. Macoupin County ahead: 71% cropland by cover. Almost nothing else. The forest that blanketed the Ozarks behind us, the wetlands of the river bottom we've just left — all that texture flattens here into an agricultural machine of astonishing efficiency and almost complete ecological replacement. The prairie grasses that once grew here, the oak savannas, the wetland swales — almost entirely gone, converted beginning in the 1830s when the steel plow made the black Illinois soil breakable. John Deere invented it here, in Grand Detour, a hundred miles north of us. One invention, and a biome vanished.

The Carbondale Formation under us is thickening as we move north. In southern Illinois these coal-bearing sequences run 350 feet deep; here in the central part of the state they're still substantial — and they were mined hard. Small shaft mines opened all through this region in the 1870s and 1880s, following the railroads that made it economical to get coal out. Towns grew around the headframes. Some of those towns are still there. Some became the ghost-town pattern we've seen across this leg — built on a single extractable resource, thriving when prices held, emptying when the seam played out or the mine flooded or the market shifted to natural gas in the mid-twentieth century.

The low farmsteads off to the left are Brighton Township — about four thousand people scattered across these section-line roads. The grid is visible from the train: perfectly square fields, roads running exactly north-south and east-west, the cadastral survey of the 1780s still organizing the landscape 240 years later. Thomas Jefferson's Land Ordinance of 1785 imposed this grid on the entire Northwest Territory — Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin — before a single settler had arrived. The surveyors came first, dividing the wilderness into townships and sections by mathematics alone, then the settlers filled in the squares. It's one of the great acts of preemptive geographic imagination in American history, and it's still completely legible out this window.

Under us now the bedrock has shifted again — out of the Carbondale Formation and into what geologists call the Missourian stage, roughly 306 to 304 million years ago. Sandstone, shale, more coal. Still the Pennsylvanian period, still the great coal-bearing interval, but a chapter older within it. The Illinois Basin accumulated these sediments in repeated cycles — sea level rose, a shallow tropical sea flooded in, left limestone; sea level fell, swamp forests colonized the shoreline, left coal; rivers buried the swamp in sand and mud, left sandstone and shale; then the sea returned. Again and again, perhaps fifty or sixty times. Each coal seam in the sequence is one of those swamp episodes. The fossil record is extraordinary: the snail Pseudozygopleura, small and tightly coiled, turns up in these rocks at 315 million years — a creature that lived in those Pennsylvanian coastal swamps and left its shell in the rock we're riding over now. The shale splits along bedding planes and the shells fall out.

Those coal seams drove the settlement of this entire corridor. The railroad came through central Illinois in the early 1850s — the Illinois Central, land-granted by Congress in 1850, the first major land-grant railroad in American history. It got 2.6 million acres of Illinois land in exchange for building the line. The railroad then sold that land to settlers to generate operating revenue, which is why the towns along this route are evenly spaced — the Illinois Central platted them at intervals calculated to maximize land sales. Each town was a product before it was a place.

Plainview — unincorporated, four miles northeast of Shipman, the kind of place that doesn't appear on most maps. A cluster of farmsteads, a grain elevator visible on the horizon. In 1880 there might have been a general store, a blacksmith, a school section. The school is likely consolidated somewhere else now, the store gone, the blacksmith's trade obsolete for a century. This is the quiet version of the ghost-town pattern — not abandoned dramatically, but slowly depopulated by the same forces that emptied the more spectacular ruins further west: mechanization, consolidation, the automobile making the county seat accessible. The landscape doesn't scar. The fields just absorb it.

We're approaching Carlinville, and as we do the geology makes one more step. The Bond Formation appears ahead — Kasimovian age, 305 to 304 million years old, the youngest of the coal-bearing sequences in this part of Illinois. Shale, sandstone, limestone, coal, in the same rhythmic cycles as below. The Kasimovian stage sits right at the top of the Pennsylvanian period; above it, the geological record in Illinois goes largely missing — erosion stripped away whatever came next. So the rocks visible here represent almost the last chapter of a 30-million-year saga of swamp forests and shallow seas.

Here's what those swamp forests actually were. Not trees as we'd recognize them. Scale trees — Lepidodendron — thirty meters tall, with bark that looked like overlapping scales, relatives of the humble club mosses we find today in wet forest floors. Giant horsetails along the margins. Ferns the size of trees. No flowering plants, no grasses — those hadn't evolved yet. The air had more oxygen than today, possibly 35%. Insects grew enormous: dragonflies with two-foot wingspans, millipedes six feet long. And the trees fell, and fell, and the swamp preserved them, and three hundred million years later we burn them in power plants to light our houses. The entire modern coal economy is a compressed window into that strange, oxygen-rich world.

Carlinville coming up on both sides — the county seat of Macoupin County, and one of the more architecturally interesting small towns in Illinois. The courthouse visible from the train, built in 1870, cost $1.3 million — an extraordinary sum that sent the county into debt for forty years and became a national scandal. The contractor was a state senator; the final price was six times the original estimate. It remains one of the largest courthouse domes in Illinois, which is either admirable or infuriating depending on your tolerance for nineteenth-century public graft. Platted in 1829, incorporated in 1837 — the same year Lovejoy was killed at Alton. Old enough to have sent men to both the Mexican War and the Civil War, young enough that the courthouse corruption predates those wars' outcomes.

Just past the station, on South Charles Street, is a building worth noting: the Carlinville Chapter House, built 1909 to 1910 as a meetinghouse for the American Woman's League. The AWL was a national organization founded by Edward Lewis, publisher of the Woman's Home Companion, as a way to sell magazine subscriptions — members could earn shares by signing up subscribers, and enough shares bought chapter house construction. At its peak the AWL had chapters in hundreds of small American towns. It collapsed in 1912 when Lewis's publishing empire failed, but the buildings survived. Carlinville's is on the National Register of Historic Places. An organization that grew out of a circulation scheme, built physical infrastructure that outlasted it by more than a century. The magazine is gone. The building stands.

North of Carlinville the land opens further — we're entering the Central Corn Belt Plains now, the ecoregion that covers the heart of Illinois and Iowa and Indiana, one of the most agriculturally productive landscapes on earth. The transition from the Interior River Valleys behind us is subtle — a little flatter, the soils even darker and richer, the wetlands fewer. This is the till plain, scraped flat by Pleistocene glaciers and left with a deep deposit of glacial drift that weathered into the black mollisols that grow corn better than almost anywhere. The glaciers that did this retreated only 12,000 years ago — yesterday in geological time. The landscape we're watching through the window is geologically brand new, overlying coal-age rock that is 300 million years old.

The elevation has been climbing since St. Louis — we're at roughly 650 feet now, up from 433 at the segment start, and we'll reach about 814 feet before the leg is done. Not dramatic. But the watershed has shifted: the creeks here drain north and east into the Illinois River system rather than directly to the Mississippi, organizing themselves around the continental tilt that the glaciers partly reshaped. Water finds its way. It always does.

Off the right window, Virden Township — incorporated in 1870, three thousand people, a grain elevator and a water tower. Virden itself, the town, was the site of the Virden Massacre in 1898: mine operators trying to break a United Mine Workers strike imported Black workers from Alabama as strikebreakers; armed confrontation at the mine shaft killed four miners and four guards. It was one of the bloodiest labor actions in Illinois history and helped consolidate union power in the Illinois coalfields — these same coal seams we've been riding over. The coal under these fields didn't just fuel the industrial age. It was fought over, bled over, organized over. The placid farmland out the window sits on top of all of it.

The soil out there is darker than it looks from a distance — nearly black in the furrows where last week's rain hasn't dried yet. That's the Mollisol, the prairie grassland's gift: centuries of root death and decomposition pressed into the topsoil. We're rolling across the Central Corn Belt now, 663 feet above sea level, and we've been here a while. The bedrock under us is Bond Formation — shales and sandstones and thin coal seams laid down in a shallow tropical sea around 305 million years ago. That's the floor. The topsoil is the ceiling. Everything economic in this county lives in the twelve inches between them.

The route we're on follows old corridors in a way that rewards attention. Before the railroad, before the telegraph, the land between Chicago and St. Louis was crossed by a web of stage lines — rough, unreliable, expensive. The Illinois Terminal Railroad came through here in the early twentieth century as an interurban electric line: fast, cheap, frequent, connecting small towns the steam railroads bypassed. That's the same impulse the Butterfield Overland Mail had two thousand miles west of here — find the gap, stitch the towns together, carry the letters. The interurban lasted until the automobile made it obsolete. Same impulse, different death.

Auburn sits just ahead — a town of about six thousand that has survived where others haven't, partly because it's close enough to Springfield to catch its orbit. The pattern out here is persistence by proximity. Towns that anchored to something larger — a county seat, a state capital, a railroad junction — held on. The ones that didn't have been slowly subsiding for a century, their grain elevators rusting, their main streets down to a bar and a gas station. Auburn has the grain elevator and the school, which in downstate Illinois counts as thriving.

Around 1820, the year before Sangamon County was formally organized, a man walking from the Ohio River to central Illinois would cross a prairie that still had no roads, no fences, no towns. Just tall grass and the river traces. The Kickapoo people had been here for generations; the Potawatomi before them. Sangamon County was named for the river — a word likely from the Potawatomi meaning something like "where there is plenty to eat," which tells you something about what the bottomlands offered before anyone plowed them. The county was platted in 1821, the same year the Santa Fe Trail opened for business in Missouri — two corridors opening simultaneously in opposite corners of the new American interior. One was in Illinois, heading toward a state capital that didn't exist yet. One was in Missouri, heading toward a foreign country. Both were bets on movement becoming permanent.

Around this milepost the bedrock steps slightly older — Missourian-age sandstones and shales, maybe 306 million years old, coal seams threaded through. We won't see any of it; the glacial till covers everything. But if you could peel back the surface, you'd find a Pennsylvanian-period swamp forest compressed into thin black bands. Those coal seams drove a modest mining economy across southern and central Illinois well into the twentieth century — another resource that arrived by geology and departed by exhaustion.

The rail trail a mile ahead follows the old Illinois Terminal corridor — 8.3 miles of it converted from interurban right-of-way into a walking and cycling path. That's the life cycle of a transportation corridor: stagecoach, steam railroad, electric interurban, automobile, then back to foot traffic on the abandoned grade. We keep finding new uses for the geometry that a surveyor established a century or more ago. The path doesn't go anywhere urgent anymore. It goes somewhere pleasant. That's a different kind of victory.

Springfield sits just ahead — the state capital of Illinois, population around 114,000, and one of those American cities where the nineteenth century is still architecturally loud. Abraham Lincoln practiced law here for twenty-four years before the 1860 election pulled him east. His law office is still on the square. His home is still standing on Eighth Street. The city has been running on Lincoln ever since — a one-name economy of memory and tourism. But Springfield was also, for a long stretch, a real industrial city: coal mines, railroads, meat packing, a Pillsbury mill. The Lincoln Memorial Garden on Lake Springfield opened in 1936, designed by Jens Jensen, the landscape architect who believed that a midwestern garden should look like the Midwest actually looked — not like an English park. Prairie plants, no exotics. A radical idea in 1936.

Sangamon County spreads wide to our right as we curve into Springfield — 67 percent developed land, the highest we've seen on this leg. This is what proximity to a state capital does: it pulls in government workers, health systems, law firms, insurance companies. Illinois's government apparatus is concentrated here in a way that keeps the economy insulated from the crop price swings that gut the counties on either side. Springfield didn't need a railroad boom or a coal seam to survive. It needed a constitutional convention in 1837 to choose it as capital, and that was enough.

The station stop coming up gives us a moment to think about what Lincoln himself said about Springfield when he left it in February 1861, boarding a train not entirely unlike this one. He gave a short speech on the platform — extempore, no notes — that ended: "I now leave, not knowing when, or whether ever, I may return." He never did return alive. He came back in May 1865 in a funeral train that wound 1,654 miles from Washington through seven states, stopping in cities so people could file past the open casket. The train passed through cities that had been burning with celebration two weeks earlier, after Appomattox. By the time it reached Springfield, the country had lurched into a different kind of history. The city buried him on May 4th. The casket is still here, in Oak Ridge Cemetery.

Springfield — state capital, Lincoln's city, 114,000 people on the Sangamon River. If anyone's getting on or off, this is the stop. The station is modest for a capital city, a reminder that Amtrak inherited a railroad empire built for freight and only coincidentally serves passengers. Springfield once had a Union Station worthy of its political stature. What we have now works. The Sangamon River is just east — the river that gave the county and the Potawatomi word its name, still flowing toward the Illinois River, still moving in the direction water has always moved here: east and south, toward the Mississippi.

Leaving Springfield, we cross into Logan County — population 28,000, median income just under the state median, about 40 percent cropland. The bedrock swings back to Bond Formation here — the Kasimovian shales and sandstones we started the segment on. The land is flatter than anything we've seen since Indiana. Elevation holds around 600 feet, and it will stay there. The glacier pressed this entire region into a pool table in the last ice age, scraping off whatever topographic ambition the bedrock had. What's left is the best farmland on earth. Illinois grows about a billion bushels of corn a year. It doesn't look like a billion bushels. It looks like a quiet green grid.

The community called Mount Fulcher sits at the junction of old Route 66 and Interstate 55 — which is to say, it sits at the junction of the old corridor and the corridor that replaced it. Route 66 was already a palimpsest when it opened in 1926: it followed mail routes and wagon tracks and the old Pontiac Trail. The interstate followed Route 66's geometry while destroying its economy. Motels, diners, filling stations that had survived for thirty years on the traffic of travelers suddenly found themselves a quarter-mile from an on-ramp that didn't stop. Mount Fulcher is unincorporated. No census count. It persists the way small crossroad places persist: quietly, without being noticed.

The fossil record under us here — Laevigatosporites vulgaris, a fern spore found in these Pennsylvanian-age coals — tells us this was swamp forest around 307 million years ago. Tree ferns thirty meters tall, standing in warm, oxygen-rich air near the equator. Illinois was equatorial then; the continent was drifting north. The coal seams those forests became were what the industrial Midwest ran on for a century. A fern spore compressed into the rock we're riding over is the same fern spore that heated the factory that made the steel for a railroad that we're now sitting in. The chain is real. It's just very long.

The small creek crossing on our left is Kickapoo Creek — it rises up in McLean County to the north and runs south to join Salt Creek, which joins the Sangamon, which joins the Illinois, which joins the Mississippi. Every drop of water from this drainage ends up in the Gulf of Mexico. The Kickapoo people were here before the county, before the state, before the survey lines. They were removed — most of them to Kansas, then Oklahoma — in the treaty era of the 1830s. The creek kept their name. That's how the American landscape works: the people are gone, the word stays, fading into a geographic label nobody stops to read.

Logan County was organized in 1839, named for John Logan, a physician and Illinois state legislator. The county seat, Lincoln, has the distinction of being the only city in the United States named for Abraham Lincoln before he became president — and Lincoln himself was present at the christening in 1853, participating in the ceremony that dedicated the town by squeezing juice from a watermelon onto the ground. He was a lawyer then, riding the Eighth Judicial Circuit. He later joked that he never knew anything named Lincoln that amounted to much. He was wrong about the city. It's still here.

Lincoln, Illinois — county seat of Logan County, population around 14,000. Named for the man before anyone knew what the name would mean. The town has a small Lincoln-before-Lincoln heritage to it — the watermelon anecdote is on the historical markers. The station stop here is brief. The town's economy is now anchored in health care and retail, like most of the small county seats we've passed through. It has survived a century of agricultural consolidation, the death of Route 66 traffic, the shrinkage of the farm labor force, by being just large enough to be indispensable to the county around it. One hospital, one high school. Enough.

Over the next hour, the landscape ahead will hold its flatness — Logan County gives way to Tazewell and Woodford counties, and we'll stay on this great glacial plain almost all the way to Chicago. The Sangamon watershed drains away to the east now; we'll cross into the Illinois River watershed shortly. The rivers are heading the same direction we are: north. The land ahead is more developed, closer to the Chicago suburban fringe. The cropland thins. The road intersections multiply. We're moving from the working agricultural interior toward something denser, busier, louder — the long approach to the city. But that's still a couple of hours out. For now, the fields. The flat horizon. The particular quiet of central Illinois in the growing season, when there is nothing to see and everything to think about.

The Bond Formation is still under us as we cross out of the heart of Logan County — the same shales and sandstones that started this segment, thin coal seams, tropical-sea sediment from 305 million years ago. The biome is Central Corn Belt Plains, which will hold for a while yet. Elevation around 600 feet, barely varying. The great flat middle of the country. We've come sixty miles since Macoupin County and the land has barely changed — that sameness is itself a story, a geological one: the glacier did this, erasing every variation the bedrock might have offered, leaving a surface so level that water doesn't know which way to run. The rivers here meander in great lazy loops because the land gave them no direction. They figured it out eventually. So do we.

The soil out here is dark almost to black — not painted, not stained, just saturated with carbon. This is the deep organic legacy of ten thousand years of prairie grass dying and composting into itself, layered into some of the most fertile ground on earth. Below that soil, three hundred million years of Pennsylvanian seabed — the Bond Formation, a layered sandwich of shale, sandstone, and thin coal seams laid down when Illinois sat at the equator and a shallow inland sea advanced and retreated again and again. The land is so flat because the same glaciers that built the soil planed it. We're riding a tabletop made by ice.

We're well into the humid east now — and it matters to say what that means. The great hydrological divide we've been crossing for the last several hundred miles isn't a single ridge you step over; it's a gradient, a slow tipping of the continent's drain. West of the Mississippi, water fights to reach the sea. Here, it doesn't. Rain that falls on this field will find the Illinois River, then the Mississippi, then the Gulf, with very little argument. We've traded the landscape of scarcity for the landscape of plenty — and the towns ahead will show it. No ghost towns in McLean County. The ones that stuck are still here.

The village of McLean slips by ahead — 743 people, down from 830 a decade ago. Founded in 1855, right at the moment the railroad was stitching these Illinois towns together for the first time. Every one of these small Illinois villages has the same origin story: the railroad surveyor arrived, drove stakes, and a town materialized almost immediately — a general store, a grain elevator, a church. The difference between McLean and the ghost towns we saw earlier in the leg is not ambition. It's water. It's soil. The corn belt forgave almost every failure of capital or timing. The desert Southwest did not.

The railroad made these Illinois towns, and it's worth sitting with how fast that happened. In 1836, Lexington was platted. In 1854, Chenoa. In 1855, McLean. One after another, new towns snapping into existence like a string of firecrackers, each one planted in a grid pattern the survey crews could lay out in an afternoon. This was the same era the California Gold Rush was pulling thousands of Americans west overland — 1848 to 1855, a tide of migration crossing exactly the kind of terrain this train crossed in its earlier miles. The irony runs deep: the very routes the forty-niners scrambled across in desperation would, within twenty years, be civilized into rail lines, the stage roads first, then the steel. The towns that lasted were the ones that hitched themselves to iron.

Off to our left, the geometry of Dale Township — fields plowed into long rectangles aligned to the cardinal points, a product of the Public Land Survey System that divided most of the country west of Ohio into mile-square sections in the late 1700s. Everywhere we've passed through Illinois, that grid has governed the landscape. Every road, every field boundary, every town plat follows it. The land doesn't curve; it corners.

The bedrock under us has just shifted — around mile 2590 we crossed from the Bond Formation into Missourian-age rock, slightly older, laid down around 306 million years ago. Same sea, same climate, same equatorial Illinois. Sandstone, shale, coal — the repeating chorus of Pennsylvanian Illinois. These seams of coal are what made this part of the state matter economically before the railroad arrived, and they're why the early settlers pushed in from the south and east before the tracks came. Coal camps dotted this country through the 1880s and 1890s, rough communities that existed entirely to extract and ship what the Pennsylvanian sea had deposited. Most of those camps are gone. The coal seams are thin up here in northern Illinois — the Bond Formation thins from as much as 350 feet thick in southern Illinois to 65 feet here. Not worth it anymore. Another variety of ephemerality.

Bloomington is off to our right — a real city, 78,000 people, the county seat, the anchor of a metro area that pulls in Normal beside it. Founded in 1822, which means it predates the railroad by a generation; it was already a going concern when the tracks arrived and simply grew larger. But what Bloomington is most famous for, in retrospect, is a single speech. In May 1856, Abraham Lincoln gave what became known as his "Lost Speech" here — a passionate address against the expansion of slavery so electrifying that reporters stopped taking notes and just listened. Not a word of it was written down at the time. We know only that it moved the crowd to its feet and that Lincoln himself called it the best speech he ever gave. A speech that survives only as legend, in a city that still remembers it was there.

The Bloomington-Normal station is our stop here — and pulling away from it, the landscape opens back into that wide corn and soybean flatness. McLean County is the largest county by land area in Illinois, and most of it looks like this: eighty percent developed or in cropland, the line between them blurring when you realize that "developed" in rural Illinois often means exactly one farmstead every half mile, a grain bin, a machine shed, a pickup in the drive. Population 171,000, median income $75,000 — wealthier than the counties behind us. Finance and real estate show up as significant industries alongside the expected education and health. Illinois State University in Normal pulls a different economic gravity than the smaller county seats.

Towanda, population 431. Founded 1875 — that's ten years after the Civil War ended, right in the thick of the railroad land-grant era when lines were platting towns across the West like seeds scattered from a moving car. In Illinois, the towns that got platted in 1875 got the benefit of an already-mature rail network; they weren't founding outposts on a frontier, they were filling in the gaps. Towanda exists because there was still room for a town between Bloomington and Lexington, a place for the grain from the surrounding sections to aggregate before moving east or west. Functional. Modest. Durable.

If you look at the fossils found in the rocks under our feet — and they are there, though deeply buried — you'd find crinoids. Elibatocrinus elegans, Erisocrinus typus, Apographiocrinus typicalis — sea lilies, essentially, filter feeders that stood on stalks anchored to the shallow seafloor and swept the water with feathery arms. Three hundred and six million years old, give or take. Illinois was a warm, equatorial, shallow sea. The idea is almost impossible to hold: this flat, landlocked, hyper-productive corn country was once underwater, populated by creatures related to starfish, in a world where North America hadn't yet assembled itself into anything a modern map would recognize. The coal in those thin seams is the compressed residue of swamp forests that rose and fell along the sea's margins. We're burning — or used to burn — compressed Pennsylvanian swamp, to move trains across what used to be the bottom of that swamp's adjacent sea.

Lexington — platted 1836, the same year the Alamo fell in Texas and the same year a young legislator named Abraham Lincoln first arrived in the Illinois statehouse thirty miles south of here. There are two stories about the name: it was either named for the Battle of Lexington in 1775, where one of the town founders' fathers had fought, or it was simply the name somebody liked. Either way, by 1836 "Lexington" carried the whole freight of American founding mythology. The pattern repeats: a railroad corridor town with a Revolutionary War name, dropped onto a Pennsylvanian seafloor, surrounded by corn.

The landscape is very nearly featureless to a casual eye right now — flat to the horizon in every direction, the fields broken only by shelter belts of trees around farmsteads and the occasional grain elevator rising like a white tower above everything else. Those elevators are the architecture of the corn belt the way cathedral spires are the architecture of medieval France: the tallest structure in town, oriented to the essential function of the community, visible from miles away. The Illinois Central and other railroads built most of these towns specifically to aggregate grain. The town exists to serve the elevator; the elevator exists to serve the railroad. This stretch of Illinois was an agricultural factory before anyone called anything a factory.

Chenoa was founded in 1854 by Matthew T. Scott — a deliberate act of real estate speculation, the town created whole from open prairie so the railroad would run through it. That's not unusual; what's unusual is the name. "Chenoa" is an Algonquian word, and Scott chose it in the way mid-nineteenth century town founders often reached for Native American place names: as local color, as distinctiveness, sometimes as genuine respect, often as marketing. By 1856 it was incorporated, by 1954 it had a centennial, and today it sits at the intersection of Interstate 55, Historic Route 66, and US Route 24 — three centuries of corridor stacked on top of each other, the old Lincoln Highway alignment under the Interstate, the rail corridor running alongside. The Butterfield Overland Mail routes we've been tracing since the beginning of this leg mapped exactly this logic: find the easiest passage through the terrain, mark it, and every subsequent technology of movement will use the same line.

We're crossing from McLean County into Livingston County — the population drops noticeably, from 171,000 down to 35,000. Same crops, corn and soybeans, but now wheat appears in the mix. The land cover flips: sixty percent cropland here, forty percent developed, the reverse of what we've seen since Bloomington. This is the quieter, less metro-adjacent Illinois, the county where the county seat is the obvious center of everything and the surrounding towns are small and functional. Median income holds — $68,000 — and poverty is relatively low. It's prosperous farmland without a university or a finance sector to diversify it. Livingston County is what most of rural Illinois looks like.

Pontiac ahead — 11,000 people, the Livingston County seat, founded in 1837 and named for the Ottawa war chief Pontiac, who led a major uprising against British forts in 1763. The town was platted the same year Michigan became a state, the same year Martin Van Buren moved into the White House. It's well upstream from those events geographically but not in spirit: 1837 is peak Land Rush Illinois, the period when every inch of productive prairie was being surveyed and claimed and titled as fast as lawyers could write deeds. Pontiac stuck because it got the courthouse. Towns that got the courthouse survived; towns that didn't often didn't. One building, the seat of county government, and you had a future. Simple as that.

The soil out there — almost black, some of the most productive farmland on earth — is glacial till laid down when the Laurentide ice sheet retreated twelve thousand years ago. Beneath it, the bedrock is Missourian-age sandstone and shale laid down in a shallow inland sea around 305 million years ago. Coal seams run through those rocks. Farmers plowing here in the 1860s sometimes found chunks of it at the surface. We're riding through geology and agriculture stacked in thin, consequential layers.

The flat grid of fields you see in every direction isn't accidental — it's the Public Land Survey System, begun in 1785, that carved the continent into perfect square-mile sections. Every fence line, every road running perfectly north-south or east-west, reflects a surveyor's chain dragged across this ground before the railroad came, before most of these towns existed. The survey and the railroad together did the same work: they imposed a legible geometry on a continent that had its own older, invisible order. Route 66 would later run through this same corridor, threading the survey's grid on its way west. Corridors persist.

Around here the bedrock shifts — just slightly older, the Carbondale Formation, Moscovian age, around 310 million years ago. Shale, sandstone, coal, and limestone, built in a vast coal swamp that stretched across what would become the American Midwest. The coal measures of Illinois made this state an industrial engine before anyone thought of oil. The rooftops and fields look the same out either window, but the ground beneath us just quietly changed eras.

The Illinois coal seams in this part of the state fueled a particular transformation. In the 1880s and 1890s, coal towns sprouted along every rail line — not just mining settlements but company towns, with company housing, company stores, and company doctors. Many of them are gone now, or nearly so. The transition from coal to petroleum, from steam to diesel, from rail freight to truck freight — each one erased another set of towns that had seemed permanent. What the railroad made, its own evolution unmade.

Dwight sits right on an original stretch of Route 66 — the old road still runs through town, recognizable if you look. But before Route 66, there was the railroad, and Dwight's story runs with it. The town was platted in 1854, named for a Chicago and Alton Railway promoter, and by 1892 it had built a handsome brick station that would stand for more than a century. That station operated continuously until 2016 — one hundred and twenty-four years. Most towns would be glad to have a building survive that long. What's remarkable is that one kept its original function. The corridor, once established, just keeps getting used.

Dwight has another layer that fits the leg's running theme. It sits in territory that was crossed by early mail routes pushing west — the same drive to move information across a continent faster than a horse could carry it alone that eventually produced the Butterfield Overland Mail and the Pony Express. Those systems look quaint now, but they were the leading edge of a technological obsession with speed and connectivity that runs straight through to the digital present. The stagecoach stop, the railroad station, the interstate highway interchange: each generation builds its version of the same infrastructure, usually right on top of the last one.

Gardner — a village of thirteen hundred people, easy to miss through the window — is the kind of place that holds a county's agricultural memory. The fields around it are corn and soybeans now, as they've been for a hundred and fifty years, but the town's population has stayed almost flat since the 1920s. Rural Illinois has been slowly emptying since the tractor replaced the farm hand. Not a ghost town — still lived in, still functional — but not growing either. The land is more productive than ever; it just needs fewer people to work it.

There's a particular Illinois story worth knowing as we approach Braidwood. In the 1970s, Commonwealth Edison built a nuclear generating station south of Braidwood on a site chosen partly for its proximity to the Kankakee River for cooling water. The Dresden Nuclear Power Station had already been operating since 1960 just a few miles north, one of the first commercial nuclear plants in the country. This corner of Illinois became, quietly, one of the most nuclear-dense landscapes in America. The same logic that made coal towns here in the 1880s — access to rail, access to water — made nuclear plants here a century later. The energy technology changed; the geography of infrastructure didn't.

Braidwood was a coal town — founded 1867, built around the mines that ran through the Carbondale Formation shales beneath the Illinois prairie. In 1883, a mine explosion here killed sixty-nine men, one of the worst mining disasters in Illinois history. The town survived, adapted, eventually outlasted coal. The nuclear plant that carries its name sits a couple miles east and generates electricity for northern Illinois today. It's an unusual biographical arc for a small midwestern city: from coal disaster to nuclear power in a hundred years, same landscape, different risks.

The Braidwood mines are worth sitting with for a moment. The coal those miners were pulling out of the ground in 1883 was the compressed remains of a Carbondale Formation swamp — 310 million years of compression, turning tree ferns and club mosses into fuel. The men going down the shaft were harvesting sunlight stored when Illinois was a tropical wetland near the equator, before the Appalachians had been worn down, before the Rockies existed. Mining is always a form of time travel, extracting the deep past to power the present. What the Braidwood miners couldn't know was that burning that stored carbon would eventually alter the climate enough to shift the precipitation patterns their descendants would farm under.

We've crossed into Will County now, and the numbers shift dramatically. Livingston County, behind us, had thirty-five thousand people spread across a thousand square miles of farmland. Will County has nearly seven hundred thousand — one of the fastest-growing counties in Illinois — and eighty percent of its land is developed. The prairie is giving way to the suburban edge of Chicago. You can see it in the rooflines, the density of roads, the distribution centers and warehouses that start appearing between the fields. We're entering the gravitational field of the third-largest city in the country.

The geology makes a significant jump here. Around milepost 2680 the bedrock shifts from Carbondale Formation shales — 310 million years old — down to the Silurian System, dolostone and limestone laid down between 425 and 445 million years ago. That's a gap of roughly eighty-five million years, a chunk of Devonian and Mississippian time missing from the local record. The glaciers that bulldozed this landscape scraped and rearranged the surface, leaving younger rocks in some places and exposing much older ones in others. The Silurian limestone here — dolostone and reef material from a shallow tropical sea — is the same stone that Chicago's nineteenth-century buildings were quarried from. The city ahead was literally built from the seafloor that's right beneath our wheels.

Elwood is where the Joliet Army Ammunition Plant operated from World War II through the end of the Cold War — one of the largest ammunition depots in the country, sprawling across thirty-three square miles. It produced artillery shells and bombs for four wars. After the army decommissioned it in the 1990s, it became the Abraham Lincoln National Cemetery and a massive intermodal logistics junction — the largest inland port in North America by some measures. The same rail corridors that once moved munitions now move container cargo from the Port of Los Angeles to the warehouses of Chicago. Corridors persist; their cargo changes.

The Elwood intermodal junction is worth lingering on because it closes a circle we've been tracing across this leg. The containerized freight revolution that turned Elwood into an inland port was itself enabled by the standardization of shipping containers in the 1950s and 1960s — a technological shift as consequential as the railroad had been a century earlier. The Burlington Northern Santa Fe and Union Pacific lines that converge here carry more freight tonnage than most rail systems in the world. We're riding on one of those lines now. The Butterfield mail coaches of the 1850s were trying to solve the same problem these trains are solving: how do you move things reliably and quickly across a continent? Each generation builds a faster, higher-capacity answer. This is the current answer.

Joliet. Originally settled in 1834 where the Des Plaines River cuts through the Silurian limestone, it grew into a steel town in the 1850s and 1860s — originally called Juliet, renamed in 1845 after the French explorer Louis Jolliet who canoed past here in 1673. The steel industry that made the city is gone, but Joliet remade itself around riverboat gambling in the 1990s and distribution logistics in the 2000s. It's also where the Stateville Correctional Center operates — one of the largest prisons in Illinois, which put Joliet on a different kind of national map. The city that made steel now makes crossroads: of highways, rail lines, waterways, and jurisdictions. That's the Des Plaines River valley just off our right window.

The Silurian limestone that built Chicago sits just beneath us as we pull through Joliet and north toward the city. This rock — laid down in a reef-studded tropical sea when North America straddled the equator, when the first land plants were barely getting established onshore — was quarried by the millions of tons from cuts along the Illinois and Michigan Canal just north of here. The canal itself, finished in 1848, connected Lake Michigan to the Illinois River and opened the interior of the continent to Chicago's markets. The geology made the quarry; the quarry supplied the canal walls; the canal made Chicago's hinterland. From here north, the landscape densifies fast. The prairie is behind us. We're in the long approach to the city, and the lake is not far ahead.

The ground beneath us is ancient seafloor — Silurian dolostone and limestone laid down when this whole region sat under a warm shallow sea, roughly 430 million years ago. The fossils that wash out of road cuts here are trilobites: *Calymene celebra*, *Bumastus insignis*, creatures that scuttled across that seafloor before a single fish had fins strong enough to walk on land. We're rolling over the bones of an ocean. And yet everything above that bedrock is younger by a factor of a thousand — glacial till, lake sediment, the flat geometry of a place the ice sheet shaped and left, not long ago in geological terms.

The land out both windows right now is telling a story about arrival. We're entering the outer ring of the Chicago metropolitan region — the edge where the cornfields give way to warehouse clusters and subdivision rooftops. Chicago didn't grow the way other American cities did, by building outward from a river crossing or a harbor. It grew along corridors — rail corridors, most of them — and each line that poked out into the prairie became a thread that pulled towns into existence. The Burlington Northern, the Rock Island, the Illinois Central: those names are mostly gone from the letterheads now, but the towns are still there, strung along the right-of-way like beads. We've been riding one of those strings all the way across the continent. We're close now to where all the strings converge.

Look right — that's Lemont on the hillside above the Des Plaines River valley. Founded 1836, the same decade the first steam locomotives reached the prairie. Lemont's story is quarry stone: the Silurian dolostone that underlies this whole stretch is hard, buff-colored, excellent for building. In the 1830s and 40s workers — many of them Irish immigrants who came to dig the Illinois and Michigan Canal — quarried Lemont dolomite and floated it east on the canal itself. The stone became bridges, courthouse steps, Chicago storefronts. The quarrymen lived in the hillside village; the boats carried the rock. Then the canal era ended, the railroads won, and Lemont shifted into the suburban orbit. The stone is still here, just under the lawns.

Here's a moment to think about what Chicago meant — what it *was* — in the half-century after the Civil War. By 1870 the city had become the greatest railroad junction on Earth. Lines from every direction converged here: grain moving east from the Plains, lumber moving south from Wisconsin, cattle moving north from Texas on the Chisholm Trail and into the stockyards. The whole interior of the continent funneled through this city. And it wasn't an accident of geography alone — though Lake Michigan's southern tip gave it a head start — it was a deliberate technological bet made by financiers and engineers who understood that whoever controlled the junction controlled the hinterland. That bet paid off. By 1900, if you shipped a barrel of flour from Kansas, a side of beef from Nebraska, or a bushel of corn from Iowa, odds were strong it touched Chicago. We're riding the last few miles of a rail corridor that is itself one of the oldest and most important in that web. The Southwest Chief — and its predecessors, the Santa Fe's Super Chief, the El Capitan — ran from Los Angeles to this terminal for generations. What began as a mail route through Apache country became one of the premier passenger lines in American history. And now it drops us here, into the city that organized a continent.

Hickory Hills, incorporated 1951 — one of hundreds of Cook County suburbs that materialized in the postwar years when the automobile and the GI Bill together pushed the city edge outward at a pace no planner had fully anticipated. The name is aspirational: the hickory forest is long gone, cleared for farmland a century before the subdivision went in. What's left is the grid — streets named for trees that don't grow there anymore, houses that look roughly the same as houses twenty miles north or twenty miles south. Postwar suburban geography repeated itself across every American metro, as reliably as the geology repeats itself under the till. It's not without life. People raised children here, built businesses, coached little league. But the landscape has the anonymity that comes from having been made fast, from a template, at scale.

Left window, Countryside — incorporated 1960, another node in the same suburban weave, population just over six thousand. The name follows the same wishful logic as Hickory Hills: countryside is exactly what it isn't. By 1960 this land was already thoroughly developed, already absorbed. What you see out that left window is Cook County in its fully urban form: 100 percent developed land cover, by the county's own accounting. Not a single acre of cropland recorded. We've crossed an invisible but absolute threshold. From here to the terminal we are inside the city.

The Southwest Chief is about to slide into Chicago from the south and west, following the Des Plaines River corridor and then cutting through the Back of the Yards, South Lawndale, the dense residential and industrial patchwork of the city's south side. This approach hasn't changed dramatically since the Santa Fe's first trains made it in the late nineteenth century. The corridor itself is an artifact of topography — the river valley offered a grade the early railroads could follow without blasting — and so the modern train follows a path first chosen by surveyors who were following the logic of the land. That's the palimpsest at work: the glacier laid down the valley, the river cut it, the surveyors followed the river, the railroad followed the surveyors, and we follow the railroad. Layers of decision, each one inheriting the constraint of the one before.

Left window — or what's left of it: the Crawford Generating Station site, South Lawndale, Chicago. The plant went up in 1924, coal-fired, enormous. For most of the twentieth century it burned coal shipped in from downstate Illinois and Indiana, feeding power into the city's grid. Residents of the surrounding neighborhood — disproportionately Latino and lower-income — lived with the particulate matter, the sulfur dioxide, the health burden that comes from being adjacent to a major industrial emitter. That's where Chicago's coal story ends differently from the boom-and-bust extraction towns we've passed earlier on this leg: the coal there was mined in ghost towns we've long since left behind; the cost of burning it was paid by people who lived in the shadow of the stack. Crawford stopped generating power in 2012. The plant came down in 2020. The lot is being redeveloped now. What exactly that means for the neighborhood is still being negotiated.

In the last miles now. Lake Michigan is off to our left — you can't see it from the train, but you feel it in the light, in the way the sky opens up to the northeast, in the damp that's different from the humidity of the Mississippi watershed we've been crossing. Chicago sits on the continental divide between two great drainage systems, a fact so counterintuitive it takes a moment to register: the city straddles the split between water that flows to the Gulf of Mexico and water that flows to the Atlantic via the St. Lawrence. The Illinois and Michigan Canal — built with the Lemont dolomite we saw back at mile 2702, dug in part by those same Irish quarrymen — connected the two systems artificially in 1848. Chicago became the hinge on which the continent turned. One waterway to the east, one to the south, and this single city at the junction. The train has carried us across the full span of that continent — from the Pacific to this hinge point. We made it.

Union Station ahead — the great hall Burnham's firm imagined and Graham, Anderson, Probst and White finished in 1925. The waiting room's coffered ceiling, the marble columns, the light falling through the skylights. It was built to receive the full convergence of American rail traffic and it does that still, even in a diminished era of train travel. The Southwest Chief arrives here as it has for decades, sliding in from the desert Southwest, carrying passengers who watched the land change from red sandstone to green corn, from 5,000-foot altitude to lake-level, from the silence of the Painted Desert to the noise of the second city. The mail routes that first marked this corridor are gone, replaced by FedEx and fiber optic. The stagecoach stops are ghost towns or strip malls. But the corridor itself persists. The train is still here. And so are we.

58.text: The clock above the concourse reads 1954 in its bones — poured concrete, broad canopy, that postwar confidence that rail would carry the nation forward forever. New Orleans Union Passenger Terminal replaced six separate depots that once scattered passengers across the city. The Illinois Central alone had its own house here; now we share the same platform with the Crescent and the City of New Orleans. The train we're on is headed north on one of the most storied rail corridors in America — the IC main line, the track that generations called simply the Panama Limited route. We're rolling now.

Underneath us — right now, and for the next fifty miles — the earth is almost entirely young. Cenozoic rock: the broad category for everything laid down in the last 66 million years, after the dinosaurs cleared the stage. Here in the Mississippi Alluvial Plain, that means sediment that arrived by water, grain by grain, flood by flood. The Mississippi River built this land. It built Orleans Parish. It built the floor beneath this station. The river still adjusts its meanders seasonally, still deposits fine silt on the floodplain after every high water. We're riding across a landscape that is, in geologic terms, barely finished.

The Mississippi Alluvial Plain is the biome we're in — a vast, low, flat province of river-deposited soils stretching from southern Illinois to the Gulf. It is extraordinarily fertile and extraordinarily wet. The alluvium here runs deep. Drive a post into the ground anywhere in New Orleans and you are driving it into sediment that the river carried from Montana and Minnesota and Ohio, mixed and sorted and dropped here over millions of years. The city floats on it, essentially. So does everything we'll see until we climb, slowly, onto higher ground north of mile fifty.

To our right, the Pontchartrain Center — a modest arena that opened in 1991, hosting concerts and hockey and the ordinary civic life of Kenner, Jefferson Parish's largest community. Jefferson Parish wraps around New Orleans on the west and south; it's the suburban ring, more prosperous on average than Orleans, and it sits on the same alluvial floor. The parish seat is Gretna, across the river. We pass through the edge of this suburban landscape quickly — subdivisions, a warehouse district, the geometry of a mid-century American suburb pressed up against an ancient river delta.

The Illinois Central Railroad — the line beneath our wheels — was platted and built in the 1850s, and by the 1860s it ran from Chicago to Cairo, Illinois, where it connected south toward the Gulf. It became the arterial corridor for what historians call the Great Migration: roughly six million Black Americans who left the rural South between 1910 and 1970, riding trains like this one north toward Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland. The IC was not the only route, but it was among the most traveled.

Think about what that means geographically. The train left from towns we'll pass through in the next hour — from parishes like this one, from the sugarcane fields of St. John the Baptist, from the small cities of the Mississippi interior. It arrived, sixty or so hours later, in Chicago. The same distance by foot would have taken weeks. The railroad compressed it into a single night and a day. Families who had never left their county could, for a few dollars, step into a different world. That compression — geographic, economic, social — is part of what made the Migration so rapid and so transformative. We're traveling its southern end right now, moving north on the same right-of-way.

Out the left window: Norco. The name derives from New Orleans Refining Company — the plant that has dominated this town since the early twentieth century. Today it's a Shell and Valero complex, one of the larger petrochemical facilities on the lower Mississippi. The river we've been tracking since New Orleans curves close here, and the refineries sit on its bank for the same reason the sugar plantations did a century earlier: river access, flat land, proximity to transportation. The geology that laid down this alluvial plain also concentrated the organic material — ancient sea life, compressed over millions of years — that eventually became the oil and gas now processed at facilities like this one.

Cancer Alley, some call this stretch of the river between New Orleans and Baton Rouge. Eighty miles of petrochemical plants and the communities that live alongside them. The air quality data for St. Charles Parish puts it among the highest industrial pollution exposures in the country. The people who live in Norco — population just under three thousand — are the descendants of the same labor that worked these riverbanks when the commodity was cane sugar rather than crude oil. The crop changed. The economic structure did not change much at all.

St. John the Baptist Parish begins around mile twenty-four, and it is — according to the land cover data — one hundred percent wetland. Every acre. The parish seat is Edgard, an unincorporated cluster on the west bank. The largest community is LaPlace, on the east bank where we're traveling. What you're seeing out the windows now, if you look away from the industrial corridor, is what the lower Mississippi always looked like before drainage and levees: cypress swamp, standing water, floating mats of vegetation, the occasional heron working a shallow ditch.

Sugarcane has been grown here since the colonial period. The crop survives in St. John the Baptist Parish, though only as a fragment of the plantation economy that once covered these bottoms. Cane requires a frost-free growing season — this far south, the climate just barely allows it. Every degree of latitude north we travel over the next hour makes cane cultivation less viable. By the time we reach Hammond, we're at the edge of cane country. Beyond that, it's a different agricultural world.

Ahead and to either side, the land opens into one of the stranger crossings on this route. The Manchac Swamp Bridge — that's the highway structure you can see in the distance, carrying Interstate 55 and U.S. Route 51 over the swamp on concrete pilings — was completed in 1979. It is miles long. The swamp it crosses is the backwater between Lake Pontchartrain and Lake Maurepas, two broad, shallow lakes connected by the Manchac Pass.

We cross the swamp on a rail trestle that predates the highway bridge by decades. The Illinois Central laid track through here in the railroad's great expansion era; the engineers had no good options — the swamp had to be bridged or crossed on fill, and fill in this terrain sinks. So the trestle. Our train moves through the cypress canopy at track level, water visible between the ties on both sides in wet season. The Interstate 55 corridor runs nearly parallel to us all the way to Chicago — the freeway and the railroad, the same corridor, the same route, each era's preferred technology of movement.

The Manchac Swamp marks something of a threshold. Behind us: New Orleans and its parishes, the deep alluvial delta, the city that has always been a port and a destination. Ahead: the higher ground of the Florida Parishes — the southeastern corner of Louisiana that never flooded with the Red River deposits, that was settled differently, that has its own personality.

The Florida Parishes were, briefly and peculiarly, actually part of Spanish West Florida even after the Louisiana Purchase. The United States acquired them in 1810 through a short-lived rebellion — the Republic of West Florida lasted seventy-four days — and added them to the new state. Tangipahoa Parish, which we're entering around mile forty-eight, sits in the heart of that old West Florida territory. It was settled by Scots-Irish farmers coming south from the Carolinas and Tennessee, not by the French Creole planters who defined the river parishes. Different people, different crops, different churches. Strawberries rather than cane; Baptist rather than Catholic.

The Illinois Central ran through this country and founded towns along its right-of-way. Ponchatoula, just ahead, was platted as a railroad town. Hammond, our stop, was named for a man who sold timber rights to the IC in 1818 — though the railroad itself arrived decades later, it was the railroad that made the town.

Ponchatoula, population around seventy-five hundred — this is strawberry country. The Ponchatoula Strawberry Festival draws tens of thousands each spring, and the parish ships strawberries to markets across the region. The town was incorporated in 1820, which puts its founding right at the moment the Santa Fe Trail was opening up to the west and the country was just beginning to understand the size of what it had purchased. Ponchatoula is a Choctaw word, meaning something like "hanging hair" — a reference, probably, to Spanish moss. We'll see the recurring pattern as we move north into Mississippi: Indigenous place names preserved in the geography long after the nations that gave them were displaced. The placenames are a kind of memory that the land holds even when the history books pass over it.

Around us as we come into Tangipahoa Parish: twenty-eight percent wetland, twenty-eight percent forest. The landscape is starting to lift. We are, almost imperceptibly, climbing out of the alluvial plain.

At roughly mile fifty, the bedrock geology beneath us shifts — from that broad Cenozoic category of older sedimentary rock to genuine Holocene alluvium: clay, sand, and gravel deposited in the last eleven thousand years, since the end of the last ice age. That is geologically instantaneous. The fossils found in this zone reflect it: Rangia cuneata, a brackish-water clam; Littoraria irrorata, the marsh periwinkle; Mytilopsis, a small mussel. All are creatures of the coastal interface, of brackish marshes and tidal flats. They lived here when sea level was slightly higher, or when the river was depositing differently. They're in the sediment beneath the strawberry fields.

Beyond mile sixty — just past Hammond — the geology shifts again to Pleistocene prairie terraces: older, higher, drier ground, laid down between two and a half million and eleven thousand years ago. Light gray to light brown clay and sandy clay, the geologic survey says. That older, firmer surface is what lets Hammond sit a full twenty feet above sea level — modest by most standards, but here, on this coastal plain, it's the high ground. It's why Hammond was the place the IC chose for a depot rather than the swampier lowlands south of it.

Hammond, Louisiana — population around twenty-one thousand, the largest city in Tangipahoa Parish. Out the left window you'll see Southeastern Louisiana University, established here because Hammond had the rail connection and the slightly higher ground. The campus opened in 1925, during the same decade that the Great Migration was accelerating northward through this very station.

The IC depot here was a separation point — literally. Jim Crow laws required segregated waiting rooms, segregated cars, segregated everything. Black passengers who boarded here for Chicago entered through one door and exited through another. They rode in the colored car, usually directly behind the locomotive, where the smoke and cinders were worst. The same train, the same tracks, the same northward journey — divided. What the Migration represented was, among other things, the decision to make that journey one-way. To not come back to the separate door. Hammond is forty-five miles from New Orleans and forty-five miles from Baton Rouge, almost exactly equidistant. For a century it was a market town for the Florida Parishes. For the IC, it was a stop. For the people who passed through its depot heading north, it was a threshold.

We're climbing now, though you'd never feel it — a few hundred feet over the next hundred miles, spread so evenly the grade is nearly unmeasurable. But the land is telling us. The cypress swamp has given way to mixed pine and hardwood. The soil is firmer, better drained. The Pleistocene prairie terraces are taking over from the Holocene alluvium. We're leaving the Mississippi Alluvial Plain — that vast, young, river-built province — and entering the Southern Coastal Plain: a broader, older, drier ecoregion that stretches east to the Carolinas and north into Tennessee. The transition happens around mile fifty, and by the time we reach mile sixty it's visible in the tree line, in the color of the soil visible along the cuts, in the way the farmhouses sit up on slightly higher ground.

The watershed divide is still fifty miles ahead — around mile one hundred and ten, we'll cross from the Mississippi watershed into the South Atlantic-Gulf watershed, from water that drains to the Mississippi delta into water that drains more directly to the Gulf through shorter rivers. That crossing is invisible from the window. But it's real, and it matters: we are, slowly, moving off the map that the great river drew.
